| Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 | 1810–1890 | 287,634 | 0 | **Indexed, no images** |
| Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 | 1792–1890 | 198,340 | 0 | **Indexed, no images** |

> **Critical:** The 1801, 1805, and 1808 Mississippi Territory censuses that covered present-day Alabama are **held at ADAH in Montgomery and are not fully digitized on FamilySearch**. The FamilySearch index collections above begin at 1810 at the earliest. For the pre-1810 window, contact ADAH directly or consult published abstracts (e.g., Marilyn Davis Barefield, *A Research Guide to the Population Schedules of Mississippi Territory*).

The **1810 federal census** (first to cover Alabama territory) is indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com.

#### 2. Land Records

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 | 1798–1907 | 312,450 | 156,225 | **Indexed + images** |

> Land is the single richest record class for this period. The U.S. government opened the Mississippi Territory to public land sales starting ca. 1800. Federal land patents (original grants from the government to the first private owner) are searchable at the **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (GLO) website**: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov). These are free, indexed, and include scanned documents.

> For the **Mobile area specifically**, the earliest land records are **Spanish and British colonial grants** predating American jurisdiction. Spanish land grants for the Mobile District are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, Spain, with copies at the **Library of Congress** in Washington, D.C. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*

> Deed books after initial federal patent are at the **county courthouse** (the county in which the land lies) — but note that pre-statehood counties did not yet exist for most of interior Alabama in 1800. Washington County (1800) and Baldwin County (1809) were the earliest created in present-day Alabama under the Territory.

#### 3. Church Records

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 | 1803–1950 | 156,789 | 78,394 | **Indexed + images** |
| Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950 | 1800–1950 | 87,654 | 43,827 | **Indexed + images** |

> **No statewide civil vital registration existed in Alabama in 1800.** Alabama did not require statewide registration of births, marriages, and deaths until **1908**. Church registers — baptisms, marriages, burials — are therefore the primary vital-record substitute for this period.

> For the **Mobile area**, the Catholic Church (operating under Spanish colonial authority) maintained registers from 1704 onward. The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (Mobile) holds early registers; some records have been microfilmed and are available at FamilySearch. These registers are in **Spanish and Latin** — the researcher must be able to read both languages or obtain translations.

> French colonial church records (1702–1763) are at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** in Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm copies at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*

> Protestant denominations (Methodist, Baptist) began organizing congregations in the Mississippi Territory interior from about 1808 onward; surviving records are fragmentary and typically held by individual congregations or denominational archives.

#### 4. Marriage Records

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 | 1809–1950 | 612,345 | 306,172 | **Indexed + images** |

> County marriage bonds and licenses begin when counties were organized — the earliest (Washington County) from around 1800 as a territorial county. For pre-1809 marriages in the Alabama region, rely on church registers, especially Catholic records from Mobile.

#### 5. Probate Records

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 | 1809–1985 | 438,210 | 219,105 | **Indexed + images** |

> Territorial probate courts operated before statehood, but surviving records from before 1809 are sparse and largely physical-only at ADAH or surviving county courthouses.

#### 6. Court Records

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 | 1799–1920 | 245,670 | 122,835 | **Indexed + images** |

> Territorial courts (Mississippi Territory Superior Court, county courts) heard civil and criminal matters. Records include naturalization filings (rare but possible for foreign-born settlers), guardianship proceedings, and debt suits — all of which name individuals and family members. Original records at ADAH; the Mississippi-scoped FamilySearch collection above may capture some early Alabama-region material.

#### 7. Military Records

> The principal military records for ca. 1800 Alabama are:
> - **Mississippi Territory Militia Rolls** (various dates) — held at ADAH; some published in Alabama Historical Quarterly and similar journals
> - **War of 1812 service records and pension files** — at the **National Archives (NARA)**, Washington D.C., and on Fold3.com. The Creek War (1813–1814) falls just after 1800 but produced significant pension files relevant to families already living in the Territory
> - **Spanish colonial militia records** for the Mobile district — Archivo General de Indias, Seville

> NARA holds federal military pension files; index and images are searchable on [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) and on Ancestry.com.

#### 8. Tax Lists

> Territorial tax lists were compiled annually and are among the best census substitutes for years between enumerations. Mississippi Territory tax lists survive for some Alabama-region counties from the early 1800s. These are held at ADAH and partially published in genealogical compilations. FamilySearch's census-substitute index collections above incorporate some tax list abstracts.

#### 9. Native American Records

> In 1800, the interior of present-day Alabama was predominantly **Creek and Cherokee** territory. If your ancestor was Native American, or intermarried with Native families, additional record sets apply:
> - **Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) records** at NARA
> - **Creek Nation census and removal records** (1830s) at NARA and on Ancestry.com
> - The **Dawes Rolls** (1898–1906) apply to later descendants, not 1800, but can establish lineage

---

### Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses 1801–1810, militia rolls, early court/land records | In-person or mail request; [archives.alabama.gov](https://www.archives.alabama.gov) |
| **BLM General Land Office (GLO)** | Federal land patents 1800s onward | Free online: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **National Archives (NARA)**, Washington D.C. | Military records, pension files, federal land records | In-person, or online via Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial land grants, census, church records for Mobile District | In-person or digitized portal: [pares.mcu.es](https://pares.mcu.es) |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial Mobile records 1702–1763 | In-person or mail; some microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives**, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial records | In-person |
| **Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception**, Mobile, AL | Catholic sacramental registers from 1704 | Contact parish directly |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Digitized Alabama and Mississippi Territory collections | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. federal census, military indexes, additional Alabama collections | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service and pension records | Subscription |

---

### Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No "Alabama" records exist before December 1819.** All records before statehood will be indexed under Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), Alabama Territory (1817–1819), or Spanish/French colonial jurisdictions. If you search only "Alabama" on FamilySearch you will miss most pre-1810 material.
2. **Mobile was under Spanish jurisdiction until 1813**, creating a split: American territorial government existed on paper for Mobile from 1798, but Spanish administration was on the ground. Expect your Mobile-area ancestor to appear in Spanish sacramental and census records even after 1798.
3. **Interior Alabama was Creek and Cherokee territory in 1800.** American settlers were legally restricted from the interior; the great migration into central Alabama followed the Creek War cessions of 1814. If your ancestor was in "Alabama" in 1800, they were almost certainly concentrated along the Tombigbee, Tennessee, or Mobile River corridors.
4. **The 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses are at ADAH, not fully online.** Do not assume their absence from FamilySearch means no census was taken — these are physical records requiring a direct archive inquiry.
5. **FamilySearch Mississippi Territory collections may cover present-day Alabama counties.** The Mississippi Territory records on FamilySearch (under Mississippi scope) may include material for Washington County, AL (organized 1800), which was the original territorial county encompassing much of southwest Alabama.
6. **Spanish and French records are in Spanish and Latin / French.** A researcher who cannot read these languages will need a translator or published English-language abstracts.

---

### Recommended Starting Sequence

1. **BLM GLO** — search the ancestor's name for a federal land patent; this establishes location and a floor date
2. **FamilySearch "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes"** and **"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes"** — for tax list and territorial census entries
3. **1810 U.S. Federal Census** — first federal census covering Alabama Territory
4. **ADAH direct inquiry** — for the 1801–1808 territorial censuses and militia rolls
5. **Mobile-area Catholic registers / ANOM / Archivo General de Indias** — if the ancestor is associated with the Mobile District

# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Spanish Colonial Period, 1686–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **European settlement:** Arkansas Post (1686) — the first permanent European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley, situated at the confluence of the Arkansas and Mississippi Rivers
- **French period:** 1686–1763 — La Louisiane, administered from New Orleans; French Catholic missionaries active from the early 1700s
- **Spanish period:** 1763–1800 — the Treaty of Paris ceded the territory to Spain; administered as part of the Province of Louisiana (Upper Louisiana), with the commandant at Arkansas Post the local authority
- **Return to France / U.S. acquisition:** Spain secretly re-ceded to France in 1800; the Louisiana Purchase transferred the region to the United States in 1803; Arkansas Territory was carved out in 1819; statehood in 1836
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post — the sole significant European settlement throughout this period; population was small (a few hundred European settlers, soldiers, and traders at any time, plus enslaved persons and indigenous contacts)
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, military garrison
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish soldiers and administrators, a small contingent of Acadian exiles (post-1755), enslaved Africans, and sustained contact with Quapaw, Osage, and other Native nations
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — French Capuchin and Jesuit missionaries, continuing under Spanish administration
- **Language of records:** French (early period); Spanish (post-1763 civil/military records); Latin (sacramental registers)

---

## Boundary changes

- **Before 1763:** The territory was part of French Louisiana, administered from New Orleans. Records created in this period follow French colonial administrative channels.
- **1763–1800:** Spanish Louisiana, Upper District. Arkansas Post functioned as a military-civil post; no county system existed. All civil authority flowed through the post commandant and the Governor-General in New Orleans.
- **1803–1819:** U.S. Territory of Orleans / District of Louisiana, then Missouri Territory. Spanish-era land claims were adjudicated by U.S. boards of land commissioners — those proceedings (post-1803) are a key secondary source for confirming Spanish-era grants.
- **1819:** Arkansas Territory created, beginning a recognizable county system. **Records before 1819 do not follow county lines** — search by post/settlement name (Arkansas Post), not by county.

---

## Available record types

### Church / sacramental records
- **What exists:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials recorded by Catholic missionaries and priests at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s onward through the Spanish period
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group **008814402** — "Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)," covering **Arkansas Post, 1763–1800**, 64 images
  - **Digitization level: Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image
  - **Language: Spanish** — researcher must read Spanish to use this volume
- **Physical/microfilm holdings:** Surviving registers are held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** and in transcribed form at the **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock)
- **Note:** French-period registers (pre-1763) are less intact; what survives is held by the Diocese and the Arkansas History Commission. No FamilySearch volume for the French period was returned by the survey.

### Spanish colonial censuses (padrones)
- **What exists:** Periodic *padrones* (household enumerations) conducted by the Spanish commandant at Arkansas Post, listing heads of household, family members, enslaved persons, and sometimes ages and occupations
- **Where held:** **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock) holds the primary Arkansas-based copies; **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) holds the original administrative records ([FamilySearch Wiki — Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)); **Library of Congress** holds microfilm of selected colonial Louisiana records
- **Digitization level: Physical/microfilm only** — no FamilySearch indexed collection or browse-only volume for padrones was returned in this survey
- **Language: Spanish**

### Land concessions and grants
- **What exists:** Spanish land grants (*concesiones*) issued by the post commandant or Governor-General; recorded in notarial or administrative registers
- **Where held:** **Arkansas History Commission**; **Archivo General de Indias** (Papeles de Cuba series, which covers Spanish Louisiana); **Bureau of Land Management — General Land Office (GLO)** website holds U.S. confirmations of Spanish-era claims filed after 1803
- **Post-1803 confirmation records:** After the Louisiana Purchase, Congress authorized boards of land commissioners to confirm valid Spanish grants. The proceedings name grantees and often describe the original grant in detail — a crucial secondary source for tracing Spanish-period landholders even when the original concession is not found. These U.S.-period confirmation records are at **NARA** (Record Group 49) and partially online at the GLO website
- **Digitization level: Physical/microfilm only** (original Spanish records); **online** (GLO confirmations)
- **Language: Spanish** (original grants); English (U.S. confirmation proceedings)

### Military post records
- **What exists:** Troop rosters, muster rolls, correspondence, and commandant's journals from the Arkansas Post garrison under both French and Spanish regimes
- **Where held:** **Archivo General de Indias** (Papeles de Cuba and Santo Domingo series); **Arkansas History Commission**; **NARA** (for post-1803 U.S. Army records at Arkansas Post)
- **Digitization level: Physical/microfilm only** for the colonial period
- **Language: Spanish / French**

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **No civil vital registration existed during this period.** The Catholic sacramental registers described above are the functional equivalent. U.S. statewide civil registration in Arkansas did not begin until 1914. There is no pre-1800 civil birth, marriage, or death record series in the American sense.

### Census records (U.S. period)
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870* (collection ID 2085124) — begins in 1819, after U.S. territorial organization. **Does not cover the Spanish period.**
- No federal census reached Arkansas before the U.S. territorial period (1819 is the earliest U.S. enumeration).

### Probate and court records
- **No U.S.-style probate or court system existed** before 1803. Inheritance and estate disputes were handled through the post commandant. Surviving records of this type (if any) are within the military/civil post records at the **Archivo General de Indias** and **Arkansas History Commission**.
- Post-1803 U.S. probate records begin with Arkansas Territory (1819).

### Land records (U.S. period — for confirming Spanish claims)
- After 1803, U.S. territorial courts adjudicated Spanish land claims. Check **NARA RG 49** (General Land Office records) and the **BLM GLO website** (glorecords.blm.gov) for confirmed patents tracing back to Spanish grantees.

### Military records (U.S. period)
- For ancestors who served in or around Arkansas Post after 1803, **Fold3** and **NARA** hold U.S. Army records. Spanish-era military service records are at the **Archivo General de Indias**.

### Cemetery records
- Formal burial registers follow the Catholic sacramental series above. Physical grave markers from this period at Arkansas Post are scarce. **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) covers some later burials at Arkansas Post but sparse coverage for the colonial period.

### Newspaper records
- No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800. The earliest Arkansas newspaper dates to the territorial period. **Not applicable for this time window.**

### Immigration / emigration
- Entry into Spanish Louisiana required a passport (*licencia de viaje*) and loyalty oath; records of settlers arriving at Arkansas Post may appear in the post commandant's correspondence at the **Archivo General de Indias**. Acadian exiles resettled in Louisiana after 1755 — some filtered into the Arkansas Post area; their resettlement lists are in the Papeles de Cuba series.

### Tax records
- Spanish colonial tax lists, when they survive, are embedded in post administrative records at the **Archivo General de Indias**. No separate digitized tax series was returned for this period.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Coverage for this period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | 1 browse-only volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763–1800, 64 images (image group 008814402) | Free — browse only, no name index |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S. confirmations of Spanish-era land claims, post-1803 | Free |
| **NARA Online** (catalog.archives.gov) | Some U.S. territorial-period records; RG 49 land records | Free |
| **Fold3** | U.S. military records post-1803 | Subscription |
| **Ancestry** | No collection specific to pre-1800 Arkansas was returned in this survey | Subscription |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial padrones, land concessions, military records (transcripts & microfilm); French Catholic register transcripts | In-person; some finding aids online at [www.thestatelibrary.com/ahc](https://www.thestatelibrary.com/ahc) |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records: Papeles de Cuba (Louisiana administration), Santo Domingo series; padrones, land grants, military rosters, church confirmations | In-person; microfilm at select U.S. libraries; partial digitization via PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) — free online |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of selected colonial Louisiana records | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original or microfilm sacramental registers from Arkansas Post missions | Contact the Diocesan Archives ([littlerockdiocese.org](https://www.littlerockdiocese.org)) |
| **NARA — Southwest Region** (Fort Worth, TX) | Post-1803 U.S. territorial records; RG 49 land commission records | In-person / mail requests |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types are documented as existing but have **no online name-indexed collection** for the pre-1800 period:

- **Spanish colonial padrones (censuses)** — physical/microfilm at Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias; not digitized on FamilySearch
- **Spanish land concessions** — original documents in Archivo General de Indias (partially accessible via PARES); transcripts at Arkansas History Commission
- **Military post records and commandant's correspondence** — Archivo General de Indias; not in any indexed online database
- **French-period sacramental registers (pre-1763)** — Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission; the single FamilySearch volume covers only 1763–1800

---

## Known record losses

- Settlement at Arkansas Post was attacked and burned multiple times (notably 1749 and 1783), which likely destroyed some locally-held records. The surviving colonial record base is incomplete.
- The dispersal of authority between the post commandant and New Orleans means records were not always kept in one place — some were sent up the chain to New Orleans and ultimately to Spain, others remained locally and were lost.
- Many records passed through multiple hands (French → Spanish → American) with attendant losses at each transition.

---

## Research tips

1. **The FamilySearch sacramental register (image group 008814402) is your most accessible starting point**, but it must be browsed image by image — 64 pages covering 1763–1800 — in Spanish. Use it first before traveling to repositories ([FamilySearch Wiki — Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).

2. **The Archivo General de Indias' PARES portal** (pares.mcu.es) has partially digitized the Papeles de Cuba series, which covers Spanish Louisiana administration including Arkansas. Search free online before planning a trip to Seville.

3. **U.S. land-claim confirmations are a backdoor into the Spanish period.** If your ancestor held land at Arkansas Post, their confirmed claim filed after 1803 will name them, describe their original grant, and sometimes cite the Spanish concession date — giving you a documentary anchor in the American record system even when the original Spanish record is in Spain.

4. **All colonial Arkansas records are in Spanish or French (or Latin for sacramental entries).** If you cannot read these languages, plan to work with a translator or hire a specialist in Spanish colonial paleography.

5. **Sacramental registers recorded Native Americans and enslaved persons** as well as European settlers — baptismal and marriage entries routinely name godparents and witnesses, expanding the network of identifiable individuals ([FamilySearch Wiki — Arkansas Genealogy, Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)).

6. **Think regionally, not just locally.** Arkansas Post was the only significant settlement; ancestors may also appear in New Orleans colonial records (held at the Louisiana State Archives and the Historic New Orleans Collection) or in Missouri (Upper Louisiana records at the Missouri State Archives), as the same colonial administration covered the whole region.

7. **Acadian research:** If your ancestor was an Acadian exile resettled in Louisiana post-1755, the resettlement and census lists in the Papeles de Cuba series are the first place to look. The Center for Louisiana Studies (University of Louisiana at Lafayette) holds significant Acadian-Louisiana collections.

8. **DNA evidence** can complement the thin documentary record — particularly for families of mixed French-Native or French-African heritage common at Arkansas Post, where the paper trail often stops abruptly.

---

**Summary of digitization coverage:** The pre-1800 Arkansas record base is almost entirely in physical or microfilm form. Only **one FamilySearch volume** (the 1763–1800 sacramental register, browse-only, in Spanish) is digitized online. For padrones, land grants, and military records, you will need to engage the **Arkansas History Commission** and the **Archivo General de Indias** — either in person, through the PARES portal, or via a professional researcher based in Seville.

## 🗺️ Ohio (Northwest Territory Era) — Locality Research Guide
**Place:** Ohio / Northwest Territory, United States
**Period:** c. 1785–1820 (focus: c. 1790, pre-statehood)

---

### 1. Jurisdictional History & Boundary Changes

In 1790, "Ohio" did not yet exist as a legal entity. The land was part of the **Northwest Territory**, created by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Researchers must navigate three overlapping jurisdictional layers:

| Period | Governing Body | County Structure |
|--------|---------------|-----------------|
| Pre-1787 | Unorganized / Virginia claims | None |
| 1787–1788 | Northwest Territory (no counties) | None |
| 1788 | Northwest Territory | **Washington County** organized — covered most of present Ohio |
| 1790 | Northwest Territory | **Hamilton County** carved from Washington County (SW Ohio) |
| 1800 | Indiana Territory split off | Additional counties organized |
| **1 March 1803** | **Ohio statehood** | 17 counties at statehood |

**The critical rule:** Any record created c. 1790 will be filed under **Washington County** (most of the state) or **Hamilton County** (southwestern Ohio) — not under "Ohio." Boundary shifts were rapid; you must pin the ancestor's location to determine which county had jurisdiction. Early court and land records for the territorial period are held at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus. (Source: [Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory))

#### Three Land Survey Districts — A Geographic Split

Ohio contains three distinct survey systems, each with its own land records and repository. Which one applies depends on *where within Ohio* the land was located — this is a **geographic split**, not a temporal one. If the ancestor's exact location is unknown, search all three:

| District | Area | Survey Type | Records Held At |
|----------|------|-------------|----------------|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between Scioto & Little Miami rivers | Metes-and-bounds | Virginia State Library, Richmond, VA |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio (Cleveland area) | Rectangular grid | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland, OH |
| **U.S. Military District / Seven Ranges** | Eastern Ohio | Federal rectangular | BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) |

(Source: [Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records))

---

### 2. Records Available — With Access Levels

#### 🟢 Land Records — FIRST PRIORITY for 1790

Land records are the single richest source for pre-statehood Ohio — they document presence, neighbor networks, and often family relationships through witness names.

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840* ([collection 1542187](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187)) — 234,567 indexed records, 117,283 images — **indexed + images** ✓
- **FamilySearch Digitized Volume** (image group **005112233**): *Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799* — 51 images — ⚠️ **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be examined image by image with no search capability)
- **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov): Federal land patents — searchable online, free
- **Virginia State Library** (Richmond, VA): Virginia Military District warrants — physical; some digitized
- **Western Reserve Historical Society** (Cleveland, OH): Connecticut Western Reserve land records — physical

#### 🟡 Tax Records

Tax duplicates are the primary name-list substitute for the absent 1790 census in this region.

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850* ([collection 1987542](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542)) — 345,890 indexed records, 172,945 images — **indexed + images** ✓ *(starts 1800; no FamilySearch-indexed tax collection covers 1790–1799)*
- **FamilySearch Digitized Volume** (image group **005112240**): *Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803* — 73 images — ⚠️ **12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** — the majority must be browsed image by image
- **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus): Holds earliest territorial tax lists predating 1800 — physical/microfilm

#### 🟢 Church Records — Primary Substitute for Vital Records

There was **no civil vital registration** in Ohio in 1790. Statewide birth and death registration did not begin until **1867** (county level). Church records — Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Quaker congregations all came early into the territory — are the primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials.

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950* ([collection 2246917](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917)) — 678,234 indexed records, 339,117 images — **indexed + images** ✓ (dates to 1787)
- **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus): Original church registers — physical
- Denominational archives: Local churches and regional repositories

#### 🟢 Marriage Records

County-level marriage bonds and registers began with Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790).

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013* ([collection 1803785](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785)) — 1,523,678 indexed records, 761,839 images — **indexed + images** ✓ (dates to 1789)

#### ⛔ Census Records — Gap at 1790 (Critical)

Ohio was **not included in the 1790 federal census**. The first federal enumeration covered the original states, Vermont, and parts of the Southwest Territory — but not the Northwest Territory. Ohio residents first appear in the **1800 federal census**. There was no territorial census for this area. **Tax lists (see above) are the best available name-list substitute for 1790–1800.**

#### ⚠️ Death Records — Gap for 1790

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001* ([collection 1417891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1417891)) — starts 1840, **well outside the 1790 target period.** Useful only for later descendants.
- For the 1790 period: church burial registers and cemetery records (FindAGrave: findagrave.com) are the primary sources.

#### 🟡 Military Records

Many early Ohio settlers were **Revolutionary War veterans**. Pension applications and bounty land warrants often name wives, children, ages, and places of origin — making them one of the richest biographical sources for this era.

- **Fold3** (fold3.com): Revolutionary War pension and bounty land files — online, subscription
- **NARA** (archives.gov): Service records and pension files — physical; some digitized
- *Note:* Bounty land in the Virginia Military District was specifically granted to Virginia veterans — warrants are at the Virginia State Library

#### 🟡 Court & Probate Records

Washington County Court (from 1788) and Hamilton County Court (from 1790) hold the earliest territorial court records: naturalizations, guardianships, estates, and civil cases.

- **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus): Primary repository for territorial-era court records — physical

#### 🔴 Newspapers

Coverage for 1790 is essentially absent. The first Ohio newspaper, the *Centinel of the North-Western Territory*, began publication in Cincinnati in **November 1793**. **Newspapers.com** holds some early Ohio papers, but content before 1793 does not exist for this territory.

### 4. Research Quirks & Critical Warnings

1. **Boundary-change rule (1790):** All of Ohio in 1790 belonged to either Washington County or Hamilton County. Records will be filed under one of these two — not under "Ohio." Search both if the ancestor's specific location is unknown.
2. **No 1790 census for Ohio:** The Northwest Territory was not enumerated. Tax lists (from 1800 on FamilySearch; earlier at Ohio History Connection) are the best substitute.
3. **Three land districts, three repositories:** The Virginia Military District (Virginia State Library), Connecticut Western Reserve (Western Reserve Historical Society), and U.S. Military/Seven Ranges (BLM GLO) each have separate records. This is a geographic split — which repository applies depends on where the land was located. Search all three if uncertain.
4. **No civil vital registration until 1867:** Church records are the only systematic vital-record source for the 1790 period.
5. **Territorial Land Records volume is browse-only:** Image group 005112233 (51 images, 1788–1799) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — every image must be browsed manually.

7. **Virginia-origin families:** Many early Ohio settlers — especially in the Virginia Military District — came from Virginia. Check Virginia county records for the family *before* their Ohio arrival.
8. **After 1800, check Indiana Territory:** When the Indiana Territory was split from the Northwest Territory in 1800, some northwestern Ohio counties briefly came under Indiana Territory administration before Ohio statehood in 1803.

## Ohio (Northwest Territory Era) — Locality Research Guide
**Place:** Ohio / Northwest Territory, United States
**Period:** c. 1785–1820 (focus: c. 1790, pre-statehood)

### Jurisdictional History
In 1790, Ohio was part of the Northwest Territory (Northwest Ordinance, 1787). Washington County organized 1788 (most of Ohio); Hamilton County organized 1790 (SW Ohio). Ohio achieved statehood 1 March 1803. Records from 1790 are filed under Washington or Hamilton County — not Ohio.

### Land Survey Districts (Geographic Split)
- Virginia Military District (Scioto–Little Miami): metes-and-bounds; warrants at Virginia State Library, Richmond VA
- Connecticut Western Reserve (NE Ohio): rectangular grid; records at Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland OH
- U.S. Military District / Seven Ranges (E Ohio): federal rectangular; patents at BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov)
Sources: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records

### Key Collections on FamilySearch
- Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840 (col. 1542187) — 234,567 indexed records — INDEXED + IMAGES
- Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950 (col. 2246917) — 678,234 indexed records — INDEXED + IMAGES
- Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013 (col. 1803785) — 1,523,678 indexed records — INDEXED + IMAGES
- Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850 (col. 1987542) — 345,890 indexed records — INDEXED + IMAGES (starts 1800)
- Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001 (col. 1417891) — starts 1840, outside 1790 target period

### Digitized Volumes
- Image group 005112233: NW Territory Territorial Land Records 1788–1799, 51 images — BROWSE-ONLY (0% indexed)
- Image group 005112240: Washington County Tax Records 1799–1803, 73 images — 12% indexed, mostly browse-only

### Key Repositories
- Ohio History Connection, Columbus OH: territorial court, land, tax, church records
- BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov): federal land patents — free online
- Virginia State Library, Richmond VA: Virginia Military District warrants
- Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland OH: CT Western Reserve records
- NARA (archives.gov): military records, post-1800 census
- Fold3 (fold3.com): Revolutionary War pension/bounty land files

### Critical Gaps
- No 1790 census coverage for Ohio (Northwest Territory not enumerated)
- No civil vital registration until 1867; church records are the only source
- Newspaper coverage begins November 1793 at the earliest

Ohio has three land survey districts with three separate repositories: Virginia Military District records are at the Virginia State Library (Richmond, VA); Connecticut Western Reserve records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland, OH); U.S. Military District / Seven Ranges patents are at the BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov). This is a geographic split — which repository applies depends on where the land was located; search all three if uncertain.

No civil vital registration existed in Ohio until 1867 (statewide). Church records (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker) are the only systematic source for births, marriages, and burials in the 1790 period.

FamilySearch image group 005112233 (Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799, 51 images) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only, every image must be examined manually.
FamilySearch image group 005112240 (Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803, 73 images) is only 12% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — the majority must be browsed image by image.
Many early Ohio settlers in the Virginia Military District came from Virginia. Check Virginia county records for the family before their Ohio arrival.
After 1800 some northwestern Ohio counties briefly fell under Indiana Territory administration before Ohio statehood in 1803 — check Indiana Territory records if the location was on the western edge.
Early court and land records for the territorial period are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory).
Ohio County Death Records collection (1417891) begins in 1840 — well outside the 1790 target period; use church burial registers and FindAGrave for pre-1840 deaths.

## Ohio (Northwest Territory Era) — Locality Research Guide
**Place:** Ohio / Northwest Territory, United States
**Period:** c. 1785–1820 (focus: c. 1790, pre-statehood)

### Jurisdictional History
In 1790, Ohio was part of the Northwest Territory (Northwest Ordinance, 1787). Washington County organized 1788 (most of Ohio); Hamilton County organized 1790 (SW Ohio). Ohio achieved statehood 1 March 1803. Records from 1790 are filed under Washington or Hamilton County — not Ohio.

### Land Survey Districts (Geographic Split)
- Virginia Military District (Scioto–Little Miami): metes-and-bounds; warrants at Virginia State Library, Richmond VA
- Connecticut Western Reserve (NE Ohio): rectangular grid; records at Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland OH
- U.S. Military District / Seven Ranges (E Ohio): federal rectangular; patents at BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov)
Sources: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records

### Key Collections on FamilySearch
- Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840 (col. 1542187) — 234,567 indexed records — INDEXED + IMAGES
- Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950 (col. 2246917) — 678,234 indexed records — INDEXED + IMAGES
- Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013 (col. 1803785) — 1,523,678 indexed records — INDEXED + IMAGES
- Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850 (col. 1987542) — 345,890 indexed records — INDEXED + IMAGES (starts 1800)
- Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001 (col. 1417891) — starts 1840, outside 1790 target period

### Digitized Volumes
- Image group 005112233: NW Territory Territorial Land Records 1788–1799, 51 images — BROWSE-ONLY (0% indexed)
- Image group 005112240: Washington County Tax Records 1799–1803, 73 images — 12% indexed, mostly browse-only

### Key Repositories
- Ohio History Connection, Columbus OH: territorial court, land, tax, church records
- BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov): federal land patents — free online
- Virginia State Library, Richmond VA: Virginia Military District warrants
- Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland OH: CT Western Reserve records
- NARA (archives.gov): military records, post-1800 census
- Fold3 (fold3.com): Revolutionary War pension/bounty land files

### Critical Gaps
- No 1790 census coverage for Ohio (Northwest Territory not enumerated)
- No civil vital registration until 1867; church records are the only source
- Newspaper coverage begins November 1793 at the earliest

# 📍 Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **Formed** | California admitted to the Union **9 September 1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely — a direct product of Gold Rush population pressure. Prior to 1848: Mexican jurisdiction. 1846–1850: U.S. Military Government. |
| **County system** | 27 original counties established at statehood in 1850; the system expanded rapidly throughout the 1850s–1860s as the Mother Lode was settled. |
| **Key Gold Rush counties** | El Dorado (Placerville), Placer (Auburn), Nevada (Nevada City), Tuolumne (Sonora), Calaveras (San Andreas), Amador (Jackson), Mariposa |
| **Population** | ~300,000 migrants arrived by 1855 (Wikipedia, *California Gold Rush*). Population was overwhelmingly male and transient. |
| **Economy** | Placer and hardrock gold mining; maritime trade through San Francisco; agriculture in valleys |
| **Ethnic composition** | Extremely diverse: American (East and South), Mexican, Chilean, Chinese (large influx from 1850 onward), French, German, Irish, Italian, Australian, and indigenous California peoples |
| **Religions** | Catholic (dominant pre-statehood and among Hispanic population); Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian; Jewish congregations in San Francisco and Sacramento from the early 1850s |
| **Key events** | Gold at Sutter's Mill (24 January 1848); statehood (1850); 1852 California State Census; rapid county formation |

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Pre-1848:** Records created under Spanish colonial (Mission era, 1769–1821) and Mexican (1821–1848) governance — in **Spanish and Latin**. The Mission system maintained its own registers; Mexican civil records are minimal.
- **1846–1850:** U.S. Military Government; minimal formal genealogical record creation.
- **1850:** 27 original counties created simultaneously at statehood. County-level records begin here.
- **1850s–1860s county subdivision:** Many Gold Rush counties were carved up. Amador County split off from parts of Calaveras and El Dorado in 1854; Alpine County formed in 1864. ⚠️ **Quirk: If your ancestor was in a large original county, check whether the exact locale was later assigned to a new county — records created before subdivision stay in the original county, while later records go to the successor.**

---

## Available Record Types

### 📋 Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Level:** County
- **Registration start:** County-level registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in **1850**, but **statewide registration did not begin until 1905**. Compliance in the Gold Rush era was poor — especially for deaths of transient miners.
- **What exists on FamilySearch:**
  - **Births:** *California, County Births, 1850–1919* (collection [2017276](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276)) — **789,456 records, indexed + images** ✅
  - **Marriages:** *California, County Marriages, 1850–1952* (collection [1452832](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832)) — **567,890 records, indexed + images** ✅
  - **Deaths:** County death registers exist but are sparsely covered for the 1850s. No indexed FamilySearch death collection appeared in this survey for the Gold Rush period.
- **Gaps:** Registration compliance was weak 1848–1860. Births and deaths of itinerant miners were routinely not registered.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records; cemetery inscriptions; probate files naming heirs; newspaper obituaries; mortality census schedules (1850, 1860).

---

### ⛪ Church Records
- **Mission records (pre-statehood background):** FamilySearch holds *California, Mission Records, 1769–1850* (collection [1804372](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372)) — **98,765 indexed records** covering the Franciscan Mission system. **Language: Spanish and Latin.** Relevant primarily for Hispanic families already in California.
- **Post-1850 Catholic:** Held at the Archdiocese of San Francisco, Diocese of Monterey, and Diocese of Sacramento archives; some FamilySearch microfilm available.
- **Protestant:** Scattered at denominational archives and local congregations; coverage is thin given the transient Gold Rush population.
- **Jewish:** Earliest congregations (Sherith Israel and Emanu-El, San Francisco, both 1851) hold registers at the congregations themselves and at the Western Jewish History Center, Bancroft Library.

---

### 🗳️ Census Records
| Census | Years | Access Level | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| California State Census | **1852** | **Indexed + images (88%)** + full-text ✅ | FamilySearch IGN 006601001 (522 images) — the single most important census source for Gold Rush researchers |
| U.S. Federal Census | **1850** | Indexed + images (Ancestry, FamilySearch) | **Partially destroyed** — some county returns are missing ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records)) |
| U.S. Federal Census | **1860** | Indexed + images ✅ | Full coverage; covers settled population as the Rush wound down |
| Mortality Schedules | **1850, 1860** | Indexed (FamilySearch, Ancestry) | Lists persons who died in the year before each census — valuable for miners who died and left no other record |

> **Key tip:** The 1852 California State Census is the most accessible entry point for Gold Rush migrants. It was taken specifically because the 1850 federal census was acknowledged to have missed much of the rapidly-arriving population.

---

### ⚖️ Probate and Court Records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration (intestate), guardianship files, naturalization petitions, civil suits, mining disputes.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Many Gold Rush miners died intestate and without family nearby — look for **administration files**, not wills.
- **Where held:** County superior courts and county archives; California State Archives (Sacramento). Primarily **physical or microfilm; minimal digitization.**
- **Naturalization records (pre-1906):** Could be filed in any court of record — county, district, or federal. Search county court records AND federal district court records. NARA (San Bruno) holds federal court naturalizations.

---

### 🌎 Land Records
- **Survey system:** California is a **federal-land state** — original land patents were distributed by the U.S. federal government, not the state.
- **Federal land patents:** BLM/GLO website ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) — free, searchable online.
- **Mining claim registers:** County recorder's offices documented claim filings and transfers. FamilySearch holds **340 browse-only images** for San Francisco county, 1849–1855 (IGN: 006601002) — **⚠️ 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image.** Registers for other Mother Lode counties remain physically at county recorders' offices.
- **Mexican land grants:** Holders were required to file claims with the Board of Land Commissioners after 1851. Records are at NARA (San Bruno) and the Bancroft Library. **Language: Spanish.**
- **County deed books:** After an original patent, subsequent property transfers were recorded at the county level in deed books — held at county recorders, partially on FamilySearch microfilm.

---

### 🎖️ Military Records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) — many Gold Rush miners were veterans; Civil War (1861–1865) — California remained in the Union with multiple volunteer units.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Mexican War), Civil War muster rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C.) for service/pension; [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) for online access; California State Archives for adjutant general records.
- **Note:** Mexican War bounty land warrants sometimes appear in California land transfer records — a useful cross-reference.

---

### ⛏️ Mining-Specific Occupational Records
*(A Gold Rush-specific record class with no equivalent in most other localities)*

- **Mining claim registers:** Filed at county recorders' offices — critical for identifying Gold Rush miners. The FamilySearch San Francisco volume (IGN: 006601002, browse-only) is the only currently digitized example; other counties' registers are physical only.
- **Ditch company and water rights records:** Essential for placer operations; held at county recorders and water boards.
- **Corporate mine employment rolls (post-1855):** As hardrock mining took over, company records occasionally survive at the Bancroft Library and company archives.

---

### 🚢 Immigration and Arrival Records
- **Primary port:** **San Francisco** — the vast majority of ship arrivals came here. Ship passenger manifests are held at **NARA Pacific Region (San Bruno, CA)** and partially digitized on Ancestry.com. ([Source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))
- **Sacramento port:** FamilySearch holds **298 browse-only images** of Port Arrival Registers, 1849–1858 (IGN: 006601003) — **⚠️ 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image.**
- **Overland migrants:** No single arrival record exists. Look for overland trail diaries at the **Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** and **California State Library**, and for Missouri River departure records at Missouri State Archives.
- **Naturalization records:** See Probate and Court Records above. Chinese men were legally barred from citizenship (1790 Naturalization Act) and do not appear in naturalization files.

---

### 📰 Newspaper Records
- **Key papers:** *Alta California* (San Francisco, 1849–1891); *Sacramento Union* (1851–); *Sacramento Bee* (1857–); numerous short-lived mining-camp papers throughout the Mother Lode.
- **Where held:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription); **California Digital Newspaper Collection** ([cdnc.ucr.edu](https://cdnc.ucr.edu)) — free access to many 19th-century California newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries; marriage notices; mining claim transfers; legal notices; **"Letters remaining at the Post Office" columns** — these lists, printed regularly in San Francisco papers, functioned as a missing-persons directory for the transient Gold Rush population and are a unique finding tool for otherwise-undocumented miners.

---

### 🗳️ Great Registers (Voter Registration)
- **What they are:** California's Great Registers are county voter registration rolls recording name, age, birthplace, occupation, and **physical description** — the most detailed individual identification source in 19th-century California.
- **Date range:** Begin **1866** — just outside the target period, but men who arrived in the 1850s and remained will appear in the first registers.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *California, Great Registers, 1866–1910* (collection [1923340](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340)) — **1,345,678 indexed records** ✅
- **Limitation:** Women and non-citizens (including all Chinese men) are absent.

---

### 💸 Tax Records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessment rolls (from 1850).
- **Access:** Primarily physical or microfilm; held at county assessors' offices, California State Archives, and county historical societies.
- **Substitute value:** Annual rolls allow year-by-year tracking of presence and accumulated assets. Miners who owned equipment or livestock appear even if they did not own real property — an excellent surrogate for missing census years.

---

### 🪦 Cemetery Records
- **Notable Gold Rush cemeteries:** Mission Dolores (San Francisco); Sacramento Historic City Cemetery; Gold Hill Cemetery (El Dorado County); numerous county "miners' cemeteries" along the Mother Lode.
- **Online coverage:** [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) — broad coverage, though many rural mining camp cemeteries are incompletely photographed.
- **Physical records:** Sexton registers at county/city offices; transcription indexes at county genealogical societies.
- **Gap:** Many transient miners were buried in unmarked or abandoned camp cemeteries. Expect significant gaps.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Collections for This Place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org) | County Births 1850–1919 (789,456 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (567,890 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (98,765 records); 1852 State Census (88% indexed, 522 images); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1,345,678 records); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (browse-only, 340 images); Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 (browse-only, 298 images) | Free |
| [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census 1850 & 1860; San Francisco passenger lists; California collections | Subscription |
| [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery inscriptions including Gold Rush-era cemeteries | Free |
| [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) | Alta California, Sacramento Union, Mother Lode papers | Subscription |
| [BLM GLO](https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for California | Free |
| [CA Digital Newspaper Collection](https://cdnc.ucr.edu) | Digitized 19th-c. California newspapers | Free |
| [NARA archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) | San Francisco ship passenger manifests; federal court naturalizations | Free catalog; some records fee-based |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **California State Archives** (Sacramento) | State-level records; Mexican land grant records; adjutant general files | In-person; some records online |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush manuscript collections; overland trail diaries; corporate mine records; Mexican land grant diseños | In-person; online finding aids |
| **California State Library** (Sacramento) | 19th-c. newspapers, directories, and manuscript collections | In-person; microfilm via interlibrary loan |
| **NARA Pacific Region** (San Bruno, CA) | San Francisco ship arrival manifests; federal court records; federal land office records | In-person; mail requests |
| **County recorder's / clerk's offices** | Deed books; mining claim registers; county court records | In-person; mail |
| **California Genealogical Society** (Oakland) | Statewide records and research library | In-person; some records online |
| **Chinese Historical Society of America** (San Francisco) | Chinese community records, clan association records | In-person |
| **County genealogical societies** (each Mother Lode county) | Local cemetery transcriptions; obituary files; local histories | Varies |

---

## Records NOT Online

- **County probate records (1850s):** Physical only at county courthouses and California State Archives; not digitized.
- **County tax/assessment rolls (1850s):** Physical or microfilm; no major online database.
- **Mining claim registers (beyond San Francisco):** County recorders hold these physically; the FamilySearch San Francisco volume is browse-only and covers only one county.
- **Mexican land grant adjudication files:** NARA and Bancroft Library — not digitized for general online access.
- **Overland emigrant trail records:** Diaries and journals at Bancroft Library and California State Library — physical only.
- **Pre-1906 San Francisco county court records:** Largely destroyed (see Known Losses below); surviving fragments at California State Archives.
- **Chinese community records:** Clan association (tong) records; Chinese-language newspapers (e.g., *The Golden Hills' News*, 1854) — held at the Chinese Historical Society of America, not yet broadly digitized.

---

## Known Record Losses

- ⚠️ **1850 federal census — partial destruction:** Some California county census returns from 1850 are missing. ([Source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records)) **Substitute:** The 1852 California State Census (88% name-indexed on FamilySearch) partially compensates.
- ⚠️ **1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire:** Destroyed the vast majority of pre-1906 San Francisco County records — vital records, court records, probate files. **Substitutes:** Great Registers (1866–1905); NARA federal records (San Bruno); church records held outside the city; newspaper archives.
- ⚠️ **Mining camp records:** Many camps were temporary; local records (if any were kept) did not survive. No centralized miner registry ever existed.
- ⚠️ **U.S. Military Government period (1846–1850):** Generated minimal formal genealogical records.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census** — 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch (IGN: 006601001). It is the most accessible single entry point for locating Gold Rush migrants and partially compensates for the destroyed 1850 returns. ([Source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))

2. **The 1850 federal census is partially destroyed** — missing county returns are a documented fact, not a search failure. Pivot immediately to the 1852 state census, county tax rolls, and mining claim registers if your person isn't in 1850. ([Source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records))

8. **Chinese ancestors require specialized repositories** — Chinese men were barred from citizenship and do not appear in Great Registers or naturalization records. Federal census records (1850, 1860) do include Chinese residents; also check clan association records and Chinese-language newspapers at the Chinese Historical Society of America.

9. **"Letters remaining" columns in the *Alta California*** — San Francisco newspapers regularly printed the names of people for whom mail was held at the post office. These lists are a unique tool for locating otherwise-undocumented transient miners. Search via [California Digital Newspaper Collection](https://cdnc.ucr.edu) (free) or Newspapers.com.

10. **Civil registration was under-enforced before 1905** — absence from the county births or deaths collection does not mean the event didn't occur; it was simply not registered. Always seek corroborating evidence in church records, probate files, or cemetery inscriptions.

---

# 🗺 Locality Research Guide: New York City (New York County), Colonial Period (1700–1783)

## Jurisdictional Background

**Standard place:** New York, New York, United States (FamilySearch place, established from 1624)

In the 1700s, **New York City meant Manhattan Island** — the seat of British colonial *New York Province*. The city was seized from the Dutch in 1664 and renamed from New Amsterdam. The surrounding areas were **separate county jurisdictions**: Kings County (Brooklyn), Queens County, Richmond County (Staten Island), and the southern Bronx under Westchester County. Families in those areas generated records under *those* counties — not under New York City records.

⚠️ **No civil registration existed in the 1700s.** Church registers are the only systematic source for vital events (births/baptisms, marriages, and burials) in this period.

⚠️ **British occupation (1776–1783)** disrupted record-keeping during the Revolutionary War; some series have gaps for those years.

---

## Record Types & Availability

### 1. ★ Church Records — *Primary Source for Vital Events*

There is no civil vital registration for this period. Baptisms, marriages, and burials in church registers are the **only** systematic record of vital events.

**On FamilySearch:**
| Collection | Status | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| **New York, Church Records, 1640–1940** (Collection [1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)) | **Indexed + images** | 2,345,678 records; 1,172,839 images — covers entire colonial period |
| **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700–1776** (Vol. 007733180) | ⚠️ **Browse-only; in Dutch** | 211 images; **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable** |

> The Dutch Reformed registers are the oldest continuous series (beginning 1639, per the FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). The FamilySearch volume must be browsed image-by-image and **requires the ability to read 18th-century Dutch script**. There is no keyword search.

**Key denominations & physical repositories** (per FamilySearch Wiki):
- **Dutch Reformed** — also at the Reformed Church in America Archives, New Brunswick, NJ, and the New-York Historical Society
- **Anglican / Episcopal (Trinity Church)** — Trinity Church registers begin 1697; held at Trinity Church Archives, Manhattan. Trinity Churchyard is one of the best-documented colonial burial grounds.
- **Presbyterian** — First Presbyterian Church (founded 1716); held at the church and at NYGBS
- **French Huguenot** — Huguenot congregation registers are published and partially digitized
- **Jewish (Congregation Shearith Israel)** — America's oldest Jewish congregation (est. 1654); registers held at Shearith Israel

The **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** and the **New-York Historical Society** hold extensive published transcriptions and manuscript colonial church records.

---

### 2. Land Records

**On FamilySearch:**
- **New York, Land Records, 1630–1975** (Collection [2078654](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654)) — **Indexed + images.** 1,567,890 records; 783,945 images. Covers the entire colonial period.

Colonial land records include royal patents, deeds, grants, and conveyances — a key source named in the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). The **New York State Archives** holds the *New York Colonial Manuscripts*, including many provincial land grants; many have been published in the *Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York* (the "O'Callaghan volumes").

---

### 3. Probate Records

**On FamilySearch:**
- **New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971** (Collection [1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)) — **Indexed + images.** 987,654 records; 493,827 images. Begins well within the colonial period.

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** In the colonial period, wills were proved before the provincial **Prerogative Court of New York** — not a county surrogate's court. The **New-York Historical Society** published the *Abstracts of Wills on File in the Surrogate's Office, City of New York* (multiple volumes), which serves as an essential name index for colonial-era wills. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

---

### 4. Tax Records

- **New York, Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799–1804** (Collection 1678432) — indexed; **starts in 1799, after the colonial period ends.** Not directly useful but shows what format early-period rolls followed.

For the 1700s: tax assessment lists survive for some years and city wards (confirmed in FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records), but they are **physical-only** — held at the **New York State Archives** and the **New-York Historical Society**. Search NYSA finding aids at https://www.archives.nysed.gov/.

---

### 5. Military & Militia Records

Colonial New York Province maintained **militia rolls** listing men of military age — a key tool for locating colonial residents (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records). These are not yet indexed as a standalone FamilySearch collection for the 1700s city level.

**Access:**
- **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) — colonial and Revolutionary War–era New York service records
- **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/) — Revolutionary War pension files, bounty land warrants, compiled service records for New York troops
- **New York State Archives** — provincial militia rolls and state-level Revolutionary War records

---

### 6. Court Records

The **Mayor's Court of New York City** was the primary colonial-era local court (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). Court records may document civil suits, criminal cases, and family relationships.

**Access:** Mayor's Court records are held at the **New York City Municipal Archives** (31 Chambers Street, Manhattan) and partly at the **New York State Archives**. Digitization for the 1700s is limited — **physical research is likely required.**

---

### 7. Cemetery Records

**FindAGrave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) has transcribed some colonial-era burial inscriptions from New York City, though coverage for 18th-century sites is uneven. Many colonial burying grounds were later demolished or relocated. **Trinity Churchyard** is the best-documented and most accessible colonial burial ground in Manhattan.

---

### 8. Newspapers

The *New-York Gazette* (founded 1725) — New York City's first newspaper — carried genealogically relevant notices: estate advertisements, runaway servant and enslaved person notices, ship arrivals, and public announcements. **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds some 18th-century New York papers, but coverage for pre-1780 issues is limited. Physical holdings are at the **New York Public Library**.

---

### 9. Immigration & Passenger Records

New York was a major Atlantic port throughout the 1700s, but passenger manifests from this era are far less systematic than 19th-century arrivals. NARA holds some colonial ship records. The *New York Genealogical and Biographical Record* (NYGBS journal) has published passenger list transcriptions. Naturalization records before 1906 may appear in any court of record.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Colonial Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church records (indexed + images), land, probate | Free online |
| **NY Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** | Published abstracts, transcriptions, colonial records | Subscription + onsite |
| **New-York Historical Society** | *Abstracts of Wills*, manuscript church records, colonial manuscripts | Onsite; some digitized |
| **New York State Archives (Albany)** | Colonial Manuscripts, provincial tax lists, militia rolls | Onsite; finding aids at archives.nysed.gov |
| **New York City Municipal Archives** | Mayor's Court records, city records | Onsite |
| **Trinity Church Archives** | Anglican registers from 1697, burial records | Onsite; some published |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Revolutionary War service, pension, bounty land records | Fold3, Ancestry, onsite |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Church Records (general), 1640–1940 | ✅ Indexed + images | Collection 1469062 |
| Dutch Reformed Registers, 1700–1776 | ⚠️ Browse-only; **in Dutch** | Vol. 007733180; 0% indexed; must read Dutch |
| Land Records, 1630–1975 | ✅ Indexed + images | Collection 2078654 |
| Probate Records, 1629–1971 | ✅ Indexed + images | Collection 1542780; use NYHS *Abstracts of Wills* index |
| Tax Rolls (FamilySearch) | ✅ Indexed — **but 1799–1804 only** | Colonial tax lists are physical-only at NYSA/NYHS |
| Militia / Military | ❌ No indexed FS collection for this period | Fold3, NARA, NYSA |
| Mayor's Court Records | ❌ Not digitized on FamilySearch | NYC Municipal Archives, NYSA |
| Newspapers | Limited on Newspapers.com | Physical at NY Public Library |

---

## Key Quirks & Cautions

1. **No civil registration in the 1700s** — church registers are the *only* systematic vital records. A family that didn't affiliate with a congregation, or whose church records were lost, may leave no baptism, marriage, or burial record at all.
2. **Dutch Reformed registers are browse-only and in Dutch** — the one digitized FamilySearch volume (007733180, 211 images, 1700–1776) has 0% name indexing and is not full-text searchable. You must browse each image in 18th-century Dutch.
3. **Colonial NYC = Manhattan (New York County) only** — families in Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens, Staten Island (Richmond County), or the Bronx generated records under those separate county jurisdictions.
4. **Wills went to the provincial Prerogative Court, not county surrogate** — use the NYHS *Abstracts of Wills* series as your finding aid.
5. **British occupation (1776–1783) created record gaps** — some church registers and civic records are incomplete for those years.
6. **No federal census before 1790** — the first enumeration is 1790, post-colonial. For the 1700s, church and tax records are the closest substitutes for population surveys.
7. **FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages for NYC** returned only generic guides through the automated tool; the most targeted colonial-era guidance is at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.

---

This guide covers the principal record classes for 1700s colonial New York City. When you're ready to build a research plan targeting a specific ancestor or question, the **research-plan** skill can sequence the searches from most to least promising using this foundation.
