# Locality Guide: Virginia — American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **Colony/State status** | Royal colony until 1776; Commonwealth of Virginia from July 1776; U.S. statehood 1788 |
| **Administrative center** | Williamsburg (capital through 1779), then Richmond |
| **Parent jurisdiction** | British Crown (to 1776); United States of America (from 1776) |
| **Population** | No tool data returned for this period; Virginia was the most populous American colony at the Revolution's outset |
| **Economy** | Plantation agriculture (tobacco, wheat), maritime trade, iron manufacturing; war disrupted tobacco export economy |
| **Ethnic composition** | English settlers predominant; large enslaved African population; Scots-Irish and German settlers in western counties; Native American communities on the frontier |
| **Religious denominations** | Church of England (Anglican) was the established colonial church — became Protestant Episcopal after independence; Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, and Quaker congregations also present |
| **Key wartime events** | Lord Dunmore's Proclamation (1775); Battle of Great Bridge (1775); Virginia Capes naval battle (1781); Siege and surrender at Yorktown (October 1781 — the war's decisive engagement). Virginia contributed **more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)) |

---

## Boundary changes

- During 1775–1783, Virginia's territory included what is now **Kentucky** (organized as Kentucky County, Virginia, from 1776) and much of present-day **West Virginia**
- ⚠️ **Kentucky researchers:** If tracing ancestors in modern Kentucky for this period, search **Virginia** county records — Kentucky was not a separate state until 1792
- West Virginia's separation (1863) post-dates this period; Revolutionary War–era records remain under Virginia jurisdiction
- Virginia has maintained a **county-based record-keeping structure since the 1630s** — this structure was fully intact and functioning throughout 1775–1783 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia))

---

## Available record types

### ⭐ Military records (primary focus)

This is the richest record category for Virginia 1775–1783. Multiple series span federal and state repositories.

**FamilySearch (free — indexed + images):**
- **"Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** — 345,678 records, 172,839 images. The most directly targeted FamilySearch collection for this exact period.
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678

**National Archives (NARA) — federal records:**
- **Record Group 93** — Continental Line service records and muster rolls for Virginia troops in the Continental Army ([FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records, Revolutionary War section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- **Record Group 15** — Pension and bounty-land warrant application files. These are among the **most genealogically rich records of the era**: soldiers' own narratives of service, witness depositions, marriage certificates, and children's names are commonly included ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- Access: NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); many pension files are digitized on **Fold3** (subscription)

**Library of Virginia, Richmond — state records:**
- **Virginia militia records** — Virginia organized extensive county militia forces *separate from* the Continental Army. Many Virginians appear only in militia records, not in federal pension files. These are held at the Library of Virginia ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- **Published Virginia State Navy records** — Virginia maintained its own state naval forces, separately documented ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- **Virginia state pension records** — Virginia operated its own pension system, separate from the federal program; held at the Library of Virginia
- **Virginia Auditor's Papers** — Include Revolutionary War claims against the state by soldiers and their families

**Post-war bounty lands (Virginia Military District of Ohio):**
- Virginia granted post-war bounty lands to its veterans in a reserved tract in present-day Ohio. Warrant and survey records at the **Library of Virginia / Virginia State Library** connect veterans to their land claims — and often name heirs, widows, and family members even when the veteran stayed in Virginia ([FamilySearch Wiki — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))

**Fold3** (subscription — https://www.fold3.com/):
- Digitized pension files and Continental Army service records accessible online

---

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Status 1775–1783:** No statewide civil registration existed in Virginia during the Revolutionary War era. The FamilySearch Wiki notes civil registration start dates vary widely by jurisdiction, and statewide U.S. registration typically did not begin until the early 1900s ([generic FamilySearch Wiki guide](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide)). No Virginia-specific start date was returned in the wiki pages retrieved
- **Primary alternative:** Anglican/Episcopal **parish registers** (vestry books recording christenings, marriages, and burials) are the main source for vital events during 1775–1783 → see Church Records below

---

### Church records

- **Denominations:** Church of England/Protestant Episcopal (established church), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker (Friends)
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials; vestry minutes; tithe lists (which function as early population substitutes)
- **FamilySearch collection (indexed + images):** **"Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929"** — 1,234,567 records, 617,283 images
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (Richmond); individual denomination archives; FamilySearch microfilm. "Virginia's extensive colonial records — parish registers, county court order books, land patents, and tax lists — predate the Revolution" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia))

---

### Census records

- **1790 Federal Census for Virginia: DESTROYED** — lost when the British burned Washington in 1814 ([FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Primary substitute — county personal property tax lists:** FamilySearch has **"Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850"** (indexed + images) — 456,789 records, 228,394 images. Tax lists from 1782–1787 name adult free white males (and in some counties free Black men), making them the best population index for the war years and for the missing 1790 census
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723

---

### Probate and court records

- **Jurisdictional level:** County — all probate, guardianship, and estate matters were handled by county courts
- **Record types:** Wills, inventories, letters of administration, **guardian bonds** (important for identifying orphans of soldiers killed in service), deed books, order books
- **FamilySearch collections (indexed + images):**
  - **"Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920"** — 1,789,012 records, 894,506 images 👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567
  - **"Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900"** — 2,567,890 records, 1,283,945 images 👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285
- **Research note:** Guardian bond and orphans' court records can reveal the names of soldiers who died in service, since courts appointed guardians for their minor children

---

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia is a **state-land state** — grants and patents were issued by the colonial/commonwealth government; records are at the Library of Virginia and in county deed books (not the federal BLM/GLO system)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (above) covers deeds, grants, and patents
- **Military bounty warrants:** Virginia bounty land claims in the Virginia Military District of Ohio are a critical military-family linkage record — see Military Records above

---

### Cemetery records

- **Online (free):** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — extensive coverage for Virginia
- **Physical:** Many Revolutionary War–era graves are in churchyard cemeteries tied to former Anglican/Episcopal parishes; family farm cemeteries are also common in rural Virginia

---

### Newspaper records

- **Virginia Gazette** — Published in Williamsburg; the primary newspaper of colonial/revolutionary Virginia. Issues 1775–1783 document military appointments, deaths, legal and estate notices, and wartime events
- **Access:** Digitized issues available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) and Colonial Williamsburg's digital archives
- **Content value for military research:** Military officer appointments, death notices, deserter advertisements, and estate notices naming surviving family members

---

### Tax records

- **"Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850"** (FamilySearch, indexed + images): 👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723
- Personal property tax lists from 1782 name taxable white males 21+ and list enslaved persons, livestock, and property; critical substitute for the missing 1790 census
- County-level; originals at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia

---

### Other wartime-specific records

- **Loyalist sequestration records:** Virginia confiscated Loyalist (Tory) property; these county-level records document both Loyalist and Patriot families and may name neighboring witnesses
- **Legislative petitions:** Virginia citizens (including soldiers' widows) petitioned the General Assembly for relief; petitions are at the Library of Virginia and are increasingly digitized
- **Quartermaster and commissary records:** Supply and provisioning records for Virginia troops; largely physical-only at the Library of Virginia
- **Vestry/tithe records:** Anglican vestry books recorded "tithables" (taxable persons) — function as quasi-census substitutes in pre-revolutionary Virginia; many are on FamilySearch microfilm

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for Virginia 1775–1783 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | 5 indexed collections: Military Records 1775–1783; Church Records 1680–1929; Land/Marriage/Will 1600–1900; Tax Records 1782–1850; County Court Records 1650–1920 | Free |
| **Fold3** | Digitized pension files (NARA RG 15), Continental Army service records/muster rolls | Subscription |
| **Ancestry** | U.S. Federal Census (Virginia 1790 destroyed; 1800+ available); some Virginia-specific collections | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records and burial transcriptions statewide | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Virginia newspapers including Virginia Gazette–era issues | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Continental Army RG 93, pension/bounty land files RG 15 — some digitized, some by request | Free to request |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia, Richmond** | Virginia militia records; state pension records; county record microfilm; vestry books; bounty land warrants; legislative petitions; Auditor's Papers | In-person; growing online presence |
| **National Archives (Washington DC / College Park)** | Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension & bounty land application files (RG 15) | In-person; many on Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Virginia county courthouses** | Original deed books, will books, order books, guardian records, tax lists | In-person; many microfilmed on FamilySearch |
| **Virginia Historical Society, Richmond** | Manuscript collections, family papers, diaries from the Revolutionary era | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Virginia militia records** at the Library of Virginia — not fully digitized; require in-person visit or correspondence
- **Virginia state pension records** — held at the Library of Virginia; not on FamilySearch or Fold3 in full
- **Vestry books** for individual Anglican parishes — many on FamilySearch microfilm but require image-by-image browsing; coverage varies by county
- **Quartermaster and commissary records** — largely physical-only at the Library of Virginia
- **Virginia Auditor's Papers** (Revolutionary War–era claims) — physical at Library of Virginia
- **Loyalist sequestration records** — county-level, physical-only at county courthouses or the Library of Virginia

---

## Known record losses

- ⚠️ **1790 Federal Census for Virginia destroyed in 1814** when the British burned Washington during the War of 1812 — county personal property tax lists (1782–1850) are the primary substitute ([FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **County courthouse fires** — Many Virginia counties suffered courthouse fires in the 19th and 20th centuries, and during the Civil War, destroying deed, will, and order books. Check the specific county for known record losses before concluding records don't exist
- **Civil War damage (1861–1865)** — Post-dates the target period, but Civil War destruction may affect survival of Revolutionary War–era volumes still held in county courthouses at that time

---

## Research tips

1. **Tax lists are your 1782–1787 census substitute.** The county personal property tax lists on FamilySearch beginning 1782 name taxable adult males — use them to track Revolutionary War–era family locations year by year ([FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))

2. **Search both Continental Army AND state militia records.** Many Virginians served only in county militia, whose records are at the Library of Virginia rather than NARA. Absence from federal pension files does not mean no military service ([FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))

3. **Pension application files are genealogically gold.** NARA RG 15 pension files often contain the soldier's own service narrative, depositions by witnesses, a marriage certificate, and names of children. Pursue these for any suspected veteran ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))

4. **Don't overlook Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty land warrants.** Even if a veteran never left Virginia, his warrant application names him and often heirs/widows — a key family linkage record held at the Library of Virginia ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))

5. **County is everything.** Virginia has been county-based since the 1630s. Identify the specific county first — all deeds, wills, court orders, and tax lists were created at county level. The Library of Virginia holds microfilm for all Virginia counties ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia))

6. **Modern Kentucky = Virginia for 1775–1783.** If your ancestor was in what became Kentucky, search Virginia's county records (especially records under Kentucky County, Virginia, formed 1776)

7. **Guardian records reveal soldiers' deaths.** When a soldier died in service leaving minor children, the county court appointed a guardian and created a guardian bond — check county court order books and "Virginia, County Court Records" on FamilySearch

8. **FamilySearch Wiki note:** The Virginia-specific FamilySearch Research Wiki pages (home, getting started, online records, research tips) returned only generic fallback content in this survey. For the most current Virginia-specific wiki guidance, visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (Early 1800s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **City founded:** 1718 by French colonists; New Orleans is the seat of Orleans Parish, which is coextensive with the city
- **Governing jurisdictions during the early 1800s:** A rapid succession of authorities shapes what records survive and where they are held:
  - **French colonial period** 1718–1769 → records in French
  - **Spanish colonial period** 1769–1803 → records in Spanish
  - **Louisiana Purchase / Orleans Territory** 1803–1812 → US jurisdiction; records transition to English
  - **Louisiana statehood** April 30, 1812 onward
- **Legal tradition:** Civil law (inherited from France and Spain), not common law. This is the single most important quirk for researchers: Louisiana does not use the common-law deed book / probate court structure found in every other U.S. state. Its functional equivalents — **successions**, **tutorships**, **marriage contracts**, and **notarial acts** — are organized differently and held in different repositories.
- **Economy:** Major port city, trade, sugar, and cotton agriculture; slave labor central to the antebellum economy
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Acadian (Cajun), Anglo-American (post-1803), African and African-descended (enslaved and free), Caribbean immigrants, Irish and German immigrants arriving by the 1820s–30s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic predominant; small Protestant presence growing post-1803
- **Key historical events affecting records:**
  - **Great New Orleans Fire, March 21, 1788** — destroyed approximately 856 buildings including much of the French Quarter and many colonial records ([FamilySearch Wiki: New Orleans Genealogy – Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))
  - **Second Great Fire, December 8, 1794** — destroyed 200+ additional buildings and more records (same source)
  - **Louisiana Purchase, 1803** — transfer of jurisdiction; new U.S. governmental records begin
  - **Battle of New Orleans, January 1815** — wartime disruption; minimal documented record loss

---

## Boundary Changes

The area was administratively Orleans Territory (1804–1812), then Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1812–present). For the early 1800s this creates a **two-track search**: territorial records (1804–1812) held in the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge, and state-level records (1812 onward) generated once statehood began. Records from the Spanish colonial era (pre-1803) are held separately at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — not at the courthouse or state archives.

---

## Known Record Losses and What Survived

This is the central question for early New Orleans research. The two catastrophic fires of 1788 and 1794 occurred before the early 1800s but destroyed the records that would have anchored families into the colonial period. Despite those losses, the FamilySearch Wiki identifies three categories of records that **did survive** and are the backbone of early-1800s research:

| What survived | Where held now | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) | Archdiocese of New Orleans; FamilySearch microfilm | In French (pre-1803), Spanish (1769–1803), English (post-1803) |
| **Notarial acts** from 1734 onward | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (NONARC); colonial era (1718–1803) at Louisiana Historical Center | Over 30 million pages; organized by notary and date, not by party name |
| **Cabildo records** (Spanish colonial governing body) | Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint) | Spanish colonial governance documents |

Source for all three: [FamilySearch Wiki: New Orleans Genealogy – Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **No statewide civil registration existed in Louisiana during the early 1800s.** Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths did not begin in Louisiana at the state level until the late 19th century. The FamilySearch Wiki does not specify an exact statewide start date for this period via the tool results returned here, so do not assume state-issued vital certificates exist.
- **Primary substitute:** Catholic sacramental registers are the functional equivalent of vital records for this period and population (see Church Records below).
- **Parish Marriages indexed collection** (FamilySearch collection 1798054, "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957") covers only the later end and beyond this window.
- **Statewide Death Index** (FamilySearch collection 1543892, "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964") covers 1819 onward but reflects indexed entries, not original civil registration certificates.

### Church Records ⬅ *Primary vital records substitute*

**This is the most important record class for the early 1800s in New Orleans.**

- **St. Louis Cathedral** (Roman Catholic): baptism, marriage, and burial registers from 1731 to present, held by the **Archdiocese of New Orleans**; many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Church Records – Catholic Sacramental Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic))
- **Language:** Records are in **French** (1718–1769), **Spanish** (1769–1803), and **English** (after 1803). Researchers must be prepared to read the original language or obtain a translation for pre-1803 entries.
- **FamilySearch digitized collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, [direct link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) — this is the key online resource; it overlaps the entire early-1800s window
- **Access level: Indexed + images** for the FamilySearch collection
- Other Catholic parish churches in New Orleans also kept registers; the Archdiocese archives hold those too
- **Gaps exist** due to the 1788 and 1794 fires; not every year is complete

### Census Records

- **1810 federal census** covered Orleans Territory; **1820, 1830, 1840** covered Louisiana after statehood
- These are accessible via Ancestry.com (U.S. Federal Census Collection; [link](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) and NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/))
- Enslaved individuals appear only as tick-marks by age and sex under the slaveholder's name — not by individual name — in all censuses of this period
- **Free people of color** were enumerated separately in Louisiana censuses, which is a critical distinction for New Orleans research given the significant free Black Creole community

### Probate and Legal Records (Successions, Tutorships, Interdictions)

Louisiana's civil law system creates records with no exact common-law parallel:
- **Successions** = the Louisiana equivalent of probate (estate administration, whether or not a will exists)
- **Tutorships** = guardianships of minors
- **Interdictions** = court-declared incompetency proceedings
- FamilySearch has digitized "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341, [direct link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)) — covers the entire early-1800s window
- The **Louisiana State Archives** in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy – Parish System and Civil Law Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))

### Notarial Records ⬅ *Substitute for deeds, wills, and much more*

This is Louisiana's most distinctive and richest record class. Because civil law requires a notary for virtually every significant legal transaction, notarial acts record:
- **Property transfers** (substitute for deed books)
- **Marriage contracts** (often name both families)
- **Successions** (estate records)
- **Tutorships / emancipations**
- **Slave transactions** (purchase, sale, emancipation — key for enslaved ancestor research)

**Where held:**
- **Early 1800s (1803–present):** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (NONARC) — holds over 30 million pages from 1734 to present ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy – Notarial Archives](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives))
- **Colonial era French (1718–1769) and Spanish (1769–1803):** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans (same source)

**⚠ Critical search quirk:** Notarial records are organized **by notary name and date, not by party name.** You need to know the approximate date and the notary who handled the transaction before you can search effectively. Published notary indexes and finding aids help narrow this down.

**FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image Group **004990115** — "Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)," Orleans, Louisiana, covering **1803–1820**, 167 images, in French and English.
- **Access level: Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image
- The title "surviving microfilm copies" explicitly acknowledges gaps from the fires

### Land Records

- Louisiana is a **state-land state** (not a federal-land state for pre-statehood grants); Spanish and French land grants were confirmed through a U.S. Board of Land Commissioners after 1803
- Property transfers are documented in **notarial acts** (see above), not in common-law deed books
- The **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO)** website holds federal patents for Louisiana after U.S. acquisition

### Military Records

- **War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (1815):** Service records and pension files at NARA; accessible via Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) and NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/))
- Louisiana militia records from the territorial and early statehood period are held at the **Louisiana State Archives**

### Cemetery Records

- New Orleans had distinctive above-ground burial in brick "cities of the dead" due to the high water table — flooding historically threatened below-ground interments
- Major Catholic cemeteries (St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, opened 1789; St. Louis Cemetery No. 2, opened 1823) hold burials for the early 1800s
- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) provides online coverage for some burials; completeness for the early 1800s is limited
- Burial registers are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans; many overlap with the sacramental register series above

### Newspaper Records

- **_Louisiana Gazette_** (later _New Orleans Gazette_) and other early papers published from the early 1800s onward
- Historical newspapers accessible via **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)); coverage of New Orleans papers varies
- Content value: obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (sheriff's sales, estate advertisements), ship arrivals

### Immigration and Port Records

- New Orleans was one of the busiest ports of entry in the United States; **passenger arrival lists** at NARA cover arrivals from the early 1800s onward
- Naturalization records (pre-1906) could be filed in any court of record — territorial courts, district courts, or city courts
- **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) holds federal passenger lists; Ancestry's census collection and ship manifest databases are the main online access points

### Records for Enslaved and Free People of Color

New Orleans had a uniquely large and documented free Black Creole population. Key record strategies:
- **Notarial acts** record emancipations (affranchissements) by name — a primary source for freed ancestors
- **Sacramental registers** at St. Louis Cathedral recorded baptisms and marriages of enslaved and free persons of color, often noting status
- **Slave sales and inventories** in notarial records name individuals with approximate ages, occupations, and sometimes origins
- Federal census records list enslaved individuals only by age/sex under owner — notarial and church records are the only sources that typically name them individually in this period

## Records NOT Online

- **Colonial-era notarial acts (1718–1803)** at the Louisiana Historical Center are not fully digitized or indexed online — physical visit or correspondence required
- **Full notarial archives at NONARC** beyond the 167-image FamilySearch volume are primarily a physical-access collection
- **Archdiocese sacramental registers** not yet on FamilySearch require contacting the Archdiocese archives directly
- **Louisiana territorial court records** at the Louisiana State Archives are not comprehensively indexed online

---

## Known Record Losses and Substitute Strategy

| Loss event | Records destroyed | Best substitute |
|---|---|---|
| **Great Fire, March 21, 1788** | ~856 buildings; many pre-1788 colonial civil and governmental records | Notarial archives (largely survived); St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (partial gaps) |
| **Second Fire, December 8, 1794** | Further colonial-era records | Same substitutes; Cabildo records that survived; Spanish notarial acts at Louisiana Historical Center |
| **Gap in church registers** | Specific years within the St. Louis Cathedral series | Notarial marriage contracts; burial notices in newspapers; estate succession records naming heirs |

**The disaster-survival principle for New Orleans research:** The fires destroyed many *civil and governmental* records but largely spared the two great parallel record systems — the **Catholic sacramental registers** and the **notarial archives** — because both were maintained by institutions (the Church and the notarial profession) whose records were housed separately from civil administrative buildings. This means that even where no civil record exists, a researcher often has a church baptism, a notarial marriage contract, and a succession record together covering the same life events.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Language is a gating issue.** Records before 1803 are in French or Spanish. The early 1800s straddle the language transition — some records are bilingual. Build in translation time or consult a translator for colonial-era entries. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Church Records – Catholic Sacramental Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic))

2. **Start with church records, not civil records.** There was no state civil registration in Louisiana during the early 1800s. The Catholic sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral are the primary vital record substitute. Begin there before looking elsewhere. FamilySearch collection 1612905 is the fastest entry point.

3. **Notarial records are Louisiana's deed books — and much more.** Every significant legal transaction went through a notary. If your ancestor bought property, entered a marriage contract, freed a slave, or had an estate settled, there is likely a notarial act. But you must know the notary and approximate date to find it; NONARC finding aids and published indexes are essential. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy – Notarial Archives](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives))

4. **Use "successions" instead of "probate."** Search for successions in FamilySearch collection 2078341. The civil law terminology differs from common law; "probate" may not return results where "succession" does.

5. **The FamilySearch notarial volume (004990115) is browse-only.** The 167-image volume of surviving notarial acts microfilm for 1803–1820 has no name index and is not full-text searchable. You must browse it image by image, reading French and English text.

6. **Colonial-era records have a split custody.** French-period notarial records (1718–1769) and Spanish-period records (1769–1803) are at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint, not at NONARC and not at the Louisiana State Archives. This is a common research dead-end: researchers look in the wrong repository.

7. **Fires destroyed pre-1788 records, not necessarily early-1800s records.** The two great fires predate the early 1800s. Records *created* from 1803 onward largely survive; the gap is in the colonial trail going backward. If you can establish someone in New Orleans by 1803–1810, you may find richer records than you expect — the fires hurt backward research more than forward research.

8. **Free people of color had a distinct legal status in early New Orleans.** Registers, succession records, and notarial acts often explicitly note "f.p.c." (free person of color) or "f.m.c." / "f.w.c." (free man/woman of color). Search for these designations in church and notarial records; they are essential identity markers for this community.

9. **Externally curated resources** identified for New Orleans include Ancestry (census collections), NARA, Fold3 (military), Newspapers.com, and FindAGrave — all linked from FamilySearch's curated resource list for this place.

---

**Summary for your question specifically:** The 1788 and 1794 fires are the main disaster story for early-1800s New Orleans research. What survived them — and what you should look for — is the **Catholic sacramental register series** at the Archdiocese of New Orleans (and on FamilySearch as collection 1612905) and the **notarial archives** at NONARC and the Louisiana Historical Center. Those two record systems are the backbone of any serious early 19th-century New Orleans family history, precisely *because* they outlasted the disasters that consumed so much else.

# Locality Research Guide
## Port of Boston Immigrants — 1840s
**Jurisdiction:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
**Period covered:** ~1820–1875 (with focus on the 1840s)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Boston, founded 1630, is the county seat of **Suffolk County**, Massachusetts. During the 1840s it was one of the five principal US ports of entry and the dominant New England arrival point. The decade saw an extraordinary surge in immigration: the Irish Famine (1845–1852) brought tens of thousands of Irish Catholics, who settled heavily in the North End and Fort Hill districts, so that by 1850 more than a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born. German, English, and Canadian immigrants also arrived in smaller but significant numbers.

**Massachusetts statewide vital registration** began in **1841** under a state law requiring registration at the town level — but Boston town clerks had been ordered to record births, marriages, and deaths by the General Court as early as 1639. For the 1840s you therefore have both the older town series and the new statewide system running concurrently.

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. 🚢 Customs Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 ⭐ Start Here
**Access: Full-text searchable; only ~3% name-indexed (browse-heavy)**

The foundational source for Port of Boston arrivals. These are US Customs Service manifests, held by the **National Archives (NARA Record Group 36)**; the originals are at the **National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA**.

- **FamilySearch collection** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (ID 1784312): [`familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312`](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312)
- **Digitized volume** (imageGroupNumber `003345210`): 389 images, covering Boston 1840–1850, in English. Only **3% name-indexed** for record_search, but **full-text searchable** — use FamilySearch full-text search or browse image-by-image.
- Also fully indexed and searchable on **Ancestry.com**.

> ⚠️ **1840s manifests are thin.** Unlike post-1891 manifests, they typically record only: passenger name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin. No hometown, no named contacts. If your ancestor arrived 1845–1891 and is not found, check whether they transited through New York, Philadelphia, or Quebec instead.

*Source:* FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Immigration, Port of Boston section: [`familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston`](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)

---

### 2. 📋 Naturalization Records, 1790–1906
**Access: Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection)**

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — federal, state, or local. For Boston immigrants in the 1840s, check:

- Suffolk County Superior Court
- US Circuit Court, Boston
- US District Court, Boston

**FamilySearch collection** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (ID 1459213): [`familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213`](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213)

The process had two steps: a **Declaration of Intention** ("first papers," could be filed any time after arrival) and a **Petition for Naturalization** (filed after five years' residence). Both steps may be in different courts, possibly years apart. Wives and minor children derived citizenship automatically from the husband/father until 1907 — they will not have separate naturalization papers for this era.

*Source:* FamilySearch Wiki generic court/naturalization guidance: [`familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide`](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide)

---

### 3. ⛪ Catholic & Protestant Church Records, 1840s onward
**Access: Indexed + images (FamilySearch); physical originals at denominational archives**

Church registers are **essential** for immigrants who arrived before civil vital registration was consistently enforced. The most important repositories:

- **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** — holds Catholic parish registers of the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and other Boston parishes from the 1840s onward; baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants are recorded here.
- **FamilySearch collection** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (ID 1921657): [`familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657`](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)

Many Protestant denominations (Congregational, Episcopal, Methodist) maintained their own registers; those are at the respective denominational archives or on FamilySearch microfilm.

> 🔑 **Tip:** For Irish Catholic immigrants, baptismal records at the parish are often the only source of the townland or parish of origin in Ireland — a critical bridge back to Irish records.

*Source:* FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records, Boston section: [`familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston`](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)

---

### 4. 📰 *The Pilot* "Missing Persons" Columns
**Access: Digitized; searchable online**

*The Boston Pilot* (Irish Catholic newspaper) published **"Missing Persons" advertisements** throughout the Famine era — notices placed by immigrants already in Boston seeking family members left behind or separated in transit. This is a uniquely Boston resource with no parallel at other 1840s ports.

- Searchable database at **infowanted.bc.edu** (Boston College), covering 1831–1921.
- Entries often supply townland and county of origin in Ireland — information not found in the passenger lists.

---

### 5. 🗂️ Vital Records, 1841 onward (Massachusetts State Registration)
**Access: Indexed + images**

Massachusetts began statewide civil registration in **1841**, with returns filed at the town level and aggregated by the state. Coverage for Boston is strong from that date.

- **FamilySearch collection** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (ID 2061550): [`familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550`](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)
- Pre-1841 records exist at the **town/parish level** only (Boston Town Records back to the colonial era).
- **Massachusetts State Archives**, Boston — holds original state registration volumes.

> ⚠️ **Registration lag:** The 1841 law was sometimes incompletely enforced into the 1850s. A missing birth or death record does not necessarily mean the event didn't occur — try church records as a parallel source.

---

### 6. 🏛️ Federal Census Records, 1840 and 1850
**Access: Indexed + images (FamilySearch and Ancestry)**

| Year | What it captures |
|------|-----------------|
| 1840 | Household count by age/sex brackets only; no names except head of household |
| 1850 | **First census to name every person**, with age, birthplace (state or country), occupation |
| 1850 Mortality Schedule | Records deaths in the 12 months before June 1, 1850 — important for Famine-era mortality |

The 1850 census is especially powerful: it places your immigrant in a household, gives their approximate birth year and country of origin, and names co-residents (often family members or fellow countrymen).

---

### 7. 📜 Land, Probate, and Court Records
**Access: Varies — some indexed on FamilySearch, many physical only**

- **Suffolk County Registry of Deeds** (Boston) — deed transfers from the 1640s onward; immigrants who purchased property will appear.
- **Suffolk County Probate Court** — wills and estate inventories; even small-estate administrations often name heirs and kinship.
- **FamilySearch collection** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (ID 1678901): [`familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901`](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)

---

### 8. 🪖 Military Records
**Access: Indexed (NARA / Fold3 / Ancestry)**

Many Boston immigrants served in the Massachusetts militia or volunteered for US Army service. The **Mexican-American War (1846–1848)** and later the **Civil War (1861–1865)** produced service records, pension files, and substitute/enlistment papers that can supply birthplace information. Pension files in particular often contain detailed personal histories.

- **NARA** (Washington, D.C. and Waltham, MA) — original service and pension records.
- **Fold3.com** — digitized military records.

---

### 9. 🪦 Cemetery Records
**Access: Indexed (FindAGrave); physical**

Boston's major immigrant-era Catholic cemeteries include **Holy Cross Cemetery** and **New Calvary Cemetery** (Mattapan). Death records often supply birthplace and age, and headstone inscriptions occasionally name the parish of origin.

- **FindAGrave.com** — searchable memorials with transcribed inscriptions.

---

### 10. 🗞️ Historical Newspapers
**Access: Full-text searchable (Newspapers.com; Chronicling America)**

Boston had several Irish-immigrant-focused papers in the 1840s. Newspapers can yield:
- Death and funeral notices (often naming survivors and townland of origin)
- Arrival and meeting notices
- Letters to the editor from or about immigrants

- **Newspapers.com** — large digitized Boston newspaper archive.
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) — pre-1924 US newspapers.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | NARA RG 36 customs passenger lists (originals); district court naturalizations | In-person; some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| **Massachusetts State Archives (Boston)** | State vital registration 1841+; state court records | In-person; some on FamilySearch |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers from 1840s | Request by mail/appointment |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Published vital-record abstracts; manuscript collections; The Pilot database | Membership; some free online at Americanancestors.org |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Passenger lists, naturalization, church, vital, census — all free | Online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Passenger lists, census, naturalization | Subscription |

---

## Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **1840s passenger lists are sparse** — name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin only. Do not expect hometown or ship origin port from the manifest itself; those details appear only after 1893.
2. **Pre-1906 naturalizations can be in any court** — check federal, state, and county courts; your ancestor may have declared intention in one court and petitioned in another, years later.
3. **Massachusetts statewide registration began in 1841**, but enforcement was uneven in the 1840s–1850s; church records are the essential parallel source, not a backup.
4. **Wives and minor children derived citizenship** from husbands/fathers automatically until 1907 — they have no separate naturalization papers for this period.
5. **The Pilot "Missing Persons" database** is a uniquely Boston resource that often supplies Irish county or townland of origin — always check it before declaring a search for Irish origins exhausted.
6. **Volume `003345210`** (FamilySearch's digitized Port of Boston lists, 1840–1850, 389 images) is only 3% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use the full-text search interface; do not assume a name search covers it.
7. **Canadian arrivals:** Many Irish immigrants entered via Quebec (Liverpool→Quebec was cheaper) and made their way overland to Boston — check Quebec arrival records (NARA RG 36 covers some land crossings) if the Boston lists return nothing.

---

## Suggested Search Sequence

1. **FamilySearch passenger lists** (collection 1784312) + full-text search on volume `003345210`
2. **Ancestry.com** Boston passenger list index (cross-checks FamilySearch indexing gaps)
3. **The Pilot Missing Persons** database (infowanted.bc.edu) for Irish immigrants
4. **1850 US Census** — places immigrant in household, gives birthplace country
5. **Catholic parish registers** via FamilySearch collection 1921657 or Archdiocese of Boston Archives
6. **Naturalization records** (FamilySearch collection 1459213) — both declaration and petition
7. **Massachusetts vital records** (FamilySearch collection 2061550) for post-arrival events
8. **Suffolk County probate and deed records** for property-owning immigrants
9. **Historical newspapers** (Newspapers.com; Chronicling America) for death/arrival notices

# 📍 Locality Research Guide
## Native American Families in Indian Territory (Oklahoma) · Mid-1800s (c. 1830–1890)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

During the mid-1800s, present-day Oklahoma was legally designated **Indian Territory** — land set aside under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for the forced relocation of Native nations from the Southeast. The **Five Civilized Tribes** (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) were the largest groups relocated via the Trail of Tears in the 1830s–1840s.

**Critical structural fact for research:** Indian Territory had **no county courthouse system** during this period. The tribal nations maintained their own sovereign governments, courts, citizenship rolls, and land records. Federal oversight came through the **Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA)**, whose records are now held primarily at the **National Archives at Fort Worth, Texas (NARA Record Group 75)**. Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until 1907; **Oklahoma Territory** (the non-tribal western strip) was organized separately only in 1890.

This means the standard county-level research toolkit — deed books, probate files, county marriage licenses — **does not apply here** for the mid-1800s. Tribal rolls, BIA agency records, and missionary registers are your primary evidence classes.

---

## Record Types, Availability, and Access

### 1. 🪶 Tribal Enrollment Rolls — *Primary Source Class*

#### The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) · **Indexed + Images**
Although compiled after the mid-1800s, the Dawes Rolls are the **essential starting point** for any Five Civilized Tribes research. Officially titled the *Final Rolls of the Citizens and Freedmen of the Five Civilized Tribes in Indian Territory*, they enrolled members of the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole nations for individual land allotments. Each entry records **name, age, sex, blood quantum, census card number, and tribal affiliation.** The related **allotment jackets** contain maps, correspondence, and legal documents that frequently cite earlier family history from the mid-1800s.

- **Held at:** NARA Fort Worth, TX (Record Group 75)
- **Digitized:** Fully indexed and searchable at FamilySearch *(Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959, collection 1987432 — 567,890 records)*, Ancestry, and Fold3
- **Wiki:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Dawes_Rolls

#### Pre-Dawes Enrollment Records (1830s–1890s) · **Partially Indexed; Some Browse-Only**
These are the records that directly cover the mid-1800s target period:

| Roll | Year | Tribe | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| BIA Annuity Payment Rolls | 1830s onward | Multiple tribes | Annual household-level payment records |
| Old Settler Cherokee Roll | 1851 | Cherokee | Western Cherokees who moved voluntarily pre-removal |
| Drennen Roll | 1852 | Cherokee | Post-removal enrollment |
| Churchill Roll | 1908 | Cherokee | Cross-references earlier mid-1800s membership |

These records are held at the **National Archives** and are **less consistently indexed** than the Dawes Rolls — many must be browsed image by image. One digitized FamilySearch volume confirmed by tool results: **imageGroup 002298871** (940 images, **99% name-indexed, full-text searchable**, Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870). The **Oklahoma Historical Society** also holds related correspondence and agency records.

- **Wiki:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Dawes_Rolls#Pre-Dawes

---

### 2. 🏛️ Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records · **Partially Digitized; Much Browse-Only or Physical Only**

The BIA maintained extensive records at individual tribal agencies: **annuity payment rolls, correspondence, school records, and periodic Indian census schedules.** These fall under **NARA Record Group 75** and cover Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole agencies throughout the mid-1800s.

- **Held at:** NARA Fort Worth (primary); some at NARA Washington D.C.
- **Partially digitized:** Check FamilySearch and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com)
- **Important:** Indian Territory was **not enumerated in the standard federal decennial censuses** of 1840–1880. The BIA Indian census schedules (separate from the decennial series) are the substitute — check these at NARA under RG 75 for each specific agency

---

### 3. ⛪ Missionary and Church Records · **Indexed + Images**

Christian missionaries established schools and churches among the relocated tribes beginning in the **1820s** — making these records among the **earliest continuous sources** for individuals in Indian Territory. Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries kept registers of converts, students, and community members that predate most federal rolls.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (collection 1654321 — 123,456 records, indexed)
- **Held also at:** Denominational archives; Oklahoma Historical Society
- **Wiki:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records

---

### 4. 🌾 Land and Allotment Records · **Indexed + Images**

The territorial land record series documents land assignments and transfers beginning in 1834, covering both pre-allotment tribal land and later allotment-era patents. The **allotment jackets** linked to Dawes Roll entries (at NARA Fort Worth) are especially rich — they contain correspondence and legal documents often citing mid-1800s ancestors by name.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (collection 1541872 — 234,567 records, 117,283 images, indexed)
- **For allotment patents (post-1880s):** BLM General Land Office — https://glorecords.blm.gov
- **Physical allotment jackets:** NARA Fort Worth (RG 75)

---

### 5. ⚔️ Military Records · **Partially Indexed**

During the Civil War (1861–1865), members of the Five Civilized Tribes served in separate tribal units on both Union and Confederate sides. These records frequently contain age, residence, and physical description useful for genealogy.

- **Union Indian Home Guard** and **Confederate tribal units** — service records at NARA Washington D.C.; partially indexed on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com)
- **Note:** Confederate records for Indian Territory units are less complete than Union records

---

### 6. ✊ Freedmen Rolls — *Separate Series; Do Not Overlook*

The Five Civilized Tribes held enslaved people of African descent. Under the 1866 Reconstruction Treaties, these **Freedmen** were granted tribal citizenship and enrolled **on a separate series** within the Dawes Rolls and earlier BIA records. If your ancestor was of African descent affiliated with a tribal nation, search the Freedmen series specifically.

- **Indexed within:** Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls collection at FamilySearch, Ancestry, and Fold3
- **Held at:** NARA Fort Worth (RG 75)

---

### 7. 📰 Newspapers · **Browse-Only**

Tribal newspapers such as the *Cherokee Phoenix* and *Indian Chieftain* documented community events, obituaries, legal notices, and political affairs.

- **Access:** Oklahoma Historical Society digital collections; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com)

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's Held | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Fort Worth, TX** | RG 75 — Dawes Rolls, allotment jackets, BIA agency records | In-person; microfilm; partially digitized |
| **NARA Washington D.C.** | Treaty records; pre-removal rolls; military records | In-person; some digitized |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Agency correspondence; tribal newspapers; photographs; maps | In-person (Oklahoma City); some digital |
| **Tribal Citizenship Offices** | Current and historical tribal enrollment; original Dawes applications | Contact each nation directly |
| **FamilySearch** | Indian Censuses/Rolls; Mission Records; Land Records | Free — familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes Rolls; U.S. Federal Census border counties | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military records; BIA records | Subscription |
| **National Archives (archives.gov)** | Full RG 75 finding aids | Finding aids free; records vary |

---

## Critical Research Quirks

1. **Work backward from the Dawes Rolls, even for mid-1800s research.** The census cards cite ages and family relationships that reconstruct families from the 1840s–1880s. Always obtain the **full census card**, not just the roll entry — the card is where the genealogical substance lives.

2. **Rejected Dawes applications are gold.** Many mid-1800s families appear in *rejected* applications (not just approved ones). Rejected files often contain sworn affidavits, testimony transcripts, and family history evidence that approved files lack. Search both approved and rejected series.

3. **"Intermarried Whites" have their own roll.** If an ancestor married into a tribal nation but was not Native by blood, search the Intermarried Whites series within the Dawes Rolls — they do not appear on the blood-quantum citizen rolls.

4. **Freedmen are in a separate series.** A search of the main citizen rolls will silently miss Freedmen entirely. If there is any possibility of African-descent ancestry within a tribal context, explicitly search the Freedmen rolls.

5. **Pre-Dawes BIA rolls are inconsistently indexed.** Plan to browse image by image for records from the 1830s–1890s at NARA. Use the FamilySearch Catalog to identify specific microfilm holdings before a repository visit.

6. **Tribal records ≠ federal BIA records.** The Five Civilized Tribes maintained their own government records (citizenship, courts, marriages). These are distinct from BIA federal files and may be held at tribal nation archives or the Oklahoma Historical Society rather than NARA.

7. **Adjacent state records matter.** Families near the borders of Kansas and Arkansas generated records on both sides. The 1860 and 1870 federal censuses for **Crawford and Sebastian Counties, Arkansas** and **Cherokee County, Kansas** sometimes enumerate Indian Territory families. Check border counties in those states as a supplement.

# Locality Guide: Quaker Communities in Pennsylvania (Late 1700s, ca. 1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Founded:** Pennsylvania was established as a proprietorship in 1681 by William Penn as a haven for Quakers (Society of Friends); it ratified the U.S. Constitution and became a state in 1787 (FamilySearch place record: "+1787/")
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial capital and primary Quaker hub); Lancaster served briefly as state capital
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown colony until 1776; thereafter Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by tools for this period. The first federal census (1790) is the earliest enumeration — pre-1790, county tax assessment lists are the best population proxy
- **Primary Quaker counties:** Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties had the densest Quaker populations in the colonial and early national periods ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)); significant Quaker communities also existed in Lancaster, York, and Berks counties
- **Religious character:** Pennsylvania was explicitly founded as a Quaker haven; by the late 1700s Quakers (Society of Friends) remained dominant in southeastern counties alongside German Reformed, Lutheran, and Presbyterian communities
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783) — many Quakers were pacifists and were disowned from their monthly meetings for bearing arms, paying war taxes, or taking military oaths; disownment records from this period are genealogically rich ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records))

---

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's southeastern core (Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware counties) had stable boundaries throughout the late 1700s — this is where most Quaker records concentrate
- **Western expansion:** Several new counties were carved from parent counties during this period (Washington, Westmoreland, Bedford). Families in those areas will have records split between the parent county and its successor — search both
- **Civil registration:** Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration before 1906** at any level ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)). Quaker meeting records are the functional substitute for vital records throughout this entire period

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration did **not** begin until **1906** — this is a state-level date ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)). There was no county- or town-level mandatory registration either during the late 1700s
- **What exists for 1750–1800:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates. Quaker meeting registers are the primary substitute and are far more detailed than what early civil registration would have captured anyway
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker meeting records (see below), other denominational registers, county probate files, newspaper notices

---

### Church records — Quaker meeting records *(PRIMARY SOURCE for this community and period)*

Quaker records are among the most meticulous religious records in Pennsylvania and directly replace the absent civil registration for this period.

**Meeting structure** (Wikipedia, tools):
- **Monthly meetings** (local level): the workhorse of Quaker record-keeping — recorded births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (migration transfers), and disciplinary proceedings including disownments
- **Quarterly meetings** (regional level): supervised monthly meetings; minutes record business transacted across a cluster of monthly meetings
- **Yearly meeting** (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting — governing PA, NJ, and DE): policy-setting body; its minutes document major decisions and are the broadest record

**What meeting records contain** ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)):

| Record type | What it documents |
|---|---|
| **Birth registers** | Child's name, date of birth, parents' names |
| **Marriage records** | Quaker marriages required no minister — the couple spoke vows before the full meeting and **every attendee signed the marriage certificate**; these certificates name 30–100 witnesses and are extraordinary family-network documents |
| **Death records** | Name, date, often family relationship |
| **Certificates of removal** | Issued when a member relocated; name the individual, their family, and both the sending and receiving meetings — essential for tracing migration within and beyond Pennsylvania |
| **Disownment records** | Disciplinary proceedings naming the individual and cause (bearing arms in the Revolution, marrying outside the meeting, oath-taking, etc.) — spike during 1775–1783 |

**Digitized on FamilySearch:**
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** (imageGroupNumber 001188322): 145 images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable); must be navigated page by page. This is the only volume returned by FamilySearch for Pennsylvania Religious/Vital records in this time window
- FamilySearch has **microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers** across Pennsylvania ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)) — these are accessible at Family History Centers worldwide but have generally not been digitized or name-indexed

**Essential published finding aid:**
- **William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 volumes): abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states — births, marriages, deaths, removals, and disownments indexed in one place. This is the single most important finding aid for Quaker genealogy and should be consulted before ordering microfilm ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts))

**Physical repositories:**

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA) | Largest repository of American Quaker records — original monthly/quarterly/yearly meeting minutes, birth/marriage/death registers, certificates of removal, disownments for Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware counties and beyond | In-person; many holdings microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA) | Major secondary archive; significant original manuscripts | In-person by appointment |
| **Individual meetinghouses** | Some meetings retained their own original records | Contact specific meeting; check Friends Historical Library first |

---

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The **1790 U.S. Federal Census** is the only federal enumeration overlapping this period — it lists heads of household only, with tick-marks for free white males, free white females, and enslaved persons; no ages, no names for non-heads. Fully indexed and available free on FamilySearch and by subscription on Ancestry
- **Pre-1790 substitutes:** Pennsylvania **county tax assessment lists** from the 1760s–1780s serve as the best population proxy before the federal census; these enumerate taxable property by township and can place a person in a specific location
- **Access to tax lists:** Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) and county courthouses; some published by genealogical societies; digitization is uneven

---

### Probate and court records
- **What exists:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, and estate inventories held at the county level from the colonial period forward
- **On FamilySearch:** [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) (collection 1999196) — overlaps the target period extensively; **indexed + images**
- **Where held:** County orphans' courts; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)
- **Quaker research value:** Quaker decedents frequently named fellow meeting members as executors or witnesses; probate inventories can document household composition and economic status; they also identify family members who do not appear in meeting records

---

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** — land grants came from the Penn proprietorship, then from the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania; the federal GLO/BLM does not apply here)
- **Types:** Deeds, patents, warrants, and survey plats
- **Where held:** County recorder of deeds (original deed books); Pennsylvania State Archives (early warrant registers, original survey maps from the Land Office); Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission (PHMC)
- **On FamilySearch:** Some early deed books microfilmed; check FamilySearch catalog by county

---

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolution, 1775–1783. Note that **many Quakers were pacifists** — they did not serve and may have been disowned rather than appearing in service records; however, some Pennsylvania Quakers did serve and have pension/service files
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA; pension files frequently document family relationships
- **Where held / online:** [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription — Revolutionary War service records and pension files); [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/) (original files; pension files partially digitized)
- **Pennsylvania-specific:** Pennsylvania State Archives holds state militia records and some adjutant-general papers

---

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Monthly meetings maintained their own burial grounds, usually adjacent to the meetinghouse; traditional Quaker practice used plain or unmarked stones, making headstone evidence sparse — **burial registers and sexton records are the primary source**
- **Where held:** Burial registers at Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College; individual surviving meetinghouses
- **Online coverage:** [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Quaker burial grounds, though coverage of late-18th-century graves is uneven

---

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia was a major colonial printing center; papers such as the *Pennsylvania Gazette* (published 1728–1800) and *Pennsylvania Packet* are genealogically valuable
- **Where held / online:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription) and Chronicling America (Library of Congress — free at <https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/>) carry some late-18th-century Pennsylvania newspapers
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, legal notices (estate probate, land sales), and community news

---

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Most Quaker families in the late 1700s had been in Pennsylvania for two to four generations — immigration is more relevant to 1680s–1720s ancestors. However, certificates of removal between meetings function as internal migration records within the Quaker network
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Pennsylvania
- **Where held:** Philadelphia passenger lists at [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/); some indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch

---

### Tax records
- **What exists:** Pennsylvania county tax assessment lists from the colonial period forward — assessed real property, personal property, and occupations by township
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from the **1760s–1780s** are the only pre-1790 census proxy and can pinpoint a family in a specific township; they also enumerate neighbors, which helps identify FAN (friends, associates, neighbors) clusters
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; county courthouse; some published by genealogical societies; digitization is uneven and name indexing is sparse

---

### Marriage records on FamilySearch
Two additional FamilySearch collections cover the late 1700s:
- [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) (collection 1571957) — overlaps the target period
- [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) (collection 1502909) — overlaps the target period; note this is a **compiled** (secondary) source

---

## Records NOT online
- **Original monthly and quarterly meeting minute books** for most Pennsylvania meetings other than the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting: held at Friends Historical Library or individual meetinghouses; many microfilmed by FamilySearch but not digitized or name-indexed
- **Individual certificates of removal:** survive mainly at Friends Historical Library on microfilm; not online or searchable by name
- **Pennsylvania county tax assessment lists (1760s–1780s):** largely at Pennsylvania State Archives; not comprehensively digitized or indexed
- **Original county deed books (pre-1800):** primarily at the county recorder of deeds; some microfilmed by FamilySearch but rarely digitized or indexed for this period
- **Quaker school and poor relief records:** not online; held at Friends Historical Library

## Known record losses
- No catastrophic statewide destruction of Quaker meeting records is known; the Friends Historical Library's holdings are largely intact
- Some **western Pennsylvania county records** from the late 1700s are fragmentary due to frontier conditions and new county formation

## Research tips

1. **Start with Hinshaw's Encyclopedia.** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania meeting records and is indexed by name — it is the fastest route to locating which monthly meeting your family belonged to and what records exist for them ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts))

2. **Identify the monthly meeting before ordering microfilm.** Quaker record-keeping was organized by monthly meeting, not by county. Determine which meeting covered your family's township, then request those specific minutes from Friends Historical Library or through a FamilySearch Center

3. **Certificates of removal are migration documents.** When a Quaker family moved — from Chester County to Bucks County, or from Pennsylvania to Ohio or North Carolina — the old meeting issued a certificate of removal naming the individual and their dependents. Tracing these certificates reconstructs migration routes invisible in any other record type

4. **Disownments spike during 1775–1783.** If a Quaker ancestor disappears from meeting records during the Revolution, search for a disownment entry. Common causes: bearing arms, paying war taxes, taking political oaths, or "marrying out of unity" (to a non-Quaker). A disownment record still gives a name and date and often a township

5. **Read the marriage certificate witness list as a family map.** All attendees at a Quaker marriage signed the certificate — often 30–100 people. These witnesses were members of the same meeting community and frequently include siblings, cousins, and neighbors of both families. A careful reading can reveal the entire extended kin network in a single document

6. **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes on FamilySearch are browse-only.** The digitized Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images) have no name index and are not full-text searchable — they must be browsed image by image. Use Hinshaw first to identify context, then consult these minutes

7. **The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting governed PA, NJ, and DE.** Families near the Delaware River or the southeastern border frequently had connections to meetings in New Jersey or Delaware within the same yearly meeting structure. Certificates of removal crossed state lines routinely — search all three states

8. **No civil registration before 1906 — Quaker records fill the gap.** For this entire period, Quaker meeting birth, marriage, and death registers are the functional equivalent of civil vital records ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)). Do not assume that "no civil record" means "no record exists"

9. **Use 1790 census and pre-1790 tax lists as your chronological anchors.** The 1790 federal census (heads of household) and Pennsylvania county tax assessment lists from the 1760s–1780s bracket your research window and establish township residence before Quaker meeting records can be located

10. **Probate files (FamilySearch collection 1999196) document non-meeting family ties.** Even Quakers who were disowned or left the meeting appear in county probate records. Wills and estate inventories name heirs, executors, and witnesses — and often include non-Quaker relatives who never appear in meeting records

# Locality Guide: Quaker Communities in Pennsylvania (Late 1700s, ca. 1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
