- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial capital and primary Quaker hub)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown colony until 1776; thereafter Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools. The first federal census (1790) is the earliest enumeration; pre-1790, county tax assessment lists are the best population proxy
- **Primary Quaker counties:** Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties had the densest Quaker populations ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records))
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783) — many Quakers were disowned for bearing arms, paying war taxes, or taking oaths; disownment records from this period are genealogically rich

## Boundary changes
- Southeastern core (Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware) was stable throughout the period
- Western Pennsylvania: several new counties (Washington, Westmoreland, Bedford) formed from parent counties — search both parent and successor county for families in those areas
- **No statewide civil registration before 1906** ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)) — Quaker meeting records substitute throughout

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began at the **state** level in **1906** only ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)); no county- or town-level mandate existed in the late 1700s
- **What exists for 1750–1800:** None. Quaker meeting registers are the functional substitute
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker meeting birth/marriage/death registers; county probate files; newspaper notices

### Church records — Quaker meeting records *(PRIMARY SOURCE)*

Quaker records are the most meticulous religious records in Pennsylvania and replace absent civil registration for this period.

**Meeting structure** (Wikipedia):
- **Monthly meetings** (local level): births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal, disownments
- **Quarterly meetings** (regional level): supervised monthly meetings
- **Yearly meeting** (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting — governing PA, NJ, and DE): policy-setting body

**What meeting records contain** ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)):

| Record type | What it documents |
|---|---|
| Birth registers | Child's name, date of birth, parents' names |
| Marriage records | Couple spoke vows before the full meeting; **all attendees signed the certificate** — 30–100 witnesses, naming extended family and community |
| Death records | Name, date, often family relationship |
| Certificates of removal | Issued when a member relocated; names individual, family, sending and receiving meetings — essential for tracing migration |
| Disownment records | Names individual and cause (bearing arms, marrying out of meeting, oath-taking, etc.) |

**Digitized on FamilySearch:**
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** (imageGroupNumber 001188322): 145 images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)
- Many other monthly meeting minutes are on **FamilySearch microfilm** but not digitized or name-indexed ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts))

**Essential published finding aid:**
- **William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 volumes): abstracts births, marriages, deaths, removals, and disownments from Pennsylvania meetings — consult before ordering microfilm ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts))

**Physical repositories:**
- **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA): largest US Quaker archive — original minutes, birth/marriage/death registers, certificates of removal, disownment records; many microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA): major secondary archive

### Census records
- **1790 U.S. Federal Census**: first federal enumeration — heads of household only; fully indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription)
- **Pre-1790 substitutes:** Pennsylvania county **tax assessment lists** (1760s–1780s) enumerate taxable property by township; held at Pennsylvania State Archives and county courthouses

### Probate and court records
- **On FamilySearch:** [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) (collection 1999196) — **indexed + images**; overlaps the target period
- **Where held:** County orphans' courts; Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Quaker value:** Probate files name executors, witnesses, and heirs — often include non-Quaker relatives who never appear in meeting records

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds; Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** — grants from the Penn proprietorship, then Commonwealth; federal GLO/BLM does not apply
- **Where held:** County recorder of deeds (deed books); Pennsylvania State Archives (early warrant registers, survey maps)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolution, 1775–1783. Many Quakers were pacifists and were disowned rather than appearing in service records; some did serve
- **Online:** [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription) — Revolutionary War service records and pension files; [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/) (original pension files)
- **Physical:** Pennsylvania State Archives — state militia records and adjutant-general papers

### Cemetery records
- Monthly meetings maintained adjacent burial grounds; traditional Quaker practice used plain or no headstones — **burial registers are the primary source**
- **Where held:** Friends Historical Library; individual surviving meetinghouses
- **Online:** [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com/) — coverage of late-18th-century Quaker graves is uneven

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia's *Pennsylvania Gazette* (1728–1800) and *Pennsylvania Packet* are genealogically valuable
- **Online:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription); Chronicling America (LOC, free)
- **Content:** Marriage notices, death notices, estate legal notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- Most Quaker families in the late 1700s had been in Pennsylvania for two to four generations; certificates of removal function as internal migration records within the Quaker network
- **Philadelphia passenger lists** at [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/); some indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Tax records
- Pennsylvania county tax assessment lists (1760s–1780s) are the best pre-1790 population proxy; enumerate taxable property and neighbors (FAN cluster) by township
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; county courthouses; some published by genealogical societies

### Marriage records on FamilySearch
- [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) (collection 1571957)
- [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) (collection 1502909) — compiled (secondary) source

| Repository | Holdings | Access |

| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Largest US Quaker archive: minutes, birth/marriage/death registers, certificates of removal, disownments | In-person; microfilm via FamilySearch Centers |

## Records NOT online
- Original monthly and quarterly meeting minute books for most Pennsylvania meetings (other than Philadelphia Yearly Meeting): microfilmed by FamilySearch but not digitized or name-indexed
- Individual certificates of removal: at Friends Historical Library on microfilm; not searchable online
- Pennsylvania county tax assessment lists (1760s–1780s): largely at Pennsylvania State Archives; not comprehensively digitized
- Original county deed books (pre-1800): primarily at county recorder of deeds
- Quaker school and poor relief records: at Friends Historical Library

8. **No civil registration before 1906** — Quaker registers are the only vital records for this period ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records))
9. **1790 census and pre-1790 tax lists are your chronological anchors** — use both together to place families in specific townships

### Online repositories
| Repository | Holdings for Late 1700s Pennsylvania | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (browse-only); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994; Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950; Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900; microfilmed Quaker meeting records via FamilySearch Centers | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 Federal Census; some Pennsylvania records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records, pension files | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Some late-18th-century Pennsylvania newspapers | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Some historic Pennsylvania newspapers | Free |
| FindAGrave | Quaker burial ground inscriptions (coverage varies) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military pension files, Philadelphia passenger lists | Free / paid request |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |

| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Largest US Quaker archive: minutes, birth/marriage/death registers, certificates of removal, disownments | In-person; microfilm via FamilySearch Centers |

| Family History Library / FamilySearch Centers | Microfilmed Quaker meeting records from across Pennsylvania | Free at centers worldwide |

## Records NOT online
- Original monthly and quarterly meeting minute books for most Pennsylvania meetings (other than Philadelphia Yearly Meeting): microfilmed by FamilySearch but not digitized or name-indexed
- Individual certificates of removal: at Friends Historical Library on microfilm; not searchable online
- Pennsylvania county tax assessment lists (1760s–1780s): largely at Pennsylvania State Archives; not comprehensively digitized
- Original county deed books (pre-1800): primarily at county recorder of deeds
- Quaker school and poor relief records: at Friends Historical Library

## Known record losses
- No catastrophic statewide destruction of Quaker meeting records is known; Friends Historical Library's holdings are largely intact
- Some western Pennsylvania county records from the late 1700s are fragmentary due to frontier conditions and new county formation
- FamilySearch Wiki gap: The Pennsylvania-specific wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content in this survey — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records

## Research tips
1. **Start with Hinshaw's Encyclopedia.** The *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 vols.) abstracts PA meeting records by name — fastest route to locating a family's monthly meeting ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts))
2. **Identify the monthly meeting before ordering microfilm.** Records are organized by meeting name, not county; find the meeting for the family's township first
3. **Certificates of removal are migration documents.** They name the individual, their family, and both sending and receiving meetings — essential when families moved to Ohio, Indiana, or North Carolina in the late 1700s–early 1800s
4. **Disownments spike during 1775–1783.** A Quaker ancestor who disappears during the Revolution may have a disownment entry (bearing arms, paying war taxes, oath-taking) — still names them and gives a date
5. **Marriage certificate witness list is a family map.** All 30–100 meeting attendees signed the certificate; witnesses frequently include siblings, cousins, and neighbors of both families
6. **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes on FamilySearch are browse-only** (imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images) — no index, no full-text search; use Hinshaw first
7. **The PYM governed PA, NJ, and DE.** Certificates of removal crossed state lines; search all three states when tracing a southeastern Pennsylvania Quaker family
8. **No civil registration before 1906** — Quaker registers are the only vital records for this period ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records))
9. **1790 census and pre-1790 tax lists are your chronological anchors** — use both together to place families in specific townships
10. **Probate files (FamilySearch collection 1999196) document non-meeting family ties** — wills and inventories name heirs, executors, and witnesses, including non-Quaker relatives

# Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania — Genealogy Research Guide
### Late 1800s Steel Industry (c. 1870–1900) | Allegheny County

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Pittsburgh sits at the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela, and Ohio rivers in **Allegheny County**, formed in 1788. By the 1870s–1890s, Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, and dozens of smaller mills drew hundreds of thousands of workers to the city and surrounding mill towns — Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrants prominent among them.

⚠️ **Critical registration gap:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906**. For the 1870–1900 target window, there are no state birth or death registers — church records, county court filings, and city records are the primary substitutes.

---

## 1. 🏭 Industrial & Occupational Records — Pittsburgh's Signature Sources

### Company Employment Records
**Access: Physical / Fragmentary — contact repositories directly**

Survival is uneven and was never systematic. The two best-holding repositories confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki:

- **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh) — holds company records, industrial photography, and labor documentation for Pittsburgh-area employers. *(Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))*
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives** — focused on steel and iron industry records for the Monongahela Valley mill towns. Contact directly for specific employer holdings. *(Same source)*

### State Factory Inspection Reports
**Access: Physical — Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg**

Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics began publishing factory inspection reports in the 1870s, listing employers, employee counts, and working conditions. These can place an ancestor at a specific mill in a specific year.

### Union Membership Lists
**Access: Physical — labor archives**

The iron and steel unions — Sons of Vulcan, the Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers — kept membership rolls. The 1892 Homestead Strike generated particularly extensive documentation. Contact the **Heinz History Center** and **Pennsylvania State Archives** for surviving union records. *(Source: [Allegheny County — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))*

### City Directories
**Access: Partly digitized; strong physical holdings**

Pittsburgh city directories listed residents by **name, occupation, and street address** — an invaluable occupational snapshot in years between censuses. The **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds volumes from the 1810s forward. Many late-1800s volumes are digitized on **Ancestry.com** and through HathiTrust. This is the primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 census. *(Source: [Allegheny County — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))*

---

## 2. 📋 Census Records

### Federal Census: 1870, 1880, 1900
**Access: Fully indexed and digitized — FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry.com**

All three surviving censuses within the target window list occupation for each adult. These are the anchor records for steel-era family research.

⚠️ **The 1890 federal census is virtually destroyed** — substitute with city directories (1888–1892 editions), tax lists, and city health records for that decade gap.

### Mortality Schedules (1870, 1880)
**Access: Indexed — FamilySearch and Ancestry.com**

A separate census schedule recording persons who died in the year preceding the census, including **cause of death, occupation, and birthplace** — particularly valuable for tracing industrial accident deaths in Pittsburgh's mills. Available on both FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Pennsylvania State Census
Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period; the federal census is the only enumeration available.

---

## 3. 📜 Vital Records

### Births & Deaths (1870–1900)
**Access: No statewide records — church registers and city health records are the substitute**

Statewide death and birth registration did not begin until 1906. For the target window, rely on:
- **Church registers** (baptism / burial) — see §4 below
- **Pittsburgh city health records** — held at the **Allegheny County Health Department** and **Pennsylvania State Archives**

FamilySearch has [Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) — begins *after* the target window, but useful for ancestors who died post-1906.

### Marriages
**Access: Indexed + images on FamilySearch**

Three FamilySearch collections cover the 1870–1900 window at the county level (Allegheny County Courthouse, Register of Wills):

| Collection | Date Range | FamilySearch Link |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages | 1885–1950 | [Collection 1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | 1677–1950 | [Collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | 1700–1900 | [Collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) |

---

## 4. ⛪ Church Records — Often the Best Vital Source

**Access: Varies — some digitized, many physical only**

Ethnic Catholic and Protestant parishes were the social and documentary backbone of Pittsburgh's immigrant steel communities. Church registers are frequently the **only source** for births and deaths before 1906:

| Community | Parish Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Polish** | Roman Catholic | St. Stanislaus Kostka (est. 1875, Pittsburgh's first Polish parish) |
| **Slovak** | Byzantine & Roman Catholic | South Side, Braddock, Homestead parishes |
| **Croatian & Italian** | Roman Catholic | Multiple ethnic parishes per mill town |
| **German** | Lutheran & Catholic | Pre-boom establishment; strongest records |
| **African American** | AME, Baptist | Registers held at individual congregations |
| **Irish** | Roman Catholic | Multiple parishes, well-documented |

**Repository contacts:**
- **Diocese of Pittsburgh** — diocesan archives hold many parish registers
- **Heinz History Center** — microfilm of some local church records
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** — local church history collections

*(Source: [Allegheny County — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))*

---

## 5. 🚢 Immigration & Naturalization Records

### Passenger Lists
**Access: Fully indexed and digitized**

Most Pittsburgh steel workers arrived via New York (Ellis Island, open 1892) or Baltimore (pre-Ellis Island). Search on:
- **FamilySearch.org** — free, fully indexed
- **Ancestry.com** — subscription; broadest collection
- **Statue of Liberty–Ellis Island Foundation** — free, for 1892–1957 arrivals

### Naturalization Records
**Access: Physical — Allegheny County Courthouse and NARA Philadelphia**

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — federal, state, or local. For Allegheny County, search:
- **Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas** (courthouse) — holds most local declaration of intent and final naturalization papers
- **National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Region 3)** — federal court naturalizations and consolidated records
- **FamilySearch** — has microfilmed some Allegheny County naturalization records

⚠️ An ancestor may appear in multiple courts across multiple steps (declaration of intent, then final papers years later, often in a different court).

*(Source: [Allegheny County — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))*

---

## 6. ⚖️ Probate Records

**Access: Indexed + images on FamilySearch**

[Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) spans the full target window. Filed at the **Allegheny County Register of Wills**. Working-class mill workers may have modest or no estates, but probate files document heirs, real property, and family relationships — and name siblings and children.

---

## 7. 🏠 Land & Tax Records

### Property Tax Records
**Access: Physical — Allegheny County and Pennsylvania State Archives**

Annual assessment lists document which workers owned property. Many mill community workers bought row houses near the plants in Homestead, Braddock, or McKees Rocks. Held at the **Allegheny County Assessment Office** and **Pennsylvania State Archives**.

### Deed Records
**Access: Physical — Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds**

Property transactions document settlement and migration patterns within the Pittsburgh mill corridor. Useful for establishing when a family moved between mill towns.

---

## 8. 📰 Newspapers

**Access: Digitized (subscription and free)**

Pittsburgh's newspapers covered labor strikes (especially the landmark 1892 Homestead Strike), industrial accidents, and ethnic community news that frequently name individual workers and families:

- **Newspapers.com** (subscription) — largest Pittsburgh newspaper holdings including the *Pittsburgh Dispatch* and *Pittsburgh Post*
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) — selected Pennsylvania titles
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** — physical archive and microfilm of local papers

---

## 9. 🎖️ Military Records

### Civil War Veterans
**Access: Fully indexed at Fold3 and FamilySearch**

Many older Pittsburgh steel workers of the 1870s–1890s were Civil War veterans. **Pension files** at NARA are especially rich — they list spouses, children, health status, and home address across multiple decades:

- **Fold3.com** (subscription) — pension files and service records
- **FamilySearch.org** — some pension indexes, free
- **National Archives** (Washington DC / Philadelphia) — original pension files
- **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) — state adjutant general records

---

## 10. 🗂️ Repository Quick Reference

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Company/industrial records, labor collections, immigration records, church microfilm | In-person; some online via finding aids |
| **Rivers of Steel Archives** | Steel/iron industry records, mill-town documentation | In-person; contact directly |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1810s+), newspapers, local history | In-person; some digitized |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Naturalization papers, marriage licenses, probate, deeds | In-person + FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Factory inspection reports, labor records, state health records | In-person; some online |
| **NARA Philadelphia (Region 3)** | Federal court naturalizations, immigration, federal records | In-person; Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Marriages, probate, census, church microfilm — collections above | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | US Census, city directories, passenger lists, newspapers | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Pittsburgh newspapers, labor news, accident reports | Subscription |

---

## ⚠️ Key Quirks & Cautions

1. **No statewide vital registration before 1906** — births and deaths 1870–1900 are in church registers and city health records, not state files. Always check the parish first.
2. **1890 federal census is virtually destroyed** — use 1888–1892 city directories as the primary substitute for the lost decade.
3. **Company employment records are fragmentary** — survival depends entirely on the employer. Always contact Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel *before* concluding records don't exist.
4. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across multiple courts** — search Allegheny County courts, state courts, and NARA Philadelphia; a single ancestor may have papers in more than one place.
5. **Mill towns outside Pittsburgh city limits** — Homestead, Braddock, McKees Rocks, Carnegie, and McKeesport were separate municipalities with their own records, churches, and directories. Don't assume Pittsburgh city records cover mill-town ancestors.
6. **Ethnic parish records are the linchpin** — for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers, the Catholic parish register may be the *only* pre-1906 document recording a birth, marriage, or death. Identify the specific ethnic parish for the mill town where the family lived.

---

**Research sequence recommendation:** Start with the federal censuses (1870 → 1880 → 1900) to establish the family unit and occupation, then work outward to city directories (occupation/address in non-census years), church records (vital events), naturalization papers (immigration timeline), and Heinz History Center/Rivers of Steel (employer documentation). The 1892 Homestead Strike records are a bonus source if your ancestor worked at Carnegie Steel's Homestead plant.

# Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic
## Genealogy Research Guide

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Philadelphia County** was established in 1682 and has been coextensive with the City of Philadelphia since the **Act of Consolidation (1854)**, which merged the city and all surrounding townships into a single jurisdiction. **In 1793, the city proper was only one part of Philadelphia County.** Surrounding townships — Northern Liberties, Southwark, Kensington, Moyamensing, and others — were separate jurisdictions *within* Philadelphia County, each generating their own local records. A family living in Southwark in 1793 was not a City of Philadelphia resident: search at the county level, and confirm township when possible.

The **1793 yellow fever epidemic** (August–November 1793) killed approximately **5,000 of Philadelphia's ~50,000 residents** — roughly one-tenth of the population — making it one of the deadliest disasters in early American history. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)). Thousands more fled to the countryside. Both death documentation and absence-from-the-city records matter for genealogical reconstruction.

**Critical vital registration fact:** Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil vital registration until 1906**. There are no government-issued death certificates for 1793 victims. Church burial registers and congregation records are the *only* primary documentation of deaths for this period.

---

### 1. Epidemic-Specific Sources 🔴 *Start Here*

These sources name the dead and document relief efforts — unique to the 1793 outbreak and unavailable for any other research period.

| Source | Description | Access |
|--------|-------------|--------|
| **Mathew Carey, *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793)** | Published lists of the dead, organized by neighborhood; went through four editions in 1793 alone | Digitized and freely available via Google Books, HathiTrust, and the Internet Archive |
| **Committee of Philadelphia Minutes & Reports (1793)** | Records of the citizen committee chaired by Mayor Matthew Clarkson that organized relief; names those who received aid and those who died | Manuscripts at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**; partially transcribed in published sources |
| **Bush Hill Hospital Records** | Patient lists for the improvised hospital at the Bush Hill estate, managed by Stephen Girard and Peter Helm | Fragmentary; surviving records at HSP. Note: most patient documentation did not survive |
| **Free African Society Records** | The Free African Society and Richard Allen's African Methodist Episcopal congregation were central to epidemic response; their membership rolls and correspondence record Black Philadelphians' roles and losses | Published in *A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People* (1794) by Allen & Jones; originals at **Kislak Center, University of Pennsylvania** |
| **Benjamin Rush Papers** | Rush's clinical notes, correspondence, and patient lists; Rush was the most prominent physician during the outbreak | **American Philosophical Society**, Philadelphia |

---

### 2. Church Records (Primary Death & Vital Evidence)

Since civil registration did not exist in 1793, **church burial registers are the principal death record**. Philadelphia's extraordinary religious diversity means you must identify the family's denomination — do not assume any single church holds all relevant records.

| Church / Congregation | Notes | Record Location |
|----------------------|-------|-----------------|
| **Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal)** | One of colonial Philadelphia's oldest and largest congregations; burial registers survive from the 1690s | Registers held at **Christ Church Archives**; microfilm and partial indexes at FamilySearch and HSP |
| **Gloria Dei / Old Swedes' Church** | Oldest church building in Pennsylvania (1700); serves the Southwark township community; Lutheran then Episcopal | Records at the **Episcopal Diocese of Pennsylvania Archives** and HSP |
| **St. Peter's Church (Episcopal)** | Companion to Christ Church; separate burial register | Episcopal Diocese of Pennsylvania Archives |
| **St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church** | Oldest Catholic parish in Philadelphia; burial records include Irish and German immigrants | **Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives** |
| **Quaker Monthly Meeting Records** | Friends' meeting records are among the most systematic in early Philadelphia; include deaths, removals, disownments | **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** and **Haverford College Quaker Collection**; Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records partially on FamilySearch microfilm |
| **German Lutheran & German Reformed Churches** | Large German immigrant community in Philadelphia; check Zion Lutheran (German) and First Reformed | HSP; partial indexes in the *Pennsylvania German Church Records* compiled by HSP |
| **Second Presbyterian, Third Presbyterian** | Major Presbyterian congregations with burial registers | **Presbyterian Historical Society**, Philadelphia |
| **Mother Bethel AME Church** | Founded 1793 by Richard Allen; central to the African American community during the epidemic | Church archives; published membership records |

**FamilySearch note:** The `collections_search` did not surface a dedicated indexed collection of Philadelphia church burial records for 1793. Many church registers exist on FamilySearch microfilm as **browse-only image volumes** — no name index, requiring page-by-page browsing. The FamilySearch Wiki page [Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) confirms the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP) has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records; consult the GSP's *Publications* series directly.

---

### 3. Census Records

| Record | Coverage | Access & Notes |
|--------|----------|----------------|
| **1790 U.S. Federal Census** | 3 years before the epidemic; lists heads of household | Indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry; the 1790 PA schedules have some coverage gaps for certain townships |
| **1800 U.S. Federal Census** | 7 years after the epidemic; documents survivors and reconstituted households | Fully indexed on FamilySearch |
| **1810 U.S. Federal Census** | Captures the post-epidemic generation | Fully indexed on FamilySearch |

The **1790 census paired with the 1800 census** is a key strategy: heads of household present in 1790 but absent in 1800 (without an obvious age-out explanation) may have died in the epidemic or fled permanently.

---

### 4. Probate Records

Epidemic victims who left wills or died intestate generated probate records at Philadelphia County's **Orphan's Court and Register of Wills** — often within months of death.

**FamilySearch Collection:** [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — **893,214 records / 446,607 images** — indexed + images. This collection spans the 1793 period and is searchable by name. Probate records are especially valuable because they name heirs, creditors, and sometimes place of death.

The **original volumes** for Philadelphia County are also held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and the **Register of Wills, City Hall**.

---

### 5. Marriage Records

No statewide civil marriage registration existed in Pennsylvania in 1793; church registers and license bonds are the primary evidence.

| FamilySearch Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|------------------------|------------|---------|--------|--------------|
| [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | 156,023 | **Indexed + images** |
| [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | 0 | **Index only — no images**; request originals at HSP or county archives |

The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's** published *Pennsylvania Archives* series (particularly Series 2 and 6) contains extensive early marriage and vital record transcriptions.

---

### 6. Tax and Property Records

Philadelphia County tax assessment lists survive for the late 18th century and are a useful supplement when census records have gaps.

- **Provincial and County Tax Lists (1780s–1790s):** Name property owners and taxable inhabitants by ward; can confirm residence before/after the epidemic. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) and HSP.
- **Philadelphia County Deed Books:** Document property transfers — estates sold after epidemic deaths often generate deed records. Held at the **Philadelphia City Archives**; some early volumes microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Pennsylvania Land Records / Warrants & Surveys:** At the Pennsylvania State Archives; relevant for property owners across the county.

---

### 7. Newspapers

Philadelphia had an active press in 1793, and multiple newspapers published **weekly or daily lists of the dead** during the epidemic.

| Newspaper | Notes | Access |
|-----------|-------|--------|
| **Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser** | Published death lists during the epidemic | [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/); also [Chronicling America / Library of Congress](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) |
| **Federal Gazette** | Regular epidemic coverage and mortality lists | Library Company of Philadelphia; microfilm at HSP |
| **General Advertiser** | Published by Benjamin Franklin Bache; epidemic coverage | Chronicling America |

The **Library Company of Philadelphia** holds an exceptional Philadelphia newspaper collection and is free to visit on-site.

---

### 8. Military Records

Many Philadelphia men of 1793 were Revolutionary War veterans. Military records can confirm identity, establish family connections, and bridge gaps in civilian documentation.

- **Revolutionary War Service Records & Pension Files:** At **NARA** (Washington, DC); pension applications often contain detailed family narratives. Indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry.
- **Pennsylvania Revolutionary War Muster Rolls & Pay Abstracts:** In *Pennsylvania Archives* Series 5 and 6, and at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Philadelphia County Militia Records:** Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### 9. Immigration & Naturalization

Philadelphia was a primary port of entry in the late 18th century. Many 1793 epidemic victims were recent arrivals.

- **Philadelphia Port Arrival Lists (pre-1820):** Survive partially; held at NARA Mid-Atlantic (Philadelphia), HSP, and partially indexed at Ancestry. Coverage is incomplete for this era — list absence does not mean a person did not arrive by sea.
- **Naturalization Records (pre-1906):** Could appear in any Pennsylvania court of record — Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas, the U.S. District Court, or the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania. Records at NARA Mid-Atlantic and Philadelphia City Archives. No centralized index exists; requires searching individual court dockets.

---

### 10. Repository Directory

| Repository | Focus | Location / URL |
|------------|-------|----------------|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Manuscripts, church record transcriptions, Committee of 1793 papers, newspapers | Philadelphia, PA — [hsp.org](https://hsp.org) |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | City government records, deed books, early administrative records | Philadelphia, PA — [phila.gov/city-archives](https://www.phila.gov/departments/city-archives/) |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** | Tax lists, land warrants, military/militia records | Harrisburg, PA — [phmc.pa.gov](https://www.phmc.pa.gov/Archives) |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** | Church record indexes, published compilations | Philadelphia, PA — [genpa.org](https://www.genpa.org) |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society** | Presbyterian church records | Philadelphia, PA — [history.pcusa.org](https://www.history.pcusa.org) |
| **Friends Historical Library** | Quaker meeting records | Swarthmore College, Swarthmore, PA |
| **Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives** | Catholic parish registers | Philadelphia, PA |
| **Episcopal Diocese of Pennsylvania Archives** | Christ Church, Gloria Dei, St. Peter's, other Episcopal registers | Philadelphia, PA |
| **American Philosophical Society** | Benjamin Rush papers, scientific and civic records | Philadelphia, PA — [amphilsoc.org](https://www.amphilsoc.org) |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | Newspapers, pamphlets, rare printed sources (Carey's account, etc.) | Philadelphia, PA — [librarycompany.org](https://librarycompany.org) |
| **NARA Mid-Atlantic Region** | Federal naturalization records, some immigration records | Philadelphia, PA |
| **Kislak Center, University of Pennsylvania** | Free African Society records, African American community materials | Philadelphia, PA |
| **FamilySearch** | Pennsylvania Probate, Marriage, and other digitized collections | [familysearch.org](https://familysearch.org) — free |
| **Fold3** | Military service records, pension files | [fold3.com](https://fold3.com) — subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census, some Philadelphia church records, newspapers | [ancestry.com](https://ancestry.com) — subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Philadelphia newspapers of the 1790s | [newspapers.com](https://newspapers.com) — subscription |

---

### Key Research Quirks & Strategies

1. **No civil death certificates exist for 1793.** Pennsylvania's statewide death registration began in 1906. Church burial registers and Mathew Carey's published lists are your primary evidence of death during the epidemic.

2. **Identify the township, not just "Philadelphia."** Before the 1854 consolidation, Northern Liberties, Southwark, Moyamensing, and other townships were distinct jurisdictions within Philadelphia County. A person listed in a church or tax record as being from one of these townships generated records under that township's local administration — search at the county level and confirm township.

3. **Refugees' deaths may be documented outside Philadelphia.** Thousands fled to Chester, Montgomery, Delaware, and Bucks Counties during August–November 1793. If a family member cannot be found in Philadelphia records, check church registers in those surrounding counties — they may have died while sheltering elsewhere.

4. **Pair the 1790 and 1800 censuses.** Heads of household present in 1790 but missing from 1800 (with no clear explanation) are candidates for epidemic death or permanent emigration.

5. **African American families: use specialized sources.** The Free African Society and Mother Bethel AME Church records, Richard Allen's *Narrative* (1794), and the Kislak Center collections are essential for Black Philadelphia families — the standard church record series will not capture them fully.

6. **Probate is your fastest path to confirmed death dates.** Philadelphia County Orphan's Court wills and administrations filed in late 1793 and early 1794 directly document epidemic deaths with approximate dates. FamilySearch's Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 is indexed and searchable.

7. **Pre-1906 marriage evidence comes from church registers and bond/license records.** The FamilySearch compiled marriages index (1700–1900) has no images — you must go to HSP or the Philadelphia City Archives for the original documents.

8. **FamilySearch coverage of Philadelphia church burials is incomplete at the indexed level.** Many church burial registers exist on FamilySearch microfilm as browse-only image volumes. Use the GSP's published church record indexes and HSP's manuscript holdings as supplements.

## 🔥 Locality Research Guide
### Chicago / Cook County, Illinois — Families Affected by the Great Fire of 1871
**Jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois, United States · County formed: 1831
**Time period surveyed:** ca. 1840–1900

---

### ⚠️ The Core Challenge: Catastrophic Record Loss

The **Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871)** destroyed the **Cook County Courthouse**, incinerating the city's foundational genealogical records: deeds, birth and death registers, probate files, court records, and tax rolls. Roughly 3.3 square miles of the city burned; more than 100,000 residents were left homeless and many church registers were lost along with their parishes. Pre-fire genealogical research for Chicago families requires a **substitute-source strategy** rather than a direct search of civil records.

---

### Part 1 — Pre-Fire Records (before October 1871): What Survives & Where

| Record Type | What Survived | Where to Find It | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Federal Census** | 1850, 1860, **and 1870** schedules all survived — originals were held in Washington, D.C. | FamilySearch, Ancestry.com | Indexed + images online |
| **Reconstructed deeds** | Property owners re-registered under the **Burnt Record Act (1872)**; copies of pre-fire deeds were re-filed | Cook County Recorder of Deeds; Chicago Title and Trust Company records | See below |
| **Insurance company records** | Chicago Title and Trust Company assembled substitute title abstracts; invaluable for property ownership | **Chicago History Museum** | Physical access; some digitized |
| **City directories** | Chicago city directories survive from the **1840s onward** — name, address, occupation | **Newberry Library**, Chicago | Physical + some digitized via Ancestry |
| **Church registers (survivors)** | Parishes outside the burn zone kept registers; some destroyed parishes reconstructed their books | **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** (Catholic); individual denominational archives | Physical; FamilySearch has some microfilm |
| **Mortality schedules** | 1850, 1860, 1870 mortality schedules record deaths in the preceding year | FamilySearch (indexed collection) | Indexed + images |

|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cook County Birth Certificates** | 2024189 | 1871–1940 | ~1,450,000 | Indexed + images |
| **Cook County Death Records** | 1913456 | 1871–1947 | ~980,000 | Indexed + images |
| **Cook County Marriage Records** | 1871 | 1871–1920 | ~620,000 | Indexed + images |
| **Chicago Church Records** | 1803978 | 1833–1925 | ~285,000 | Indexed + images |

**FamilySearch digitized volume — post-fire property re-recordings:**
- **Vol. 009982111** · *Post-fire Property Re-recordings*, 1871–1880 · 112 images · **41% name-indexed** → partially searchable; browse images for the remainder

---

### Part 3 — Key Repositories

| Repository | Strengths | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** (Chicago) | City directories 1840s+, maps, manuscripts, Chicago newspaper runs, genealogical monographs | In-person; some finding aids online at newberry.org |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Insurance / title records, photographs, personal papers of fire survivors, Chicago Tribune archives | In-person; [chicagohistory.org](https://www.chicagohistory.org) |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County records post-1871: naturalization petitions, court files, voter registrations | In-person; index searchable at ilsos.gov/departments/archives/irad |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); many pre-fire parishes kept duplicate registers at diocesan level | By appointment; [archchicago.org/archives](https://www.archchicago.org/archives) |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward (birth, death, marriage) | cookcountyclerkil.gov |
| **National Archives — Great Lakes Region (Chicago)** | Federal census, naturalization records, military pension files, passenger lists | In-person + online via Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indexed collections listed above; microfilm of many post-fire county records | Free online |

---

### Part 4 — Record Types by Category

#### Census
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, 1870 (all pre-fire and fully surviving), then 1880, 1900 — all indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Illinois state census:** Illinois conducted state censuses in **1855 and 1865** — both predate the fire and cover Cook County. Check FamilySearch and the Illinois State Archives (ilsos.gov).
- **1880 Mortality Schedule:** captures deaths in the year June 1879–June 1880; useful if a fire victim died from injuries or was displaced and died shortly after.

#### Vital Records
- Civil registration in Cook County restarts effectively at 1871. For events before the fire, turn to church registers, census mortality schedules, and newspapers (obituaries).

#### Church Records
- The **FamilySearch collection "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925"** (id 1803978, ~285,000 records) covers multiple denominations and spans before and after the fire.
- The Archdiocese archives hold Catholic parish registers; many parishes outside the fire's path have unbroken series. For Lutheran, Methodist, and other Protestant congregations, check individual denominational archives and the Newberry Library.

#### Land & Property
- Pre-fire deeds are lost from the courthouse but **partially reconstructed** via the Burnt Record Act of 1872 (re-filed abstracts at the Cook County Recorder) and **Chicago Title and Trust Company** title chains at the Chicago History Museum.
- Post-fire deeds resume normally; the Cook County Recorder of Deeds holds the official record.
- **Federal land patents** (Bureau of Land Management / General Land Office) for original federal-land entries predate county records and were not destroyed: search at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov).

#### Probate
- Pre-fire Cook County probate files were destroyed. Reconstruct through newspaper notices (Newberry Library newspaper collection) and federal pension files if the deceased was a veteran.
- Post-fire probate resumes at IRAD / Cook County Circuit Court.

#### Military
- Civil War service records and pension files at NARA (and indexed on Fold3/Ancestry) were held in Washington — **not destroyed by the Chicago Fire**.
- Illinois Civil War regimental histories and muster rolls: Illinois State Archives and Ancestry's Illinois collection.

#### Immigration & Naturalization
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court — Cook County Circuit Court, U.S. District Court, etc. IRAD holds Cook County naturalizations. NARA Great Lakes holds U.S. District Court records.
- Passenger arrival lists: pre-fire arrivals entered mainly through New York, Baltimore, or New Orleans — search NARA / Ancestry / FamilySearch by port.

#### Newspapers
- Chicago had active newspapers before and after the fire. The **Chicago Tribune** (1847–) and **Chicago Times** (1854–) ran survivor lists, fire-damage notices, and death notices. Holdings at the Newberry Library and via **Newspapers.com** and **Chronicling America** (loc.gov/collections/chronicling-america).
- Survivor and relief lists were published in the weeks after October 8, 1871 — a direct source for displaced families.

#### Directories & Reference
- Chicago city directories (1839 onward) are at the Newberry Library and partially digitized on Ancestry — name, address, and occupation for heads of household annually.

---

### Part 5 — Substitute-Source Strategy for Pre-Fire Families

Because the courthouse was destroyed, use this layered approach:

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — the last pre-fire snapshot of Chicago households; fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
2. **Work backward through 1860 and 1850 censuses** to establish family composition and origins.
3. **Search city directories** (Newberry Library; Ancestry) for annual address and occupation data 1840s–1871.
4. **Check the Illinois 1855 and 1865 state censuses** (Illinois State Archives) for intercensal data.
5. **Search church registers** — both the FamilySearch collection and the Bernardin Archives (Catholic). Parishes outside the burn zone have continuous registers; some destroyed parishes reconstructed their books from memory or duplicates.
6. **Property owners:** Search the Burnt Record Act re-filings (Cook County Recorder) and the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection (Chicago History Museum).
7. **Fire relief records:** The Chicago Relief and Aid Society distributed aid to over 100,000 displaced persons; records may survive at the Chicago History Museum.
8. **Post-fire newspapers:** Survivor/missing-persons notices in the Chicago Tribune and Chicago Times, October–November 1871.
9. **Federal records unaffected by the fire:** Military pension files (NARA), passenger lists, and BLM land patents all survived intact.

---

### Research Quirks & Gotchas

- **The 1870 census is your pre-fire anchor.** It was taken in the summer of 1871 — just months before the fire — and the originals were in Washington; it survived completely. Make it your first stop for any Chicago family.
- **Cook County civil vital records begin at 1871**, not earlier — the fire erased prior registers. Do not assume a birth or death certificate exists for pre-1871 events.
- **Post-fire property re-recordings are only 41% name-indexed** on FamilySearch (vol. 009982111) — browse the remaining images for surnames not surfaced by search.
- **Pre-fire reconstructed court records** (vol. 009982110) are **0% indexed and not full-text searchable** — browse image-by-image only.
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company records** at the Chicago History Museum are a critical substitute for destroyed deeds and are not fully digitized — an in-person visit or research service inquiry is required.
- **The Burnt Record Act (1872)** required property owners to re-register, but compliance was voluntary in practice — a family that did not re-file has no reconstructed deed record.
- **Church records outside the burn zone** are the best source for pre-fire vital events; always check whether a specific parish was in the fire's path (~3.3 sq. mi. burn area on the north and south sides of the Chicago River).
- **Illinois state censuses of 1855 and 1865** are often overlooked — they provide intercensal household snapshots and predate the fire.

---

### External Resources

- **Ancestry.com** — U.S. Federal Census, Illinois state census, city directories, military records: [ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)
- **Find A Grave** — Cemetery records, memorial photos: [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)
- **Newspapers.com** — Historical Chicago newspapers: [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)
- **Fold3** — Military records, pension files: [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)
- **NARA** — Federal records, naturalization, passenger lists: [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)
- **FamilySearch Wiki — Cook County, Illinois Genealogy:** [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy)

---

**Bottom line:** The Great Fire makes pre-1871 Chicago research a substitute-source problem. Your most powerful tools in order are: the 1870 federal census, city directories at the Newberry Library, surviving church registers (especially at the Bernardin Archives), state censuses of 1855 and 1865, Chicago Tribune fire-survivor notices, and the Chicago History Museum's insurance/title records. For events after October 1871, Cook County civil registration resumes and FamilySearch has indexed collections totaling over 3 million records across births, deaths, marriages, and church records.

# Louisiana, French Colonial Period (1700–1769)
## Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Context

Louisiana in the 1700s passed through **two colonial powers** with a critical transition point:

- **French colonial period (1699–1762):** Administered from New Orleans (founded 1718) under the **Conseil Supérieur** (Superior Council). No civil parishes existed — settlements organized around military posts and Catholic missions. The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized religion.
- **Spanish transition (1762–1769+):** France secretly ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain in the **Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762)**, but Spain didn't establish effective control until 1769, when the Cabildo replaced the Superior Council. Civil *parroquias* (parishes) began forming under Spanish rule.
- **British West Florida (1763–1783):** The portion east of the Mississippi went to Britain. Families near that border may have records under a third, separate jurisdiction.

The critical research break point is **~1769**: before that, records are French-language, French-law documents; after, they shift to Spanish administrative conventions.

---

### 1. Catholic Parish Registers — *The Primary Source*

The Catholic Church was the **sole legal recorder** of vital events (baptisms, marriages, burials). There was **no civil vital registration** of any kind in this period — Louisiana statewide civil registration didn't begin until 1918.

- The **Code Noir** required baptism of all enslaved persons — registers document enslaved ancestors alongside free colonists.
- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans** registers survive from **1720**.
- **FamilySearch:** [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) (Collection 1612905) — **987,654 records, 493,827 images**. This is the key online collection for the French colonial period.
- Records are in **French** (with Latin in ecclesiastical formulas) — you must read French or arrange translation.
- Originals also held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) and diocesan archives.
- *Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy, French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)*

---

### 2. Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) Records

The French colonial government maintained records of **land grants (concessions), civil contracts, court proceedings, wills, and estate inventories** — the colonial equivalent of county court and probate records combined.

- **Held at:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint Building, 400 Esplanade Ave., New Orleans, LA 70116
- Partially digitized; in French
- No named FamilySearch collection for this series — access is physical or via partial digitization at the Louisiana Historical Center
- *Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)*

---

### 3. Notarial Archives

- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America — holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions **from the 1730s onward**.
- In French (1730s–1769), then Spanish after the Spanish takeover.
- Physical access: 1340 Poydras St., Suite 375, New Orleans, LA 70112
- *Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)*

---

### 4. Land Records / French Concessions

Colonial Louisiana land grants followed **French civil law**, not English common law — the documentary patterns differ significantly from Anglo-American records.

- Published digest: **American State Papers: Public Lands** series (widely digitized free on HathiTrust and Library of Congress)
- **Louisiana State Land Office** (Baton Rouge) holds additional records
- Originals: Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM (see below)
- *Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)*

---

### 5. Probate Records

- **FamilySearch:** [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) (Collection 2078341) — **456,789 records, 228,394 images**
- Covers the **late French colonial period from 1756**. For estate records before 1756, rely on Superior Council records at the Louisiana Historical Center.
- Records from 1756–1769 are in French.

---

### 6. Colonial Census Rolls

France conducted several **administrative enumerations** of the colony during the 1700s — these are distinct from post-1790 US federal censuses.

- **Held at:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France
- Online portal: [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)
- ANOM also holds administrative correspondence and military muster rolls for the entire French colonial period — it is an essential, if overseas, repository.

---

### 7. Military Records

Colonial Louisiana was a military colony; many early settlers served in or were employees of the **Compagnie des Indes** (Company of the Indies, which administered Louisiana 1717–1731).

- Company muster rolls and colonial military records: **ANOM**, Aix-en-Provence
- Some transferred records: **NARA** (National Archives, Washington DC) — [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church records 1718+; probate records 1756+ | Free online |
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old US Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records; partially digitized colonial records | In-person + partial online |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives** | Contracts, wills, marriage settlements from 1730s | In-person |
| **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge) | Some colonial and state-era holdings | In-person |
| **ANOM** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Census rolls, admin correspondence, military muster rolls — full French colonial period | Online portal + in-person |
| **NARA** (Washington DC) | Transferred colonial records; post-1803 federal records | In-person + Fold3 |
| **American State Papers: Public Lands** | Published land grant documentation | Free online (HathiTrust, LOC) |

---

### Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Coverage | Access Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Catholic church records (1718+) | Collection 1612905 — images present | Verify current name-indexing at FS |
| Probate records (1756+) | Collection 2078341 — images present | Verify current name-indexing at FS |
| Superior Council / notarial records | No named FS collection | Physical or partial online (Louisiana Historical Center) |
| ANOM census / admin records | Not on FamilySearch | ANOM online portal or in-person |
| American State Papers (land) | Widely digitized elsewhere | Free online |

**Coverage gap noted:** FamilySearch's curated external links for Louisiana 1700–1769 returned only generic repositories (Ancestry, NARA, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com). No dedicated colonial Louisiana database links were surfaced for this specific period.

---

### Critical Research Tips

1. **Language:** All records 1699–1769 are in **French** (with Latin in church records). After 1769, administrative and notarial records shift to **Spanish**. Plan for translation in both languages.

2. **No civil registration:** The Catholic Church is your only source for baptisms, marriages, and burials. Do not expect birth or death certificates for this period.

3. **Enslaved ancestors:** The Code Noir mandated baptism of all enslaved persons — Catholic registers are the primary source for tracing enslaved individuals in colonial Louisiana.

4. **No parishes as political units in the French period:** French Louisiana records are organized by **military post or settlement name** (e.g., Poste des Natchitoches, Poste des Illinois), not by parish. The civil parish system came with Spanish rule after 1769.

5. **The 1769 legal break:** Research straddling 1769 must work **two documentary traditions** — French-law records (Superior Council, French concessions, French notarial style) before, and Spanish-law records (Cabildo, Spanish grants, Spanish notarial style) after.

6. **British West Florida overlap:** Families east of the Mississippi after 1763 fell under British jurisdiction — check British West Florida and later American Mississippi Territory records separately.

7. **ANOM is essential:** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence is irreplaceable for the French colonial period — census rolls, administrative records, military muster rolls. Much of it is now partially accessible via its online portal, with in-person or scan requests needed for specific items.

8. **French concessions ≠ English land grants:** The American State Papers: Public Lands is a good published starting point, but originals are at the Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM.

---

The guide has been saved to your research project as `loc_001`. Your strongest starting point online is FamilySearch Collection 1612905 (Church Records, 1718–1925); for deeper colonial-period research, the Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans) and ANOM (France) are the indispensable physical repositories.

- **French colonial period (1699–1762):** Administered from New Orleans (founded 1718) under the **Conseil Supérieur** (Superior Council). No civil parishes existed — settlements were organized around military posts and Catholic missions. The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized religious body.
- **Spanish transition (1762–1769+):** France secretly ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain in the **Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762)**, but Spain didn't establish effective control until 1769, when the Cabildo replaced the Superior Council as governing body. Civil parishes (parroquias) began forming under Spanish rule.
- **British West Florida (1763–1783):** The portion of Louisiana east of the Mississippi went to Britain in 1763. Families near that border may have records under a third, separate jurisdiction.

The key research break is **~1769**: before that, records are French-language, French-law documents; after, they shift to Spanish administrative conventions.

---

### Available Records

#### 1. Catholic Parish Registers — *Primary Source*
- The Catholic Church was the **sole legal recorder** of vital events (baptisms, marriages, burials).
- The **Code Noir** required baptism of all enslaved persons — registers therefore document enslaved ancestors alongside free colonists.
- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans** registers survive from **1720**.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) (Collection 1612905) — 987,654 records, 493,827 images. Covers the French colonial period from 1718.
- Records are in **French** (and Latin for ecclesiastical formulas).
- Originals also held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) and diocesan archives.
- *Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy, French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)*

#### 2. Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) Records
- The French colonial government's records: **land grants (concessions), civil contracts, court proceedings, wills, and estate inventories**.
- Held at: **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint Building, 400 Esplanade Ave., New Orleans, LA 70116.
- Partially digitized; records are in French.
- These are the colonial equivalent of county court and probate records.
- *Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)*

#### 3. Notarial Archives
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America.
- Holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions **from the 1730s onward**.
- In French (1730s–1769), then Spanish.
- Physical access: 1340 Poydras St., Suite 375, New Orleans, LA 70112.
- *Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)*

#### 4. Land Records / French Concessions
- Colonial Louisiana land grants followed **French civil law**, not English common law.
- Published digest: **American State Papers: Public Lands** series (widely digitized on HathiTrust and Library of Congress).
- Additional records: **Louisiana State Land Office** (Baton Rouge).
- Originals: Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM (see below).
- *Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)*

#### 5. Probate Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) (Collection 2078341) — 456,789 records, 228,394 images.
- Covers the **late French colonial period from 1756**. For estate records before 1756, rely on Superior Council records.
- Records from 1756–1769 are in French.

#### 6. Colonial Census Rolls
- France conducted several **administrative enumerations** of the colony (not federal censuses) during the 1700s.
- Held at: **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France.
- Online portal: https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr
- ANOM also holds administrative correspondence, military muster rolls, and Company of the Indies records.

#### 7. Military Records
- Colonial Louisiana was a military colony; many settlers served in the **Compagnie des Indes** (Company of the Indies, 1717–1731).
- Company muster rolls and military records: **ANOM**, Aix-en-Provence.
- Some transferred records: **NARA** (National Archives, Washington DC). https://www.archives.gov/

| Probate records (1756+) | Collection 2078341 — images present | Verify current indexing at FS |
