# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns (Late 1800s — c. 1860–1906)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **State:** Pennsylvania, United States (admitted to the Union 1787)
- **Coal region split:** Two distinct zones generated most of the late-19th-century mining population:
  - **Anthracite (hard coal) — Northeastern PA:** Schuylkill County (formed 1811), Luzerne County, Lackawanna County (split from Luzerne in **1878**), Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia counties
  - **Bituminous (soft coal) — Western PA:** Allegheny, Westmoreland, Fayette, and Washington counties
- **Population:** No census population figures were returned by the tools for this period; consult individual county census schedules (federal 1870, 1880, 1900) for local figures.
- **Economy:** Hard-rock underground coal extraction; company towns (patch towns) dominated the anthracite region. Railroads, iron furnaces, and coke ovens were secondary employers.
- **Ethnic composition:** Waves of immigrant miners — Irish and Welsh in earlier decades, followed by Poles, Lithuanians, Slovaks, Italians, and Ukrainians from the 1880s. Each group formed distinct ethnic parishes and mutual-aid societies that created parallel record sets.
- **Religious denominations:** Irish and Polish Catholic, Welsh Congregational and Baptist, Episcopal, Lutheran, Slovak and Lithuanian Catholic, Greek Catholic (Ruthenian/Ukrainian), and Methodist congregations were all active in coal towns.
- **Key events:** Molly Maguires trials (1875–1877); United Mine Workers of America founded 1890; numerous colliery disasters throughout the period.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Lackawanna County** was carved from **Luzerne County in 1878.** Any Scranton/Carbondale-area records before 1878 will be found under Luzerne County — search Luzerne first for that area.
- **Schuylkill County** was established 1811 and remained stable throughout the target period.
- All records in the anthracite region are at the **county level**; there is no sub-county (township) civil registration in Pennsylvania during this period.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Critical fact:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906.** ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)) Before that date, most births and deaths were recorded by churches only.
- **Exceptions at county level:** Philadelphia County began registering births and deaths around **1860**; Allegheny County (Pittsburgh) around **1870.** No comparable early county registration has been documented in the tool results for the anthracite coal counties.
- **Marriage records** were kept at the **county level** from the colonial period onward — marriage licenses and bonds are held at the county courthouse. FamilySearch has digitized:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 ([col. 1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317)) | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | 312,045 | Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 ([col. 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | 156,023 | Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 ([col. 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | **0** | Name index only — no images; consult original county records |

- **Death certificates** (FamilySearch col. 2255317, 4.2 million records) begin in **1906** — the very end of this period. They are indexed + images and are valuable for families whose older members died just after the period closes.
- **Pre-1906 death alternatives:** Church burial registers, cemetery sexton records, newspaper obituaries, and the **Annual Mine Inspector Reports** (see Occupational Records below).

---

### Church Records ⭐ *Most critical source for this period*

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)), ethnic parishes were the **primary record-keepers** for coal mining families before 1906, and their registers "often contain the most detailed family data." Each immigrant ethnic group established its own parish:

- **Irish Catholic / Polish Catholic / Lithuanian Catholic / Slovak Catholic** parishes — sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations). Many records survive at the diocese or parish level; FamilySearch has microfilmed many.
- **Welsh Congregational and Baptist** — important for Scranton, Wilkes-Barre, and Schuylkill County Welsh mining communities.
- **Greek/Byzantine Catholic (Ruthenian, Ukrainian)** — serves later-arriving Eastern European miners, 1880s onward.

FamilySearch has a digitized collection for one key county:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records ([SYNTH-PA-CHURCH](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/SYNTH-PA-CHURCH)) | 1708–1985 | 1,245,830 | 607,220 | Indexed + images |

- **Language note:** Catholic sacramental registers in ethnic parishes may be in **Latin, Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, or Ukrainian** depending on congregation and era. Welsh Baptist records may be in **Welsh.**
- **Where held:** Local parishes (if the congregation still exists), diocesan archives (Diocese of Scranton; Diocese of Allentown for Schuylkill/Carbon; Diocese of Pittsburgh for western PA), Pennsylvania State Archives, and FamilySearch microfilm.

---

### Census Records

| Census Year | Notes |
|---|---|
| **1870 federal** | Lists occupation; identifies miners by name, age, birthplace, parents' birthplaces |
| **1880 federal** | Adds relationship to head of household; invaluable for family structure |
| **1890 federal** | **Largely destroyed** (fire, 1921); surviving fragments are minimal |
| **1900 federal** | Most detailed — lists month/year of birth, years in U.S., citizenship status, number of children |

- **Mortality Schedules (1850–1885):** Record individuals who died in the 12 months preceding each census. Particularly valuable since Pennsylvania lacked statewide death registration. List name, age, sex, occupation, cause of death, and birthplace. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry for 1870 and 1880.
- **Veterans' Schedules (1890):** Although the general 1890 census is gone, the Union Veterans and Widows Schedule survives for many Pennsylvania counties — useful for miners who served in the Civil War.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for this period are fully indexed on both FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

---

### Occupational Records ⭐ *Distinctive to coal mining families*

These records are **unique to this locality type** and should be searched before assuming a person cannot be traced.

**FamilySearch digitized volumes:**

| Volume | Place | Date Range | Images | Indexed? | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mine Worker Employment Cards ([002240015](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:002240015)) | Schuylkill County | 1870–1900 | 410 | **95% — fully indexed + full-text searchable** | Searchable online |
| Mine Accident Reports ([002240016](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:002240016)) | Luzerne County | 1870–1895 | 287 | **0% — browse-only images** | Must browse image by image |
| Colliery Payroll Ledgers ([002240017](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:002240017)) | Lackawanna County | 1878–1900 | 199 | **0% — browse-only images** | Must browse image by image |

> ⚠️ The Luzerne and Lackawanna volumes must be browsed page by page — no name search is possible. Knowing the specific colliery name before browsing will save significant time.

**Annual Mine Inspector Reports (from 1870):** Published by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Mine Inspection, these annual reports list every **fatal mine accident** statewide: name, age, nationality, and cause of death. They function as a de facto vital record substitute for miners killed on the job. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) and some county historical societies; not fully digitized online.

**Union Records:** The **United Mine Workers of America (UMWA)**, founded 1890, kept membership rolls and grievance files. These are held at the UMWA archives and at the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County.** ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

---

### Probate and Court Records

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 ([col. 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | 446,607 | Indexed + images |

- Probate records (wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships) are filed at the **county Register of Wills** from the colonial period onward.
- **Naturalization records** are critical for this immigrant-heavy population. Before the federal Naturalization Act of 1906, declarations of intention and petitions were filed in **any court of record** — county courts of common pleas, orphans' courts, even federal district courts. **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906)** are held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives.** ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)) Search the county where the miner lived, not necessarily where he arrived.

---

### Land Records

- **Pennsylvania is a state-land state** (not federal-land). Land grants originate with William Penn (1681); the **Pennsylvania State Land Office** (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records. ([Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))
- **County deed books** at the county courthouse (Recorder of Deeds) document property transfers.
- **Tax records** (assessment lists, tax duplicates) survive from the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties and serve as excellent **census substitutes** — especially valuable for the destroyed 1890 census years. Held at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (not rectangular township survey).
- Note: Coal miners in patch towns often *rented* company housing and did not own land, so land records may be sparse for this population. Tax records are more likely to document them.

---

### Military Records

- The primary conflict overlapping this period is the **Civil War (1861–1865)**. Many adult male miners in the 1870s–1890s were veterans.
- **Service records and pension files** at NARA (Washington, D.C. and regional offices); searchable via Fold3 (subscription) and some free FamilySearch collections.
- **Pennsylvania State Archives** holds adjutant general records and regimental histories.
- **1890 Veterans' Schedule** (survives even where the regular census does not) — lists name, rank, unit, disabilities, and widow's name.
- **Spanish-American War (1898):** Younger miners may have served; draft and service records at NARA.

---

### Cemetery Records

- **Online:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves have broad Pennsylvania coverage including most coal county cemeteries. Both are free to search.
- **Physical records:** Sexton burial registers at individual cemeteries; many ethnic parishes maintained their own burial grounds with separate registers.
- **Key local cemeteries:** Each coal town typically had at least one Catholic cemetery and one Protestant cemetery; some larger towns had separate ethnic sections.

---

### Newspaper Records

- Coal mining newspapers were active and covered mine accidents, strikes, and community news extensively — **obituaries and accident notices are a primary death source** before 1906.
- **Online access:**
  - **Newspapers.com** (subscription) — broad Pennsylvania coverage
  - **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) — includes many Pennsylvania papers of the period
  - **Pennsylvania State Library** (Harrisburg) holds microfilm of many local papers
- Key papers to seek: *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville/Schuylkill County, from 1825), *Scranton Republican*, *Wilkes-Barre Times-Leader*, and various ethnic-language papers (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak) for later decades.

---

### Immigration / Emigration Records

Many late-19th-century coal miners were recent immigrants. Per the FamilySearch Wiki, miners arrived predominantly through **Philadelphia** and **New York (Ellis Island, opened 1892; Castle Garden before that).** ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

- **Passenger arrival lists** at NARA; searchable free on FamilySearch and via Ancestry/MyHeritage (subscription). Examine the full manifest — family members including children are listed together.
- **Naturalization records:** As noted above, filed in county courts (pre-1906); Schuylkill County records at Pennsylvania State Archives. Search the coal county's court of common pleas, not just federal courts.
- **Passports:** Unusual for this population; most did not obtain them.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Relevant Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | County marriages 1677–1950; Probate Records 1683–1994; Schuylkill County Church Records; Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill, indexed); Luzerne Mine Accident Reports & Lackawanna Payroll Ledgers (browse-only); Death Certificates 1906+ | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1870–1900); mortality schedules; passenger lists; Pennsylvania vital records | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records statewide | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Pennsylvania newspapers | Subscription |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Civil War and Spanish-American War military records | Subscription |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Passenger lists; federal naturalization post-1906; military records | Free to search; some fees for copies |
| **Chronicling America** (loc.gov/chroniclingamerica) | Digitized Pennsylvania newspapers | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector reports; naturalization records (incl. Schuylkill Co.); Land Office records; tax records; military records | In-person; some records available via mail or online request |
| **County Courthouses** (Register of Wills, Recorder of Deeds, Prothonotary) | Probate records; deeds; marriage records; court naturalizations | In-person or mail |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | UMWA records; local mining collections; newspapers; family files | In-person |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum / Lackawanna Coal Mine** (Scranton) | Mining history collections; company records | In-person |
| **Diocese of Scranton Archives** | Catholic parish sacramental registers for Lackawanna/Luzerne region | Contact by mail; access restrictions vary |
| **Diocese of Allentown Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill and Carbon counties | Contact by mail |
| **Local parish churches** | Sacramental registers still held by active parishes | Contact individual parish |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following exist and are genealogically valuable but are **not fully available in any online database:**

- **Annual Pennsylvania Mine Inspector Reports (1870–1906)** — fatal accident lists with names, ages, nationalities; physical at Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Company employment records, payrolls, and personnel files** — fragmentarily held at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties; not systematically digitized
- **UMWA membership rolls and grievance files (1890+)** — at UMWA archives and Historical Society of Schuylkill County
- **Ethnic-language Catholic parish registers** for many parishes (Lithuanian, Polish, Slovak, Ukrainian) — held at individual parishes or diocesan archives; limited online presence
- **Luzerne County Mine Accident Reports and Lackawanna Colliery Payroll Ledgers** — digitized images exist on FamilySearch but are **browse-only** (0% indexed); no name search is possible

---

## Known Record Losses

- The **1890 U.S. Federal Census** is largely destroyed (fire, 1921). The Veterans' Schedule partial survivals and the 1885/1895 state censuses (where they exist for neighboring states) partially compensate; Pennsylvania did not conduct a mid-decade state census in 1885 or 1895.
- **Statewide birth and death registration** did not begin until 1906, meaning **no civil vital records exist for the entire late-1800s period** except in Philadelphia and Allegheny counties. Church registers and Mine Inspector Reports are the primary substitutes.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with church records, not vital records.** Because Pennsylvania had no statewide birth/death registration before 1906, ethnic parish registers are the only formal vital record source for most coal mining families. Identify the ethnic background first — it determines which denomination's archives to search. ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))

2. **Lackawanna County records before 1878 are in Luzerne County.** If you're researching the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878, search Luzerne County deed, probate, court, and marriage records. ([place_search result])

3. **The Annual Mine Inspector Reports are a de facto death register.** For any miner who died underground, the annual report for that year lists name, age, nationality, and cause of death — often the only death record that exists. Request copies from the Pennsylvania State Archives.

4. **Search county courts for naturalization, not just federal courts.** Before 1906 immigrants could naturalize in any court of record. For coal counties, the Court of Common Pleas is the most likely repository. Schuylkill County records (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

5. **Tax records substitute for the missing 1890 census.** Pennsylvania county tax assessment lists and duplicates survive from the colonial era and are held at county courthouses and the State Archives. They can place a family in a specific township in the 1890s when no census exists.

6. **The Schuylkill County Mine Worker Employment Cards (FamilySearch vol. 002240015) are 95% name-indexed** — search these directly by name. The Luzerne and Lackawanna volumes must be browsed image by image; know your colliery before starting.

7. **Chain migration is the rule, not the exception.** Coal mining communities were built on chain migration — villages in Ireland, Wales, Poland, or Slovakia sent multiple families to the same patch town. Research neighbors and associates in the same colliery; they may be siblings, cousins, or godparents whose records fill gaps in your direct line.

8. **Ethnic-language newspapers are an overlooked source.** Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, and Ukrainian papers published in Pennsylvania coal towns carried obituaries, arrival notices, and community news. Many are on microfilm at the State Library of Pennsylvania (Harrisburg).

9. **Probate records document family relationships.** Even miners without real property left estates — tools, furniture, life insurance payouts. The county Register of Wills may hold an administration file naming spouse, children, and sometimes siblings or parents. FamilySearch col. 1999196 covers Pennsylvania probate 1683–1994 with 446,000+ images.

10. **Pennsylvania is a state-land state.** Land patents and warrants originate with the Penn family and the Commonwealth, not the federal government. The Pennsylvania State Land Office (Harrisburg) holds the foundational land records; county deed books hold transfers. ([Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))

---

**Quick-start search sequence for a coal mining ancestor:**
1. Federal census (1880 or 1900) — establish family, birthplace, and colliery/township
2. Schuylkill Employment Cards (indexed, FamilySearch) **or** county-level Luzerne/Lackawanna volumes (browse-only)
3. Church baptism/marriage registers for the ethnic denomination — contact parish or diocese
4. County marriage records (FamilySearch indexed collections)
5. Annual Mine Inspector Reports (Pennsylvania State Archives) if ancestor died in a mine accident
6. County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records
7. FindAGrave / local cemetery sexton records for death date
8. Newspapers.com / Chronicling America for obituaries and accident notices

# 📜 Locality Research Guide: Massachusetts, Early 1600s Puritan Settlements
**Jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States | **Period:** c. 1620–1700
**Survey date:** 25 August 2026

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Early colonial Massachusetts comprised **two distinct, separate jurisdictions** that must each be searched:

| Jurisdiction | Active | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Plymouth Colony** | 1620–1691 | Separate colony; absorbed into Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691 |
| **Massachusetts Bay Colony** | 1628–1691 | Puritan charter; governed Boston and surrounding towns |
| **Province of Massachusetts Bay** | 1691+ | Royal charter replaced both colonies |

**Counties did not exist until 1643**, when Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and Suffolk Counties were formed. Before that date, the General Court (the colonial legislature/court) and individual towns were the only civil authorities generating records. This matters for researchers: events before 1643 will appear in town or General Court records, not county records.

Governor John Winthrop led the **Great Migration of ~20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640** (Wikipedia). The colony mandated towns to record vital events (births, marriages, deaths) starting in **1639** — making this one of the earliest civil registration mandates in North America. That town-level mandate predates statewide registration by two centuries; **statewide registration did not begin until 1841**.

---

## Record Types, Availability & Access

### 1. 📋 Town Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (ID: 2061550)
  → [familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)
- **Coverage:** ~3.46 million records, ~1.73 million images; date range 1620–1890
- **Access level:** Digitized with images on FamilySearch; verify name-index coverage for individual towns before assuming full searchability
- **Published compilations:** The **Tanner–Corbin "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is widely available in libraries and at NEHGS (source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy, Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Key repository:** Town clerks' offices (originals); Massachusetts Archives (Boston) for colony-level oversight records

### 2. ⛪ Church Records (Congregational / Puritan)
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (ID: 1921657)
  → [familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)
- **Coverage:** ~987,654 records, ~493,827 images; date range 1630–1920
- **What they contain:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, disciplinary actions (excommunications, admonishments) — the Congregational church was the **established church of the colony**, so these records overlap with and supplement town vital records (source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records, Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Published:** Many early church records appear in the **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** series and local historical society publications
- **Key repositories:** Individual church archives; NEHGS; Massachusetts Archives

### 3. ⚖️ Probate Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* (ID: 1678901)
  → [familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)
- **Coverage:** ~567,890 records, ~283,945 images; date range begins 1635
- **What they contain:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration — typically filed at county probate courts (post-1643); pre-county records are in General Court files
- **Key repositories:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives

### 4. 🏡 Land Records (Deeds & Grants)
- **No specific FamilySearch collection for this period appeared in tool results** — treat as a potential browse or physical-only gap online
- Land records were recorded at the **county level from the 1630s** in "remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds." Before 1643, land grants came from the colonial government (General Court) (source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Key repositories:** County Registries of Deeds; Massachusetts Archives (colonial-era grants); Bureau of Land Management GLO (federal patents, later period)

### 5. 🏛️ Colony & Court Records
- The **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) holds **original colony records, governor's correspondence, and court records from the 1620s onward** — this is the premier repository for the colonial period (source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- The **General Court** served as both legislature and highest court; its records are at the Massachusetts Archives
- County courts (post-1643) held civil, criminal, and equity proceedings that name family members

### 6. 🚢 Passenger & Immigration Records
- The FamilySearch collection *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists* (1820–1891) **falls entirely outside the 1600s target period** and is not a primary source for early settlers
- **For the Great Migration (1620–1643):** Use the **Great Migration study series** (Robert Charles Anderson, NEHGS/AmericanAncestors.org) — it documents every known settler who arrived 1620–1643, with sources and family reconstructions (source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- Early ship manifests and passenger lists for the colonial period are published in volumes such as *The Great Migration Begins* and are not available through standard online passenger-list collections

### 7. ⚔️ Military Records
- Colonial militia muster rolls and King Philip's War (1675–1676) records exist at **NARA** (archives.gov) and the **Massachusetts Archives**
- **Fold3.com** holds some colonial military records, though coverage for the 1600s is limited
- No FamilySearch collection specific to 1600s Massachusetts military records appeared in tool results

### 8. 🪦 Cemetery & Burial Records
- **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) includes colonial-era gravestones — New England has a strong tradition of documented early burial grounds
- Many colonial-era gravestones were transcribed by the **Bay State Historical League** and local historical societies
- Physical burial grounds in towns such as Boston, Salem, Plymouth, and Cambridge have published inscriptions

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Original colony records, General Court minutes, court files, land grants, vital registration oversight; 1620s onward | In-person & digital catalog: archives.lib.state.ma.us |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Largest genealogical research library in New England; manuscript collections; Great Migration series; published genealogies | In-person (Boston) + online: AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |
| **FamilySearch** | Town Vital Records 1620–1890, Church Records 1630–1920, Probate Records 1635–1991 | Free online: familysearch.org |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Deed books from 1630s; remarkably complete runs | County courthouse + some online |
| **County Probate Courts** | Wills, inventories, guardianship from 1635 | County courthouse; partially on FamilySearch |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Military records; some federal-era colonial materials | In-person (Waltham, MA regional branch) + Fold3 |
| **Plymouth Colony Archive** | Plymouth Colony records 1620–1691, published & indexed separately | Published volumes; online via NEHGS |

---

## Published Compilations — Critical Starting Points

These published sets are essential for the early 1600s and are widely held in libraries:

- **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series (Tanner–Corbin) — 200+ towns abstracted; the foundation of Massachusetts vital research
- **Robert Charles Anderson, *The Great Migration Begins* and *The Great Migration*** (NEHGS) — every known settler 1620–1643 with full source documentation
- ***Records of the Colony of New Plymouth*** — published and indexed; separate from Massachusetts Bay Colony records
- **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** publication series — includes published church registers

---

## ⚠️ Key Research Quirks

1. **Plymouth Colony is separate** — its records are published and indexed independently from Massachusetts Bay Colony. Never assume a single search covers both. The merger into the Province of Massachusetts Bay occurred in 1691; use that date as your dividing line.

2. **"1841" is the statewide date, not the only registration date** — towns were recording vital events under the 1639 General Court mandate. Do not conclude there are no 1600s vital records because "Massachusetts didn't register until 1841." That figure refers to *statewide* civil registration only.

3. **Counties did not exist before 1643** — events before that year will be in town or General Court records, not county records. Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and Suffolk are the original four counties (1643).

4. **Congregational church records are not optional supplements — they may be the primary record.** The Congregational church was the established church of the colony; for many early families, church registers predate or duplicate town clerk entries, and in some cases are the only surviving record.

5. **The Great Migration Name Index (NEHGS) is the required first lookup** for any family arriving before 1643 — it is the most thoroughly documented and sourced starting point for early settlers.

6. **Online collections for this period have real gaps** — land records for the colonial period did not appear in FamilySearch collections_search results and may require physical or microfilm access at county registries or the Massachusetts Archives.

7. **No census records exist for the 1600s** — the federal census begins in 1790; no colonial enumeration equivalent survives for Massachusetts. Tax lists, militia musters, and town and church membership lists serve as census substitutes.

---

## Records Outside the Target Period (Background Context Only)

| Collection | Date Range | Why Listed |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts, Passenger Lists | 1820–1891 | Outside 1600s; use Great Migration series instead |
| Massachusetts, Naturalization Records | 1790–1906 | Outside 1600s; not applicable to colonial settlers |
| U.S. Federal Census | 1790+ | Outside 1600s |

---

## Recommended Research Strategy

1. **Start with NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org** — search the Great Migration Name Index for any settler arriving 1620–1643
2. **Search FamilySearch Town Vital Records** (collection 2061550) for births, marriages, deaths
3. **Search FamilySearch Church Records** (collection 1921657) alongside vital records — they are complementary, not duplicates
4. **Search FamilySearch Probate Records** (collection 1678901) for wills and inventories, which often name all children
5. **Go to county deed books** at county registries or via FamilySearch microfilm for land transfers; connect to colony land grants at the Massachusetts Archives for pre-1643 events
6. **Consult the Massachusetts Archives directly** for court records, General Court files, and governor's correspondence
7. **Check the Tanner–Corbin "Vital Records to 1850" published volumes** for your specific town — these abstract the town clerk originals
8. **Plymouth families:** Use *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* in published form; search Plymouth County probate and land records as a separate trail from Massachusetts Bay Colony records

---

This is one of the **best-documented colonial populations in North America** for the 1600s — town-level registration from 1639, remarkably complete probate and land record runs, and a major dedicated published series (Great Migration) make Massachusetts early settler research highly tractable compared to other colonial regions.

## 📍 Oklahoma Territory Locality Research Guide — Land Run Era (ca. 1880–1910)

### Jurisdictional Context

The area that became Oklahoma passed through three distinct jurisdictional phases that directly determine which records exist and where they are held:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-Apr 22, 1889 | "Unassigned Lands," Indian Territory | Federal land, no organized civil government for settlers |
| May 2, 1890 – 1907 | **Oklahoma Territory** (west) + **Indian Territory** (east) | Two separate jurisdictions simultaneously |
| Nov 16, 1907 | **State of Oklahoma** | 46th state; the two territories merged |

**Critical split:** Oklahoma Territory (western portion) and Indian Territory (eastern portion, governed by the Five Civilized Tribes under federal oversight) operated completely different record systems until statehood. Determine which territory your ancestor lived in before selecting record sets.

The Land Run of 1889 settled the Unassigned Lands (present-day central Oklahoma). Homestead claims were administered by land offices at **Guthrie** and **Kingfisher**. Subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 opened different areas — confirm which opening applies to your family.

---

### ⭐ 1. Land & Homestead Records — *First Stop for Land Run Families*

**What they are:** Homestead applications, proof-of-settlement affidavits (naming witnesses), final certificates, and land patents. Rejected and contested claims also survive and can contain rich family detail.

| Source | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch — Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907** | [Collection 1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872) — **indexed + images** (234,567 records, 117,283 images) | Covers both territories; name-searchable |
| **BLM General Land Office Records** | [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — free, partially indexed | Homestead patents; searchable by name and legal description |
| **NARA, Record Group 49** (General Land Office) | National Archives, Washington D.C. | Full case files; some indexed on FamilySearch and BLM site |

> **Quirk:** Claims from the 1889 opening were processed at Guthrie (central districts) or Kingfisher (western districts) land offices. Know which district your ancestor's claim fell in.

> **Quirk:** "Sooner" disputes and contested claims generated additional federal records in special case files — worth checking if your ancestor's claim was challenged.

---

### 2. Census Records

| Record | Years | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** | 1890 | Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | **Rare survivor** — the national 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire; Oklahoma Territory's special census is one of very few that survived. |
| **U.S. Federal Census** | 1900, 1910 | FamilySearch, Ancestry.com | Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory were enumerated *separately* in 1900 — search both if unsure which territory your ancestor was in |
| **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** | 1851–1959 | [Collection 1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) — **indexed + images** (567,890 records, 283,945 images) | Covers tribal rolls, Dawes enrollment, annuity rolls for Indian Territory |

---

### 3. Vital Records

**Statewide registration began October 1908**, and compliance was poor until the 1930s. For the territorial period (1889–1907), **no civil vital registration existed** — use the substitute sources below.

| Record | Coverage | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Birth & Death records** | From Oct 1908 | Oklahoma State Archives | Physical / request copies |
| **County Marriages** | 1890–1995 | [FamilySearch Collection 2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789) | **Indexed + images** — 456,789 records, 228,394 images |
| *Substitute:* Church registers | From 1889 | See §4 below | Sporadic before 1900 |
| *Substitute:* Cemetery records | From 1889 | FindAGrave.com | Searchable online |
| *Substitute:* Territorial newspapers | 1889–1907 | Oklahoma Historical Society; Newspapers.com | Obituaries, marriage notices |

---

### 4. Church & Mission Records

Methodist, Baptist, and Catholic congregations were established in the Unassigned Lands beginning in 1889. Mission records in Indian Territory predate the Land Run by decades.

| Collection | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch — Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965** | [Collection 1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321) — **indexed + images** (123,456 records, 61,728 images) | Includes early mission registers for Indian Territory |
| Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church Archives | Historical registers | Oklahoma City — contact for access |
| Diocese of Oklahoma City Archives | Catholic parish registers | Oklahoma City — contact for access |

---

### 5. Indian Territory — Five Civilized Tribes Records

If your ancestor was in **eastern Oklahoma** (Indian Territory), the tribal record system is paramount. The Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) maintained their own courts, censuses, and land records.

| Record | Notes | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Dawes Commission Rolls, 1898–1914** | Enrolled tribal citizens; essential for Indian Territory families | FamilySearch [Collection 1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432); NARA Fort Worth (RG 75) |
| **Annuity Payment Rolls** (pre-1900) | List heads of household, sometimes families | NARA RG 75, M234; partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3 |
| **Tribal Court Records** | Civil/criminal cases, probate, land allotments | NARA at Fort Worth (RG 75); Oklahoma Historical Society |
| **Individual tribal archives** | Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole nations maintain their own archives | Contact each nation directly |

> **Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Five Civilized Tribes Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records)

---

### 6. Territorial Court Records (Oklahoma Territory, 1890–1907)

District court files include civil and criminal cases, **probate records**, **naturalization papers**, guardianships, and name changes — all potentially naming family members.

- **National Archives at Fort Worth** (RG 75) — primary repository
- **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City)

> **Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

| Source | Access |
|---|---|
| Service records, pension files | [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) (subscription); NARA |
| Draft registrations (WWI era) | NARA; Ancestry.com |

---

### 8. Newspapers

Territorial newspapers are invaluable for the 1889–1907 period when vital registration didn't exist — obituaries, marriage notices, land claim news, and town histories.

- **[Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)** — subscription; Oklahoma titles available
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — holds physical territorial newspaper runs
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) — some Oklahoma territorial papers digitized

---

### 9. Departure-State Records — *Don't Skip These*

According to the FamilySearch Wiki, most Land Run settlers came from **Kansas, Texas, and Missouri**. Tracing your ancestor's origins before 1889 requires searching those states. Look for:
- Kansas and Missouri census records (1880 federal census)
- Texas state census (1880)
- Birth, marriage, and church records in the state of origin

> **Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (Oklahoma City) | 1890 special census, territorial records, newspapers, land run claim files |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City) | Birth/death from 1908, territorial and state government records |
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Tribal records (RG 75), territorial court records |
| **NARA, Washington D.C.** | General Land Office homestead files (RG 49) |
| **BLM — glorecords.blm.gov** | Land patents, online and free |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Four collections listed above, all indexed + images |

---

### Research Quirks Summary

1. **Two-territory split:** Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east) had entirely separate record systems 1890–1907. Identify which territory your ancestor lived in first.
2. **The 1890 census survives here:** Oklahoma Territory's special 1890 census is a rare national survivor — use it.
3. **No territorial vital registration:** Births and deaths weren't civilly registered before October 1908. Church records, newspapers, and census are the substitutes.
4. **Land run opening matters:** Five separate openings (1889, 1891, 1892, 1893, 1895) each have their own land office records and affected different areas.
5. **Dawes Rolls for Indian Territory families:** If your ancestor was in eastern Oklahoma, the Dawes Commission enrollment (1898–1914) is the key identity record.
6. **Search departure states:** Kansas, Texas, and Missouri records are essential context for pre-1889 origins.

---

entry.guide_markdown:
## Oklahoma Territory Locality Research Guide — Land Run Era (ca. 1880–1910)

### Jurisdictional Context

The area passed through three distinct phases:
- **Pre-Apr 22, 1889:** Unassigned Lands within Indian Territory; no organized civil government for settlers
- **May 2, 1890 – 1907:** Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east, Five Civilized Tribes) — two separate jurisdictions with different record systems
- **Nov 16, 1907:** State of Oklahoma (46th state); the two territories merged

The Land Run of 1889 opened ~2 million acres; homestead claims were filed at land offices in Guthrie and Kingfisher. Subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 opened additional areas.

### 1. Land & Homestead Records ⭐ First Stop
- **FamilySearch — Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907** [Collection 1541872] — indexed + images (234,567 records, 117,283 images)
- **BLM General Land Office Records** — glorecords.blm.gov — free, partially indexed
- **NARA Record Group 49** — full homestead case files including proof-of-settlement affidavits with witnesses

### 2. Census
- **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** — Oklahoma Historical Society; rare survivor of the destroyed 1890 federal census
- **U.S. Federal Census 1900, 1910** — Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory enumerated separately in 1900
- **FamilySearch — Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** [Collection 1987432] — indexed + images (567,890 records, 283,945 images)

### 3. Vital Records
Statewide registration began October 1908; compliance poor until 1930s. No civil registration for territorial period (1889–1907).
- Birth/death from 1908: Oklahoma State Archives
- County marriages from 1890: **FamilySearch Collection 2134789** — indexed + images (456,789 records)
- Substitutes for pre-1908: church registers, census, cemetery records, territorial newspapers

### 4. Church & Mission Records
- **FamilySearch — Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965** [Collection 1654321] — indexed + images (123,456 records)
- Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church Archives (Oklahoma City)
- Diocese of Oklahoma City Archives (Catholic registers)

### 5. Indian Territory — Five Civilized Tribes
- **Dawes Commission Rolls, 1898–1914** — FamilySearch Collection 1987432; NARA Fort Worth RG 75
- **Annuity Payment Rolls** — NARA RG 75 M234; partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3
- Individual tribal archives: Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole
- Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records

### 6. Territorial Court Records (1890–1907)
- National Archives at Fort Worth (RG 75): district court cases, probate, naturalization
- Oklahoma State Archives
- Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts

### 7. Newspapers
- Newspapers.com (subscription); Oklahoma Historical Society; Chronicling America (free)

### 8. Military
- Fold3.com; NARA

### 9. Departure-State Records
Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri — search those states' 1880 census and vital records for pre-1889 origins.
- Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (circa 1700–1819)

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

The territory that is today Alabama had no single governing authority around 1800 — it was a layered jurisdictional patchwork, and which records exist for any given family depends entirely on where in the region they lived and when.

**Colonial succession (Mobile area and Gulf Coast):**
- **French**: 1702–1763. Mobile was the administrative capital.
- **British**: 1763–1780. Mobile passed to Britain after the Seven Years' War.
- **Spanish**: 1780–1813. Spain retook Mobile during the American Revolution; the Mobile District remained under Spanish authority until U.S. forces seized it in April 1813.

**American territorial period:**
- **Mississippi Territory**: 1798–1817. Created from territory ceded by Georgia and Spanish West Florida. Originally a narrow strip along the 31st–32nd parallels; expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to encompass the full area of present-day Mississippi and Alabama. Present-day Alabama was the *eastern* portion of this territory.
- **Alabama Territory**: 1817–1819. When Mississippi became a state in August 1817, the eastern half was organized separately as the Alabama Territory.
- **Statehood**: Alabama was admitted to the Union on December 14, 1819.

**Population context:** American settlement in present-day Alabama ca. 1800 was extremely sparse and concentrated along the Mobile coast, the lower Tombigbee River, and (after 1805 land cessions) the Tennessee River Valley. The Creek and Cherokee nations controlled most of central and northern Alabama until the Creek War of 1813–1814 opened those territories to rapid Anglo-American settlement. Per Wikipedia, "The region saw significant migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia after the Creek War of 1813–1814." The 1810 federal census is the first to more substantially enumerate what is now Alabama. No population data was returned by the FamilySearch place_population tool for this period and place.

---

## Boundary Changes

| Period | Governing Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French Louisiana / Mobile District | French records created |
| 1763–1780 | British West Florida | British records created |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish Mobile District | Spanish records created; Mobile held after 1798 even as U.S. took north |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory (eastern portion) | American-era records begin; present-day Alabama was NOT a separate political unit |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory | First time Alabama existed as its own jurisdiction |
| 1819– | State of Alabama | County-level record creation stabilizes |

**Critical researcher quirk:** Records for ancestors living in present-day Alabama between 1798 and 1817 are filed under the *Mississippi Territory*, not Alabama. FamilySearch collections scoped to Mississippi cover this territorial period. These are not separate research trails — they are one continuous documentary record of the same territory, split across two place labels at 1817. Search both. See [FamilySearch Wiki: Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** There was **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths in the Alabama region around 1800 — neither territorial nor colonial governments required it. Alabama did not institute statewide civil vital registration until **1908**. County-level registration began in some counties earlier (marriage bonds and licenses at the county courthouse begin with county formation, mostly 1809–1819 for territorial-era counties), but births and deaths were not civilly registered.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the only systematic vital record source for this period. For the Mobile area, Catholic sacramental registers go back to the French colonial era.
- **Holding level:** No civil registration exists at any level for circa 1800.

### Church Records
Church records are the **primary vital record substitute** for this entire period.

- **Catholic Church (Mobile area):** The oldest and most complete records in the region. Mobile's Cathedral Parish (Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception / Cathedral of the Assumption) has sacramental registers dating to the French colonial period — baptisms, marriages, and burials recorded in French, then Spanish, then English. These are the richest pre-1800 genealogical records in the state.
  - **French colonial originals**: Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France — **physical only**
  - **Microfilm of French records**: Mobile Municipal Archives — **microfilm, in person**
  - **Spanish colonial records (Mobile District):** Church registers, census returns, and land grants held at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain — **physical only** — with copies at the Library of Congress. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
  - **Language of records:** French (colonial era), Spanish (1780–1813), Latin (sacramental formulae throughout)
- **Protestant denominations:** Methodist and Baptist circuit riders were active in the territory ca. 1800–1810, but congregational records from this early period are scattered, sparse, and survival is uneven.

**FamilySearch collections covering church records:**

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396) | 1803–1950 | 156,789 | 78,394 | Indexed + images |
| [Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891) | 1800–1950 | 87,654 | 43,827 | Indexed + images |

The Mississippi-scoped collection covers church records from the territorial period and may include records from present-day Alabama counties. The Alabama collection's earliest records (from 1803) fall within the pre-statehood window.

### Census Records
- **Federal census:** The 1800 federal census enumerated the Mississippi Territory, but the present-day Alabama portion was barely settled; coverage is extremely thin. The **1810 federal census** is the first to substantially enumerate Alabama settlements (Madison County/Huntsville area, Washington County/Mobile area).
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted census enumerations in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** that covered present-day Alabama. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)), these are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery. These are the single most important census-substitute source for the 1800–1810 window.

**FamilySearch collections covering census/substitutes:**

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756) | 1810–1890 | 287,634 | 0 | **Index only — no images** |
| [Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171) | 1792–1890 | 198,340 | 0 | **Index only — no images** |

⚠️ Both census/substitute collections are **index-only** — there are no linked images. The index entries point to original records held at ADAH and other repositories.

### Land Records — *The Richest Source for This Period*
Alabama is a **federal-land state** (land originally owned by the U.S. government and distributed via federal land offices, not state grants). This makes federal land records the single most important documentary source for proving an ancestor's presence in pre-statehood Alabama.

- **Federal land offices in present-day Alabama:**
  - **St. Stephens Land Office** (Washington County, south Alabama): opened 1807 — served the lower Tombigbee and Mobile areas
  - **Huntsville Land Office** (Madison County, north Alabama): opened 1811 — served the Tennessee Valley
- **BLM General Land Office Records** (glorecords.blm.gov): Alabama federal land patents are searchable by name online — **indexed + images**, free.
- **Colonial-era grants:** The earliest land records are Spanish and British colonial grants concentrated in the Mobile area. These are held in the colonial archives cited above (AGI Seville; Library of Congress copies). ([FamilySearch Wiki: Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **Tax lists:** Territorial tax lists function as critical census substitutes and document land ownership. Per the FamilySearch Wiki, territorial records include tax lists alongside land grants, militia rolls, and court records. These are held at ADAH.

**FamilySearch collection covering territorial land records:**

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) | 1798–1907 | 312,450 | 156,225 | Indexed + images |

This collection's date range begins in 1798 — the first year of the Mississippi Territory — and is the primary FamilySearch resource for territorial-era Alabama land records. It is scoped under Mississippi but covers the full territory, including present-day Alabama.

### Probate and Court Records
- Territorial courts in present-day Alabama began generating records ca. 1799–1800 in Washington County (the first U.S. county organized in present-day Alabama).
- Court records include wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, and civil cases that name family members and provide relationship evidence when vital records are absent.

**FamilySearch collections:**

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) | 1809–1985 | 438,210 | 219,105 | Indexed + images |
| [Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) | 1799–1920 | 245,670 | 122,835 | Indexed + images |

The Mississippi-scoped court records collection begins in 1799 and covers the territorial court system, which would have jurisdiction over present-day Alabama counties.

### Marriage Records
Civil marriage bonds and licenses begin with county formation. The first territorial-era Alabama counties (Washington, Baldwin, Madison) were organized between 1800 and 1808.

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) | 1809–1950 | 612,345 | 306,172 | Indexed + images |

The earliest marriages in this collection (from 1809) fall within the pre-statehood window.

### Military Records
- **Creek War (1813–1814):** Militia and volunteer service records. The defeat of the Creek Nation opened central Alabama to American settlement.
- **War of 1812:** Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants — many Alabama Territory settlers served.
- **Territorial militia rolls:** Cited by the FamilySearch Wiki as part of the territorial records held at ADAH. ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **NARA:** War of 1812 and Creek War service records and pension files at the National Archives (Washington, D.C. and Atlanta regional). Pension files in particular are extraordinarily rich — they contain biographical statements, family details, and sometimes marriage certificates.
- **Fold3.com:** Military records (subscription).

### Tax Records
Territorial-era tax lists are among the most important sources for present-day Alabama ca. 1800. They document who owned property (or was subject to poll tax) in years without federal or territorial census coverage, and they name individuals the federal census may have missed.
- Per FamilySearch Wiki, territorial records include tax lists. ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- Original records held at ADAH. Some have been transcribed and published by the Alabama Genealogical Society.

### Cemetery Records
- Coverage on FindAGrave and BillionGraves for the pre-1820 period is extremely sparse — most graves from this era were marked with wooden markers that have not survived.
- Catholic cemeteries in Mobile have the region's oldest documented burials.
- Church cemetery transcription projects at local historical and genealogical societies are the best source.

### Newspapers
- Very few newspapers were published in the Alabama region before statehood. The *Mobile Centinel* (later *Mobile Gazette*) was among the earliest.
- Alabama newspaper digitization for this period is minimal. Check the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) for what is available.

### Immigration and Emigration
- Most settlers arriving in the Alabama region ca. 1800 came **overland** from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia — not by ship. Per Wikipedia, migration from these states accelerated after the Creek War of 1813–1814.
- Mobile is a port: French-era passenger arrivals may exist in colonial archives for early Mobile settlers, but these are in overseas repositories.
- No NARA passenger list records are relevant for the vast majority of Alabama settlers at this period (overland migration left no federal arrival record).
- Naturalization records for foreign-born settlers would have been filed in any territorial court of record.

---

## Digitized Browsable Volumes — Special Note

You asked specifically about digitized, browsable volumes that can be read image by image even without a name index. **The `volume_search` tool returned zero results** for both "Alabama, United States" and "Mississippi Territory, United States" for the 1700–1820 period. This is a real coverage gap: FamilySearch's records management system does not currently list any standalone digitized image volumes specifically tagged to pre-statehood Alabama or the Mississippi Territory for this period.

For pre-1803 records (the true colonial era), digitized browsable material requires going to the overseas repositories mentioned above or their microfilm copies.

---

- **Multiple sovereignty transitions in Mobile:** Records were disrupted and scattered across the French-to-British, British-to-Spanish, and Spanish-to-American transitions (1763, 1780, 1813). Some records were removed by departing administrations; others were lost entirely.
- **Frontier record-keeping in the interior:** Northern and central Alabama in 1800 were a sparsely settled frontier where formal record-keeping was minimal or nonexistent. - **Creek War (1813–1814) disruption:** The conflict destroyed some settlement records in central and southern Alabama.

1. **Work the two territorial trails together.** Ancestors in present-day Alabama before 1817 left records under "Mississippi Territory." After 1817 they appear under "Alabama Territory." 2. **Land records are your anchor.** Alabama is a federal-land state with records at the BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov). If your ancestor obtained land after 1807 (St. Stephens office) or 1811 (Huntsville office), a federal land patent likely exists and is searchable by name for free.

3. **The territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 fill the gap** between the sparse 1800 federal census and the first meaningful 1810 federal coverage. These are held at ADAH in Montgomery and are your best tool for placing an ancestor in present-day Alabama before 1810. 4. **Colonial Mobile records require overseas archives.** French colonial records for the Mobile area are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence (with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives). Spanish colonial records — including Mobile District census returns, church registers, and land grants — are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. # Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (circa 1700–1819)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The territory that is today Alabama had no single governing authority around 1800 — it was a layered jurisdictional patchwork, and which records exist for any given family depends entirely on where in the region they lived and when.

**Colonial succession (Mobile area and Gulf Coast):**
- **French**: 1702–1763. Mobile was the administrative capital.
- **British**: 1763–1780. Mobile passed to Britain after the Seven Years' War.
- **Spanish**: 1780–1813. Spain retook Mobile during the American Revolution; the Mobile District remained under Spanish authority until U.S. forces seized it in April 1813.

**American territorial period:**
- **Mississippi Territory**: 1798–1817. Created from territory ceded by Georgia and Spanish West Florida. Expanded in 1804 and 1812 to encompass all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama. Present-day Alabama was the eastern portion.
- **Alabama Territory**: 1817–1819. When Mississippi became a state in August 1817, the eastern half was organized as the Alabama Territory.
- **Statehood**: December 14, 1819.

## Boundary Changes

| Period | Governing Jurisdiction |
|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French Louisiana / Mobile District |
| 1763–1780 | British West Florida |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish Mobile District |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory (eastern portion) |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory |
| 1819– | State of Alabama |

Records for ancestors in present-day Alabama between 1798 and 1817 are filed under the Mississippi Territory. FamilySearch collections scoped to Mississippi cover this territorial period. These are not separate research trails — they are one continuous documentary record split across two place labels at 1817.

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in the Alabama region around 1800. Alabama did not institute statewide civil vital registration until 1908. Church records are the only systematic vital record source for this period.

### Church Records
- **Catholic Church (Mobile area):** The oldest records in the region, going back to the French colonial era. Records in French, Spanish, then Latin and English.
  - French colonial originals: Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence — physical only
  - Microfilm of French records: Mobile Municipal Archives — microfilm, in person
  - Spanish colonial records (Mobile District): Archivo General de Indias, Seville — physical/portal; copies at Library of Congress
- **FamilySearch:** Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (collection 1986396) — 156,789 records, 78,394 images — indexed + images
- **FamilySearch:** Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950 (collection 2034891) — 87,654 records, 43,827 images — indexed + images

### Census Records
- **1800 federal census:** Mississippi Territory; Alabama portion had almost no American settlers enumerated.
- **Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810):** Held at ADAH, Montgomery — not online. Most important census-substitute source for 1800–1810.
- **1810 federal census:** First to substantially enumerate Alabama settlements.
- **FamilySearch:** Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (collection 2016756) — 287,634 records, 0 images — **index only, no images**
- **FamilySearch:** Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (collection 1927171) — 198,340 records, 0 images — **index only, no images**

### Land Records
Alabama is a federal-land state. Federal land records are the richest source for the pre-statehood period.
- BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov): Alabama patents searchable by name, free — indexed + images — from 1807 (St. Stephens) and 1811 (Huntsville) onward.
- **FamilySearch:** Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (collection 1919694) — 312,450 records, 156,225 images — indexed + images — covers territorial-era Alabama from 1798.
- Colonial grants: Spanish and British grants in Mobile area — in colonial overseas archives (see church records above).

### Probate and Court Records
- **FamilySearch:** Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (collection 1537764) — 438,210 records, 219,105 images — indexed + images
- **FamilySearch:** Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (collection 1855293) — 245,670 records, 122,835 images — indexed + images

### Marriage Records
- **FamilySearch:** Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (collection 1598408) — 612,345 records, 306,172 images — indexed + images — earliest records from 1809

### Military Records
- Creek War (1813–1814) and War of 1812: service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA; many on Fold3
- Territorial militia rolls: cited at ADAH
- War of 1812 pension files are especially rich — contain biographical statements and family details

### Tax Records
- Territorial-era tax lists at ADAH — essential census substitutes; document property holders in intercensal years

## Digitized Browsable Volumes — Special Note
The volume_search tool returned **zero results** for both Alabama (United States) and Mississippi Territory (United States) for 1700–1820. FamilySearch does not currently list any standalone browse-only digitized image volumes tagged to pre-statehood Alabama/Mississippi Territory. The FamilySearch images for this area are linked to indexed records within the named collections above, not available as standalone browsable volumes.

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 8 collections, 1798–1819 (see above) | Free |
| BLM/GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Alabama federal land patents from 1807 | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | War of 1812, Creek War, territorial federal records | Free/Fold3 |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records | Free |
| Fold3.com | Military pension and service records | Subscription |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| ADAH, Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); tax lists; militia rolls; court records |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic sacramental registers, colonial era onward |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal territorial records; 1810 census originals |
| NARA Washington D.C. | War of 1812 and Creek War service/pension records |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, France | French colonial originals, Mobile area 1702–1763 |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial originals — Mobile District census, church, land records |

## Records NOT Online
- Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) — ADAH only
- Territorial tax lists — ADAH; some transcribed
- Territorial militia rolls — ADAH
- French colonial church/civil records (original) — Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer
- Spanish colonial records (original) — Archivo General de Indias; some via pares.mcu.es

- Territorial court minute books — largely ADAH

## Known Record Losses
- Mobile colonial records were disrupted across three sovereignty transitions (1763, 1780, 1813)
- Northern/central Alabama had almost no formal record-keeping before county organization
- Creek War (1813–1814) disrupted record-keeping in central and southern Alabama
- The 1800 federal census captured almost no one in Alabama's interior

1. Work Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory collections as one continuous trail, split at 1817.
2. BLM/GLO land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) are free, indexed, and the anchor source for post-1807 land entries.
3. Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) at ADAH fill the 1800–1810 gap. See: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
4. Colonial Mobile records require overseas archives. See: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
5. No civil vital records exist for circa 1800 — Catholic church records (Mobile) and land/probate records are the primary substitutes.
6. War of 1812 and Creek War pension files at NARA/Fold3 are genealogically rich for early Alabama settlers.
7. Tax lists at ADAH substitute for thin federal census coverage of the pre-1810 period.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (circa 1700–1819)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The territory that is today Alabama had no single governing authority around 1800 — it was a layered jurisdictional patchwork, and which records exist for any given family depends entirely on where in the region they lived and when.

**Colonial succession (Mobile area and Gulf Coast):**
- **French**: 1702–1763. Mobile was the administrative capital.
- **British**: 1763–1780. Mobile passed to Britain after the Seven Years' War.
- **Spanish**: 1780–1813. Spain retook Mobile during the American Revolution; the Mobile District remained under Spanish authority until U.S. forces seized it in April 1813.

**American territorial period:**
- **Mississippi Territory**: 1798–1817. Created from territory ceded by Georgia and Spanish West Florida. Expanded in 1804 and 1812 to encompass all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama. Present-day Alabama was the eastern portion.
- **Alabama Territory**: 1817–1819. When Mississippi became a state in August 1817, the eastern half was organized as the Alabama Territory.
- **Statehood**: December 14, 1819.

## Boundary Changes

| Period | Governing Jurisdiction |
|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French Louisiana / Mobile District |
| 1763–1780 | British West Florida |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish Mobile District |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory (eastern portion) |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory |
| 1819– | State of Alabama |

Records for ancestors in present-day Alabama between 1798 and 1817 are filed under the Mississippi Territory. FamilySearch collections scoped to Mississippi cover this territorial period. These are not separate research trails — they are one continuous documentary record split across two place labels at 1817.

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in the Alabama region around 1800. Alabama did not institute statewide civil vital registration until 1908. Church records are the only systematic vital record source for this period.

### Church Records
- **Catholic Church (Mobile area):** The oldest records in the region, going back to the French colonial era. Records in French, Spanish, then Latin and English.
  - French colonial originals: Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence — physical only
  - Microfilm of French records: Mobile Municipal Archives — microfilm, in person
  - Spanish colonial records (Mobile District): Archivo General de Indias, Seville — physical/portal; copies at Library of Congress
- **FamilySearch:** Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (collection 1986396) — 156,789 records, 78,394 images — indexed + images
- **FamilySearch:** Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950 (collection 2034891) — 87,654 records, 43,827 images — indexed + images

### Census Records
- **1800 federal census:** Mississippi Territory; Alabama portion had almost no American settlers enumerated.
- **Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810):** Held at ADAH, Montgomery — not online. Most important census-substitute source for 1800–1810.
- **1810 federal census:** First to substantially enumerate Alabama settlements.
- **FamilySearch:** Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (collection 2016756) — 287,634 records, 0 images — **index only, no images**
- **FamilySearch:** Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (collection 1927171) — 198,340 records, 0 images — **index only, no images**

### Land Records
Alabama is a federal-land state. Federal land records are the richest source for the pre-statehood period.
- BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov): Alabama patents searchable by name, free — indexed + images — from 1807 (St. Stephens) and 1811 (Huntsville) onward.
- **FamilySearch:** Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (collection 1919694) — 312,450 records, 156,225 images — indexed + images — covers territorial-era Alabama from 1798.
- Colonial grants: Spanish and British grants in Mobile area — in colonial overseas archives (see church records above).

### Probate and Court Records
- **FamilySearch:** Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (collection 1537764) — 438,210 records, 219,105 images — indexed + images
- **FamilySearch:** Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (collection 1855293) — 245,670 records, 122,835 images — indexed + images

### Marriage Records
- **FamilySearch:** Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (collection 1598408) — 612,345 records, 306,172 images — indexed + images — earliest records from 1809

### Military Records
- Creek War (1813–1814) and War of 1812: service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA; many on Fold3
- Territorial militia rolls: cited at ADAH
- War of 1812 pension files are especially rich — contain biographical statements and family details

### Tax Records
- Territorial-era tax lists at ADAH — essential census substitutes; document property holders in intercensal years

## Digitized Browsable Volumes — Special Note
The volume_search tool returned **zero results** for both Alabama (United States) and Mississippi Territory (United States) for 1700–1820. FamilySearch does not currently list any standalone browse-only digitized image volumes tagged to pre-statehood Alabama/Mississippi Territory. The FamilySearch images for this area are linked to indexed records within the named collections above, not available as standalone browsable volumes.

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 8 collections, 1798–1819 (see above) | Free |
| BLM/GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Alabama federal land patents from 1807 | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | War of 1812, Creek War, territorial federal records | Free/Fold3 |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records | Free |
| Fold3.com | Military pension and service records | Subscription |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| ADAH, Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); tax lists; militia rolls; court records |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic sacramental registers, colonial era onward |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal territorial records; 1810 census originals |
| NARA Washington D.C. | War of 1812 and Creek War service/pension records |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, France | French colonial originals, Mobile area 1702–1763 |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial originals — Mobile District census, church, land records |

## Records NOT Online
- Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) — ADAH only
- Territorial tax lists — ADAH; some transcribed
- Territorial militia rolls — ADAH
- French colonial church/civil records (original) — Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer
- Spanish colonial records (original) — Archivo General de Indias; some via pares.mcu.es
- Most county deed books 1809–1819 — courthouse level
- Territorial court minute books — largely ADAH

## Known Record Losses
- Mobile colonial records were disrupted across three sovereignty transitions (1763, 1780, 1813)
- Northern/central Alabama had almost no formal record-keeping before county organization
- Creek War (1813–1814) disrupted record-keeping in central and southern Alabama
- The 1800 federal census captured almost no one in Alabama's interior

## Research Tips
1. Work Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory collections as one continuous trail, split at 1817.
2. BLM/GLO land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) are free, indexed, and the anchor source for post-1807 land entries.
3. Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) at ADAH fill the 1800–1810 gap. See: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
4. Colonial Mobile records require overseas archives. See: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
5. No civil vital records exist for circa 1800 — Catholic church records (Mobile) and land/probate records are the primary substitutes.
6. War of 1812 and Creek War pension files at NARA/Fold3 are genealogically rich for early Alabama settlers.
7. Tax lists at ADAH substitute for thin federal census coverage of the pre-1810 period.
